explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 8 weeks (some Australian centres extend to under 12 weeks) require full septic workup including CSF and empirical IV antibiotics regardless of low-risk biomarkers, because the Rochester, Philadelphia and Boston low-risk criteria miss approximately 1-3% of serious bacterial infections including meningitis.
key_points: Under 8 weeks: full septic workup including LP, empirical IV benzylpenicillin + gentamicin
8 weeks to 3 months: selective workup possible if well AND low-risk criteria met
Rochester low-risk: WCC 5-15, bands <1.5, urine WBC <10, stool WBC <5 if diarrhoea
CRP >20 and procalcitonin >0.5 increase risk of SBI
Listeria cover (amoxicillin/benzylpenicillin) required under 3 months
explanation.pearls: A well-looking febrile neonate is the most dangerous febrile patient in the department. Bacterial meningitis can present with normal WCC and CRP at this age.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Febrile child
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Sepsis in neonates and infants

options.rationale: Outpatient management without workup is unsafe at this age; the under-3-months febrile-infant rule overrides reassuring appearance. Would be acceptable only if the child were over 3 months, well, and meeting NICE green-zone criteria (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Febrile child

options.rationale: The AU age-cut-off for mandatory full septic workup INCLUDING lumbar puncture is under 8 weeks of age (about 56 days) regardless of clinical appearance because low-risk criteria do not exclude bacterial meningitis at this age. At 6 weeks the recommended empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin/ampicillin plus gentamicin plus cefotaxime (Listeria, Gram-negatives, CNS penetration), per RCH CPG.
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Febrile child
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Sepsis in neonates and infants

options.rationale: Omitting LP is unsafe in under-8-week infants: low-risk biomarkers do not exclude meningitis. Selective workup without LP applies only to well 8-week to 3-month infants meeting all Rochester/Philadelphia low-risk criteria (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Febrile child

options.rationale: PO amoxicillin gives inadequate CSF penetration and serum levels for neonatal sepsis or meningitis; oral therapy is never empirical cover in suspected SBI under 3 months. Would be reasonable only for a confirmed mild outpatient bacterial focus (e.g. acute otitis media) in an older well child (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Sepsis in neonates and infants

options.rationale: CXR is a focus-driven investigation, not a sepsis screen, and substitutes for none of the required cultures. Would be indicated only with respiratory signs (tachypnoea out of proportion, focal crackles, hypoxia) (Source: NICE NG143).

explanation.summary: Recognise paediatric sepsis from tachycardia disproportionate to fever, altered mental status, prolonged capillary refill and mottling - hypotension is a late sign. Deliver the 1-hour bundle: oxygen, IV/IO access, blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotic, 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus with reassessment after each, lactate, and senior/PIPER escalation.
key_points: Cold shock: cool peripheries, prolonged CR, narrow pulse pressure - common in children
Warm shock: bounding pulses, flash CR, wide pulse pressure - older children/adolescents
Antibiotic within 1 hour; do not delay for LP or imaging
Reassess after each 10-20 mL/kg bolus; watch for fluid overload (hepatomegaly, crackles)
Escalate to PIPER/NETS for transfer to PICU
explanation.pearls: A child with sepsis decompensates suddenly because they compensate well right up to the cliff edge. Trust prolonged capillary refill and altered mentation over a normal BP.

options.rationale: Adrenaline before adequate volume worsens outcomes by increasing afterload on an under-filled ventricle. Would be correct only after 40-60 mL/kg crystalloid in fluid-refractory shock, and even then peripheral adrenaline 0.05-0.1 microg/kg/min is started while central access is obtained (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Sepsis Pathway).

Three errors stacked: oral antibiotic in shock, sub-therapeutic 10 mL/kg bolus, and imaging-before-antibiotics. CT head is not required prior to antibiotics even with suspected meningitis; antibiotics are given first and CT/LP follow once stable (Source: ANZICS; RCH CPG Meningitis).

The Australian paediatric sepsis pathway requires recognition, IV/IO access, blood cultures before antibiotics where this does not delay, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour (ceftriaxone covers meningococcaemia which is the likely diagnosis given non-blanching rash and shock), a 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus with reassessment, and lactate measurement - all within the first hour (ANZICS Paediatric Sepsis Pathway; RCH CPG Sepsis).

Treating meningococcal shock as a viral fever is the cardinal sepsis miss. Antipyretic-and-observe would only be appropriate for a well-appearing child with a clear viral focus and no red flags (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Sepsis Pathway).

LP is contraindicated in shock or raised ICP and must never delay antibiotics. LP-first would be acceptable only in a stable well-perfused child with isolated meningism, normal GCS and no coagulopathy (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis).

explanation.summary: Use the Gorelick 10-point or WHO 4-sign assessment together with acute weight loss. Mild-moderate dehydration (3-7%) has 2-3 signs and preserved consciousness, tears and BP. Severe (>=10%) has obtunded mental state, deeply sunken eyes, absent tears, very prolonged CR and weak pulses.
key_points: Best single estimate of deficit: acute weight change
Most useful clinical signs: prolonged CR, abnormal skin turgor, abnormal respiratory pattern
BP is a late sign in children - compensated shock can have a normal BP
WHO: no/some/severe dehydration plans A/B/C
Gorelick >=3 signs = >5% dehydration
explanation.pearls: If the child is alert, drinking, and producing tears, severe dehydration is unlikely no matter how dramatic the diarrhoea history.

options.rationale: Multiple Gorelick signs and a measured weight deficit are present, so dehydration is clinically detectable. Under 3 percent would require fewer than 2 Gorelick signs, no measured weight loss, and intact tears, mucosae, and skin turgor (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis classification uses the Gorelick signs (sunken eyes, dry mucosae, delayed skin recoil, reduced UO, mildly prolonged CR) and weight deficit. Mild-moderate dehydration around 4-6 percent is managed with nasogastric ORS at 50 mL/kg over 4 hours (or oral if tolerating), with IV reserved for failure of NG or shock.

Severe (10 percent plus) dehydration requires obtundation, prolonged central CR over 3 seconds, weak pulses and absent tears; over-classifying triggers unnecessary IV resuscitation. Bolus saline would be correct only with shock features or true severe deficit (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

Intubation for hypovolaemic shock is reserved for failed resuscitation with persistent altered consciousness or airway compromise; this child has preserved BP, GCS and central perfusion. Decompensated shock would require absent peripheral pulses and altered mental state (Source: APLS).

Measured weight loss and clinical signs prove a deficit; calling this euvolaemic and discharging trusts appearance over weight. Reassure-only is acceptable only when serial weights and clinical exam are both normal (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: Mild-moderate dehydration (3-7%) is first managed enterally. Trial oral ORS in small frequent volumes (e.g., 5 mL every 1-2 minutes); if vomiting, give ondansetron (>=6 months) and re-trial, or switch to rapid NG rehydration at 25 mL/kg/h for 4 hours then reassess. IV is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, ileus, altered consciousness or failed enteral rehydration. Use isotonic fluids if IV is required.
key_points: Enteral first: oral then NG; both better tolerated than IV and equally effective in mild-moderate
Rapid NG: 25 mL/kg/h ORS for 4 hours = 100 mL/kg replacement
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg PO/IV reduces vomiting; one dose only
IV bolus 10-20 mL/kg 0.9% saline for shock; isotonic maintenance
Avoid hypotonic IV fluids - risk of hyponatraemic encephalopathy
explanation.pearls: An NG tube placed for rehydration is rarely refused once parents understand it avoids repeat cannulation attempts.

sources.label: PREDICT NG vs IV rehydration trial

options.rationale: IV is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, ileus, altered mental state or failed enteral therapy; in mild-moderate dehydration NG ORS is well validated and preferred. Would be correct with shock or failed NG trial (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

0.45 percent saline is no longer recommended as routine paediatric IV maintenance in Australia due to hospital-acquired hyponatraemia. Isotonic fluid (Plasma-Lyte or 0.9 percent saline with 5 percent dextrose) is standard if IV is required (Source: NHMRC Paediatric IV Fluids; RCH CPG IV Fluids).

Plain water and dilute juice lack adequate sodium and glucose, risking hyponatraemia in ongoing losses. ORS or commercial hydration solutions are required, and ED rehydration is needed given failed oral intake (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

Rapid NG rehydration with ORS (Gastrolyte) at 25 mL/kg/h for 4 hours is the RCH first-line approach for mild-moderate dehydration in children who cannot tolerate oral sips, avoiding the risks of IV access and being non-inferior to IV for time to discharge and complications (RCH CPG Gastroenteritis; PREDICT NG/IV trial).

Ondansetron enables ORS but does not replace it; single-dose-and-discharge without verified intake misses ongoing deficit. Would be appropriate only as an adjunct before a documented successful oral trial (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis (ASCIA): any acute onset illness with typical skin features PLUS involvement of respiratory and/or cardiovascular and/or persistent severe GI symptoms; or acute onset hypotension/bronchospasm/upper airway obstruction even without skin signs. Treat with IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) anterolateral mid-thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed.
key_points: Adrenaline IM is the only first-line drug
Autoinjector dosing: <7.5 kg consider IM ampoule, 7.5-20 kg = 150 microg, >20 kg = 300 microg
Positioning: supine + legs elevated unless airway compromise or vomiting
Salbutamol, oxygen, IV fluids are adjuncts
Antihistamines and steroids are NOT first-line and do not prevent biphasic reactions
explanation.pearls: If you are debating whether it is anaphylaxis, give the adrenaline. Underuse causes deaths; overuse causes transient palpitations.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: He meets ASCIA criteria for anaphylaxis (skin plus respiratory involvement with airway compromise). IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) is first-line. ASCIA autoinjector thresholds: 10-20 kg use 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr); over 20 kg use 300 microgram (EpiPen); over 50 kg use 500 microgram (EpiPen 500). At 20 kg he is at the upper edge of the 150 microgram band, so 150 microgram is correct per current ASCIA paediatric thresholds.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Treating anaphylactic wheeze as asthma delays adrenaline, and delayed adrenaline is associated with fatal anaphylaxis. Salbutamol-first is acceptable only in isolated bronchospasm without other anaphylaxis features (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway oedema, bronchospasm or hypotension and have no role as first-line. They are adjuncts after adrenaline, never the initial intervention (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: 300 microgram is the EpiPen dose for over 20 kg under ASCIA; at exactly 20 kg the 150 microgram EpiPen Jr is correct. Would be correct if the child were over 20 kg (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Action Plan).

Talking and responsive does not exclude anaphylaxis; hoarse voice and throat tightness are airway red flags requiring immediate adrenaline. Withholding while awaiting paramedics is the textbook delay-to-death error (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis = ongoing features after 2 appropriate IM adrenaline doses. Move to IV adrenaline infusion (0.1 microg/kg/min, titrate), aggressive IV fluids (up to 50 mL/kg crystalloid), prepare for early intubation given airway oedema, consider nebulised adrenaline for upper airway and salbutamol for bronchospasm. Glucagon if on beta-blockers; vasopressin if catecholamine-refractory.
key_points: IV adrenaline infusion: 0.1 microg/kg/min start, titrate 0.05-1
Continue fluid resuscitation 20 mL/kg, repeat to 50 mL/kg
Early airway control - intubation before complete obstruction
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg for upper airway oedema
Salbutamol for persistent bronchospasm
explanation.pearls: If two correctly placed IM doses have failed, the problem is absorption or severity - not the drug. Move to infusion and call ICU.

options.rationale: 1 mg IV (1:10,000) is the cardiac arrest dose and will cause hypertensive crisis, myocardial ischaemia or VF in a perfusing patient. Would be correct only in cardiac arrest, not in refractory anaphylaxis with a pulse (Source: ASCIA; ARC Paediatric ALS).

Steroids/antihistamines do nothing for refractory shock and promethazine is contraindicated under 2 years (paradoxical reactions, hypotension). Only ever adjuncts after definitive adrenaline therapy (Source: ASCIA; TGA Promethazine warning).

Refractory anaphylaxis after two correctly delivered IM doses is an indication for IV adrenaline infusion, starting at 0.1 microg/kg/min (range 0.05-1 microg/kg/min) and titrated to BP, perfusion and airway response, while continuing fluid resuscitation. Boluses of IV adrenaline outside cardiac arrest carry significant risk of arrhythmia and hypertensive crisis and are not first-line (ASCIA Refractory Anaphylaxis Guidelines).

After two failed IM doses, peripheral perfusion is poor and IM absorption unreliable; persisting with IM is the refractory-anaphylaxis pitfall. IV infusion is the next step (Source: ASCIA Refractory Anaphylaxis Guidelines).

Glucagon has a narrow niche: beta-blocked patients with refractory shock unresponsive to adrenaline. It is an adjunct, not a replacement for adrenaline infusion (Source: ASCIA Refractory Anaphylaxis Guidelines).

explanation.summary: APLS status epilepticus pathway: 0 min - ABC, oxygen, check glucose. 5 min - first benzodiazepine (IV midazolam/diazepam or buccal/IM midazolam). 15 min - second benzodiazepine. 25 min - second-line: levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg IV over 5 min OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV over 20 min. 45 min - RSI with thiopentone, transfer to PICU.
key_points: First and second benzodiazepine before moving to long-acting agent
Levetiracetam now preferred over phenytoin in many centres (faster, fewer arrhythmias, EcLiPSE/ConSEPT trials)
Check and correct glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium
Pyridoxine 100 mg IV if under 18 months and refractory
Get help early - status >30 minutes risks neurological injury
explanation.pearls: Most paediatric status responds to two doses of benzodiazepine. If you are about to give a third benzodiazepine, you are wrong - move on.

options.rationale: Re-dosing buccal once IV is in place wastes a more reliable route and risks under-dosing through ongoing buccal pooling. Buccal would be the right second dose only if IV access were still unavailable (Source: RCH CPG: Status Epilepticus).

Phenytoin/levetiracetam is the second-line step after two adequate benzodiazepine doses; only one has been given. Would be correct if two benzodiazepine doses had already failed (Source: RCH CPG: Status Epilepticus).

Phenobarbital is reserved for refractory status after benzodiazepines plus a second-line agent have failed; jumping straight to it skips the standard ladder. Would be the right step in established refractory status (Source: APLS Australia).

RSI with thiopentone is the refractory-status escalation only after benzodiazepines and at least one second-line agent fail, with airway/breathing currently maintained the patient should not be intubated yet. Would be correct in refractory status with airway compromise (Source: APLS Australia).

Per APLS Australia and RCH status epilepticus pathway, after one benzodiazepine that has failed (and 10 minutes have elapsed), the second-line is a SECOND benzodiazepine dose - IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg (or IV diazepam 0.25 mg/kg) - now that IV access is available. If that fails after a further 10 minutes, move to a second-line agent such as levetiracetam 40 mg/kg or phenytoin 20 mg/kg (RCH CPG; APLS).

explanation.summary: First unprovoked afebrile seizure in an otherwise well child: ABC, exclude provokers (glucose, electrolytes, toxins, infection, trauma), full neurological examination. If recovered and normal: discharge with first-fit clinic referral, EEG within 1-2 weeks, MRI only for focal features/under 2/refractory, safety advice, no AED. Recurrence risk approximately 40%; epilepsy is diagnosed after 2 unprovoked seizures.
key_points: EEG within 1-2 weeks of first seizure characterises syndrome
MRI for: focal seizure, under 2 years, persistent deficit, refractory
AEDs not started after single seizure (no change in long-term outcome)
Safety: baths supervised, no swimming alone, no high climbing
Australian driving rules apply to the patient (>16) not the parents
explanation.pearls: First-fit clinics exist for a reason - rushing to imaging and starting medication after one event is overinvestigation and overtreatment.

options.rationale: After a first unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure in a neurologically normal child, the standard approach is outpatient first-fit clinic review with EEG within 1-2 weeks (which informs recurrence risk), MRI only if there are focal features or under 2 years or refractory, no anti-epileptic medication after a single seizure unless recurrence risk is high, and safety counselling (no baths alone, supervised swimming, no high climbing). Parental driving is not restricted (RCH CPG Afebrile seizures).

Starting an antiepileptic after a single unprovoked seizure is the textbook over-treatment error; recurrence is around 40 percent and early AED does not improve long-term outcome. Would be considered only after a second seizure or with high-risk EEG/MRI findings (Source: RCH CPG: First Seizure; NICE NG217).

CT plus LP for a brief generalised seizure with full recovery is over-investigation: no fever, no meningism, no focal deficit, no trauma. Indicated only with persistent altered GCS, focal deficit, suspected meningitis, or trauma (Source: RCH CPG: First Seizure).

A rescue kit is not standard after a single brief seizure; first-fit pathway is EEG-led follow-up, not pre-emptive home benzodiazepines. Would be appropriate only for established epilepsy or known prolonged seizures over 5 minutes (Source: RCH CPG: First Seizure).

Same-day MRI is over-imaging for a generalised seizure with normal exam; outpatient MRI is the standard timing. Urgent MRI is reserved for focal seizures, persistent deficit, age under 2 years, or refractory seizures (Source: RCH CPG: First Seizure).

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizure: age 6 months to 5 years, generalised, <15 minutes, single in 24 hours, full recovery, with fever and no CNS infection. Management: identify and treat the febrile illness, reassurance, safety advice, no investigations beyond what the source illness requires, no anti-epileptic, antipyretics for comfort only.
key_points: Complex = focal OR >15 min OR >1 in 24 h
Recurrence risk approximately 30% overall; higher if first seizure <18 months or family history
Subsequent epilepsy risk approximately 1-2% (background 0.5-1%)
Antipyretics do NOT prevent recurrence
LP only if meningism, age <6 months, or incomplete recovery
explanation.pearls: Parents are usually traumatised by their first febrile seizure - the most therapeutic intervention is unhurried explanation that this is benign.

options.rationale: EEG and MRI are not indicated after a simple febrile seizure with full recovery and normal exam. Would be appropriate only for complex febrile seizures (focal, prolonged over 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours) (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

Routine LP for age under 2 is the legacy rule that AU guidelines have abandoned; a well, fully immunised child without meningism or persistent altered conscious state does not need CSF. Would be indicated only with meningism, persistent drowsiness, or incomplete Hib/pneumococcal vaccination (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

Scheduled antipyretics do not reduce recurrence and may delay recognition of further illness; use for comfort only. Would never be correct as a prophylactic strategy (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

This is a simple febrile seizure (single, generalised, under 15 minutes, full recovery, age 6 months to 6 years). Management is reassurance, treatment of the febrile focus, written first-aid advice and routine follow-up; no investigations are needed and no antiepileptic is indicated.

Maintenance AEDs are not used for simple febrile seizures regardless of recurrence rate; risks outweigh benefit. Considered only for very prolonged or frequent complex febrile seizures under specialist review (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

explanation.summary: Children compensate well by raising heart rate and systemic vascular resistance; hypotension is a late and pre-arrest sign. Recognise compensated shock from tachycardia disproportionate to fever, prolonged capillary refill, mottling, cool peripheries, altered mental state, and oliguria, regardless of BP. Treat with 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid boluses with reassessment after each.
key_points: Hypotension is a late sign in children - do not wait for it
Cold shock: cool peripheries, prolonged CR, narrow pulse pressure - first-line adrenaline if fluid-refractory
Warm shock: flash CR, wide pulse pressure - first-line noradrenaline if fluid-refractory
Bolus 10-20 mL/kg over 5-10 minutes; reassess after each
Stop fluid if signs of overload (hepatomegaly, crackles)
explanation.pearls: A normal BP in a sick child is reassurance you don't deserve. Look at the periphery, the lactate and the mental state.

options.rationale: No cardiac history, gallop, hepatomegaly or pulmonary crackles to suggest pump failure; mislabelling sepsis as cardiogenic delays fluid resuscitation. Would be correct with known cardiomyopathy, post-cardiac-surgery, or signs of failure (Source: APLS Australia).

BP is preserved so by definition this is compensated shock; jumping to adrenaline before fluid breaks the resuscitation order. Vasoactives are added only once 40-60 mL/kg of crystalloid has failed (Source: APLS Australia; Surviving Sepsis Campaign Paediatric 2020).

Cap refill 4 s, mottling, oliguria and lactate 3.6 is not normal; calling this 'no shock' misses compensated shock in a well-looking child. Maintenance-only would be correct with normal perfusion, vitals and lactate (Source: APLS Australia).

Warm shock shows flash cap refill, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure; this child has the opposite (cold shock). Noradrenaline-first would be appropriate in fluid-refractory warm septic shock, not cold (Source: APLS Australia; Surviving Sepsis Paediatric 2020).

Tachycardia disproportionate to fever, prolonged capillary refill, cool mottled peripheries, oliguria and an elevated lactate define compensated cold shock with maintained BP. The first-line intervention is a 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus over 5-10 minutes with reassessment after each bolus, alongside broad-spectrum antibiotics if sepsis is suspected (APLS Australia; RCH CPG Sepsis).

explanation.summary: Fluid-refractory shock after 40-60 mL/kg crystalloid requires vasoactive support. Choose adrenaline for cold shock (low cardiac output, high SVR) and noradrenaline for warm shock (high cardiac output, low SVR). Peripheral low-dose infusion is acceptable while central access is established. Watch for fluid overload (hepatomegaly, crackles, S3, increasing oxygen requirement) and stop boluses if present.
key_points: Fluid-refractory = persistent shock after 40-60 mL/kg
Cold shock -> adrenaline 0.05-0.3 microg/kg/min
Warm shock -> noradrenaline 0.05-0.3 microg/kg/min
Peripheral infusion safe at low concentrations until central access
Hydrocortisone 50 mg/m2/day or 2 mg/kg if catecholamine-resistant
explanation.pearls: If you can feel the liver, you can stop the fluid. Paediatric fluid overload is iatrogenic and worsens outcomes.

options.rationale: She has fluid-refractory septic shock with cold-shock physiology (narrow pulse pressure, mottled cool peripheries, prolonged CR) and now signs of fluid overload (hepatomegaly, crackles). Australian guidelines support starting adrenaline as first-line inotrope in paediatric cold septic shock, and peripheral infusion at low-dose concentrations (0.05-0.3 microg/kg/min) is acceptable while central access is obtained. Further large-volume fluid boluses risk worsening overload (ANZICS Paediatric Sepsis; APLS; Surviving Sepsis Campaign paediatric 2020).

Hepatomegaly and crackles signal volume overload; further large boluses worsen pulmonary oedema and hypoxaemia. Reassess after 40-60 mL/kg and switch to inotrope (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric 2020).

Noradrenaline is the warm-shock first-line; cold shock with poor cardiac output is treated with adrenaline. Would be correct in fluid-refractory shock with wide pulse pressure and warm peripheries (Source: APLS Australia).

Dopamine showed higher mortality than adrenaline in the Ventura 2015 paediatric RCT and is no longer first-line. Considered only when adrenaline/noradrenaline unavailable (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric 2020).

Hydrocortisone is an adjunct for catecholamine-resistant shock or proven/suspected adrenal insufficiency, not a substitute for inotropes. Would be added on top of adrenaline if shock persists despite escalating doses (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric 2020).

explanation.summary: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant is the most specific sign of physical abuse in early childhood. Apply the TEN-4 FACESp rule: bruises in any of these regions or in a child <=4 months are highly suspicious. Investigations: full skeletal survey (with 2-week repeat), CT head, dilated fundus exam, coagulation screen. Mandatory reporting in all Australian jurisdictions for doctors with reasonable suspicion.
key_points: Those who don't cruise rarely bruise
TEN-4: Torso, Ear, Neck, age 4 months and under
FACESp: Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Sclera, patterned
Skeletal survey at presentation and repeat at 2 weeks (occult fractures)
Mandatory reporting is by suspicion, not certainty - this is statutory
explanation.pearls: Document objectively, do not investigate the social history beyond what is clinically necessary, and let the multidisciplinary team and statutory agency lead the safeguarding process.

sources.label: AIFS Mandatory reporting of child abuse
Pierce et al. TEN-4 FACESp validation 2021

options.rationale: Normal coags do not exclude abuse, and a bleeding disorder cannot account for patterned bruising in a pre-mobile infant. Outpatient coags alone would be appropriate only if there were no concerning history/pattern and an isolated bruise with positive family bleeding history (Source: RCH CPG: Non-Accidental Injury).

Bruises in a pre-mobile infant are sentinel injuries: 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise.' Reassure-and-discharge is the textbook safeguarding failure. Reassurance is appropriate only after full workup is reassuring (Source: RCH CPG: Non-Accidental Injury).

Bruising in a pre-mobile infant meets the TEN-4 FACESp rule (Torso, Ear, Neck, age <=4 months; Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Sclera, patterned) and is a strong red flag for inflicted injury. This child has all four red-flag locations triggered. Mandatory next steps are full skeletal survey (and repeat at 2 weeks), non-contrast CT head, dilated ophthalmology examination for retinal haemorrhages, paediatric team and child protection consultation, and mandatory notification to the state child protection authority. Doctors are mandated reporters in every Australian state and territory (RCH CPG Child abuse; AAP TEN-4 FACES).
source_refs: Pierce et al. TEN-4 FACESp validation 2021

options.rationale: Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not confirmed imaging; delaying notification breaches the statutory duty under state Children and Young Persons Acts. Would never be correct to defer notification pending results (Source: NSW/Vic mandatory reporter legislation; RCH CPG).

Direct confrontation by the treating team can compromise the child's safety, the forensic investigation and ongoing therapeutic relationships; that role belongs to child protection and police. Investigation and notification proceed without confrontation (Source: RCH CPG: Non-Accidental Injury).

explanation.summary: Drowning is primarily an asphyxial injury - prioritise oxygenation. Bystander BLS for drowning: 5 rescue breaths first, then 30:2 CPR (lay rescuer) or 15:2 (two trained rescuers in a child). Post-ROSC: lung-protective ventilation with PEEP for pulmonary oedema/ARDS, normoxia, normocapnia, treat shock, rewarm to 36 degC, manage as post-cardiac-arrest syndrome. Consider VA-ECMO for refractory hypoxia or cardiac dysfunction. Late ARDS can develop up to 8 hours later.
key_points: 5 rescue breaths first in drowning (not compressions first)
Target SpO2 94-98% post-ROSC; avoid hyperoxia and hypocapnia
PEEP for pulmonary oedema/ARDS; lung-protective tidal volumes
Rewarm to 36 degC at 0.5-1 degC/h; avoid hyperthermia
Antibiotics not routine; consider if contaminated water or sepsis develops
explanation.pearls: The lungs of a drowned child can look normal at 1 hour and ARDS by 8 hours. Do not extubate to room air based on the initial CXR.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.2 Resuscitation of the drowning victim
ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric advanced life support

options.rationale: Paediatric drowning with ROSC and short submersion has documented good neuro outcomes; early withdrawal is the prognostic-nihilism error. Withdrawal discussion is appropriate only after 48-72 h of intensive care and clear secondary-survey/imaging confirmation of devastating injury (Source: ANZCOR Drowning).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.2 Resuscitation of the drowning victim

options.rationale: Hyperoxia and hypocapnia cause cerebral vasoconstriction and oxidative reperfusion injury post-arrest; target normoxia and normocapnia. Hyperventilation is acceptable only for transient management of impending herniation (Source: ANZCOR Post-Resuscitation Care).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric advanced life support

options.rationale: Induced hyperthermia worsens neurological outcomes; controlled rewarming to 36 degC is the standard. Empirical antibiotics are reserved for documented aspiration of contaminated water or clinical evidence of infection (Source: ANZCOR; RCH CPG Drowning).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.2 Resuscitation of the drowning victim

options.rationale: Drowning-related pulmonary oedema and ARDS can be delayed up to 8 hours; clear CXR does not justify early extubation when GCS is low and B-lines are present. Extubation is appropriate only with normal gas exchange, GCS over 12 and resolved B-lines (Source: ANZCOR).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.2 Resuscitation of the drowning victim

options.rationale: Post-drowning care follows ANZCOR resuscitation principles plus post-cardiac-arrest care. Five initial rescue breaths precede compressions in drowning because hypoxia is the proximate cause. After ROSC, target normoxia (SpO2 94-98%), normocapnia, lung-protective ventilation with PEEP for pulmonary oedema/ARDS, treat shock with fluids and adrenaline, and discuss VA-ECMO for refractory hypoxia or cardiac dysfunction. Rewarm to 36 degC at 0.5-1 degC/h (do not over-rewarm; mild controlled hypothermia is no longer routinely targeted but normothermia is). Antibiotics are not routine.
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.2 Resuscitation of the drowning victim
ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric advanced life support

explanation.summary: Paediatric burns >=10% TBSA need formal resuscitation. Use modified Parkland: 3-4 mL/kg/%TBSA Hartmann's over 24 hours from time of burn, half in first 8 h, half in next 16 h. Give maintenance dextrose-containing fluid IN ADDITION (children risk hypoglycaemia). Use Lund-Browder chart (not rule of 9s) for paediatric TBSA. Titrate fluid to urine output 1 mL/kg/h. Analgesia (IV morphine or intranasal fentanyl), tetanus, cover with cling film, refer to burns service.
key_points: Modified Parkland 3-4 mL/kg/%TBSA Hartmann's over 24 h
Maintenance with glucose IN ADDITION in children
Lund-Browder chart for TBSA in children
Target urine output 1 mL/kg/h
Refer >10% TBSA, face/hands/perineum, full-thickness, electrical, chemical, suspected NAI
explanation.pearls: Children dehydrate and become hypoglycaemic faster than adults - never run a burned child without glucose-containing maintenance.

sources.label: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB)

options.rationale: Colloid worsens lung water in the early capillary-leak phase of burn injury; crystalloid is mandated in the first 24 h. Albumin is added only in the second 24 h or as rescue in failed resuscitation (Source: ANZBA EMSB).
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB)

options.rationale: Two errors: omitting maintenance (children always need maintenance plus burn fluid) and using 0.9 percent saline (hyperchloraemic acidosis risk). Parkland-only would be acceptable in adults; Hartmann's plus separate maintenance is the paediatric standard (Source: RCH CPG: Burns; ANZBA).
Hypertonic saline is not standard in paediatric burn resuscitation in Australia and is studied only in specific adult settings. Would never be first-line in children (Source: ANZBA EMSB).
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB)

options.rationale: Australian paediatric burns centres use a modified Parkland formula at 3-4 mL/kg/%TBSA of Hartmann's (compound sodium lactate) over the first 24 hours from the time of burn, half in the first 8 hours and half in the next 16 hours, with paediatric maintenance fluid containing glucose given IN ADDITION because children have lower glycogen stores and are at risk of hypoglycaemia. 3 mL x 15 kg x 18 = 810 mL resuscitation fluid (RCH CPG Burns; ANZBA EMSB).
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB)

options.rationale: TBSA over 10 percent in children mandates formal burn resuscitation fluid in addition to maintenance; an 18 percent burn cannot be managed with maintenance alone. Maintenance-only is appropriate only for under-10-percent TBSA (Source: RCH CPG: Burns).

explanation.summary: Acute single paracetamol ingestion: take a 4-hour-or-later level and plot on the Australian nomogram with a single treatment line starting at 150 mg/L at 4 h. NAC indicated if level above line, OR dose >200 mg/kg (or >10 g) with no level available within 8 hours, OR staggered/repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, OR ALT elevated. Use the two-bag IV NAC regimen: 200 mg/kg over 4 h then 100 mg/kg over 16 h. After deliberate self-poisoning, mental health assessment is mandatory.
key_points: Australian nomogram: single 150 mg/L line at 4 h, log-linear to 24 h
Two-bag NAC: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h (fewer reactions vs 3-bag)
Supratherapeutic: >200 mg/kg or >10 g acute
Charcoal useful only within 1-2 h (up to 4 h for SR)
Repeat ALT, INR, paracetamol at end of NAC; continue NAC if ALT rising or INR >1.3
explanation.pearls: Never withhold NAC waiting for a perfect history. When dose, level and time are uncertain, treat - hepatotoxicity is the unrecoverable error.

sources.label: Australian Poisons Information Centre - Paracetamol poisoning guideline (Chiew et al. 2020)

options.rationale: Delaying NAC when the level is already above the nomogram treatment line costs hepatoprotective efficacy (best within 8 h of ingestion). Repeat-and-wait would be reasonable only for an asymptomatic patient with a sub-line level and uncertain timing (Source: Australian PIC Paracetamol Guideline).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre - Paracetamol poisoning guideline (Chiew et al. 2020)

options.rationale: At 4.5 hours post-ingestion the paracetamol concentration of 165 mg/L lies above the Australian 150 mg/L treatment line on the modified Rumack-Matthew nomogram (extrapolated back to 4 h would be above 150 mg/L). The reported dose also exceeds the 200 mg/kg supratherapeutic threshold. NAC is indicated. The Australian Poisons Information Centre and AMH endorse the two-bag regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h) which reduces anaphylactoid reactions versus the traditional three-bag regimen. Psychiatric assessment is required after any deliberate self-poisoning (AMH; Australian PIC; Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre - Paracetamol poisoning guideline (Chiew et al. 2020)

options.rationale: Activated charcoal needs to be within 1-2 h (or up to 4 h for sustained-release); at 5 h post-ingestion it is not useful and must never delay NAC. Would be appropriate within 1-2 hours of ingestion (Source: Australian PIC).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre - Paracetamol poisoning guideline (Chiew et al. 2020)

options.rationale: 165 mg/L at 4.5 h is above the 150 mg/L treatment line, and 230 mg/kg exceeds the 200 mg/kg dose threshold; the higher of dose-or-level governs. Would be appropriate only if BOTH dose under 200 mg/kg AND level below line (Source: Australian PIC).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre - Paracetamol poisoning guideline (Chiew et al. 2020)

options.rationale: Oral methionine is not used in Australia and transplant assessment is for established fulminant failure meeting King's College criteria, not initial presentation. NAC is the standard antidote (Source: AMH; Australian PIC).

explanation.summary: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in infants. Soft, supraglottic tissue collapses inward on inspiration, producing positional inspiratory stridor worst when supine, feeding or crying, and improving when prone or upright. Symptoms usually appear in the first 2 to 4 weeks of life, peak around 4 to 8 months, and resolve by 12 to 24 months in the majority. Severe cases (failure to thrive, apnoea, severe distress) need ENT referral and possible supraglottoplasty.
key_points: Most common cause of stridor in infants
Positional: worse supine, better prone or upright
Symptoms begin in first weeks, resolve by 12-24 months
Refer if failure to thrive, apnoea, severe distress, cyanosis
Diagnosed clinically; flexible nasoendoscopy confirms
explanation.pearls: If the stridor is positional, gradual onset, with a thriving baby and no fever, it is laryngomalacia until proven otherwise. Acute febrile stridor with a barking cough is croup.

options.rationale: Positional inspiratory stridor starting in the first weeks, worse supine and with feeding and improving prone or upright in a thriving infant without red flags is the classic laryngomalacia picture, the most common cause of infant stridor. Australian practice is observation in the absence of red flags; flexible nasendoscopy and ENT referral are reserved for failure to thrive, severe feeding difficulty, cyanotic spells, or biphasic/atypical stridor, per RCH CPG: Stridor in children.

Subglottic haemangioma gives biphasic (not purely inspiratory) stridor and often a beard-distribution cutaneous haemangioma; classically worsens with crying not posture. Would be the answer with biphasic stridor and visible facial haemangioma (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor).

Croup is acute, with barking cough, hoarse cry, fever and age 6 months to 3 years; not chronic stridor from the neonatal period. Would be correct with acute onset and barking cough (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Inhaled foreign body presents acutely with a witnessed choking episode and focal asymmetry; chronic positional stridor since birth excludes it. Would be correct with sudden-onset cough and unilateral wheeze in a toddler (Source: RCH CPG).

Vascular rings give biphasic stridor with feeding difficulty and reflux, often worse with neck extension, not improvement with prone positioning. Would be correct with feeding difficulty and stridor worse extending the neck (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor).

explanation.summary: Severity in paediatric asthma is graded clinically by ability to talk, work of breathing, SpO2 and mental state. Severe asthma is treated with continuous nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium added to the first three nebs, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg) and supplemental oxygen to keep SpO2 at or above 94%. PEFR is not used in young children to triage.
key_points: Mild-moderate: salbutamol via MDI-spacer (6-12 puffs), oral prednisolone if moderate
Severe: continuous salbutamol nebs + ipratropium x3 + oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg
Critical (silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, drowsy): IV magnesium, ICU referral
Antibiotics only if focal infection
Reassess after each intervention; trend rather than single snapshot
explanation.pearls: Speaking in phrases or single words and SpO2 below 92% on room air should immediately trigger nebulised therapy plus oral steroid in any child with known asthma.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: This is severe acute asthma by Australian severity criteria (unable to speak in sentences, SpO2 90 percent, marked work of breathing). National Asthma Council and RCH guidance: continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium added to first three nebs, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg immediately, and titrated oxygen. IV magnesium is the next step if no response.
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: MDI-spacer is mild-moderate territory; severe asthma with SpO2 90 percent demands nebulised therapy and immediate oral steroid, not registrar-gated dosing. Spacer would suit a mild attack with SpO2 over 94 percent (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma).

IV magnesium is escalation after inhaled bronchodilator plus oral steroid have failed, not first-line; skipping inhaled therapy denies definitive bronchodilation. Would be correct as second-line in severe asthma not responding to first hour of inhaled therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Antibiotics are not routine in acute asthma without focal signs or documented bacterial focus; 4-hourly nebs is sub-therapeutic for severe disease. Continuous nebs are required initially in severe asthma (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma).

Nebulised adrenaline is for croup; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (not dexamethasone) is the standard asthma steroid in Australia. Would suit moderate croup with stridor at rest (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; RCH CPG: Asthma).

explanation.summary: Correct MDI-spacer technique: shake canister, attach, lip-seal on the mouthpiece, fire ONE puff, then either 4 slow tidal breaths or one slow deep breath followed by a 5-second breath-hold, then repeat for the next puff. Wash monthly with detergent, drip-dry, do not towel-dry.
key_points: One puff at a time - multiple puffs reduce delivery
Tidal breathing (younger) or slow deep breath + breath-hold (older)
Tight lip seal on mouthpiece
Air-dry after monthly wash (preserves antistatic coating)
Mask under 4 years, mouthpiece preferred from age 4 onwards if technique is good
explanation.pearls: If asthma is uncontrolled, watch the patient use their inhaler before changing medication. Most apparent treatment failure is technique failure.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Mouthpiece is preferred over 4 years if lip seal is reliable; switching back to a face-mask reduces drug delivery in older children. Face-mask is correct only under 4 years or when lip seal fails (Source: National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Spacers are washed monthly with detergent and air-dried; towel-drying generates static that reduces drug delivery. This is the classic spacer-technique pitfall to teach families (Source: National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: 5-10 second breath-hold is enough; 30 seconds adds no benefit and most children cannot comply (Source: National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: The two most common technique errors are firing multiple puffs without separating them (drug coalesces and impacts on the spacer wall) and breaking the lip seal between breaths. The single most important correction is one puff per actuation with 4 tidal breaths and a maintained lip seal, per the National Asthma Council How to Use Your Spacer factsheet.
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: DPIs need a fast inspiratory flow that many 8-year-olds cannot generate reliably, especially when unwell. DPI would be appropriate only for a teen with confirmed adequate inspiratory flow (Source: National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Severe bronchiolitis with apnoea, hypercapnia or persistent hypoxia despite low-flow O2 is treated with stepwise escalation: low-flow nasal prong O2 -> HFNC 2 L/kg/min -> CPAP -> intubation. HFNC is now the first non-invasive step (PARIS trial), reserving CPAP and intubation for failure. Antibiotics and salbutamol are not routinely indicated.
key_points: HFNC flow rate 2 L/kg/min, FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92-96%
Indications to escalate: ongoing apnoea, rising CO2, exhaustion, FiO2 >60%
CPAP useful for type 2 respiratory failure not responding to HFNC
Intubation for failure of non-invasive support
Salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics: not routine
explanation.pearls: Recurrent apnoea in a young infant is by itself a reason to escalate from low-flow O2 to HFNC or CPAP, even without severe hypoxia.

options.rationale: Low-flow O2 does not unload respiratory muscles or prevent apnoea; nasal prongs cap out at sub-therapeutic support for type 2 failure. Would be appropriate only with mild work of breathing and SpO2 needs alone (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

Hypertonic saline and salbutamol are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis in AU guidelines; they distract from definitive escalation. Would be considered only in older toddlers with viral-induced wheeze (Source: PREDICT Bronchiolitis Guideline).

HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the first escalation step for severe bronchiolitis with respiratory failure or apnoea, supported by the PARIS trial and RCH CPG. CPAP or intubation is reserved for ongoing apnoea, rising CO2 or exhaustion despite optimal HFNC. With recurrent apnoea and a pCO2 of 65 mmHg, HFNC is initiated now with clear escalation criteria (RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; Franklin PARIS NEJM 2018).

Intubation is reserved for failure of non-invasive support (HFNC/CPAP), persistent apnoea, exhaustion or progressive hypercapnia despite optimisation. Premature intubation increases ventilator-associated complications. Would be correct after a failed HFNC trial (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

Steroids and antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated viral bronchiolitis and do nothing for impending respiratory failure. Antibiotics only with proven bacterial co-infection or sepsis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: When severe paediatric asthma fails to respond to first-line therapy (continuous salbutamol nebs, ipratropium, oral prednisolone) after 30 to 60 minutes, the next step is IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes with PICU involvement. Further failure prompts IV salbutamol or aminophylline infusions and consideration of intubation.
key_points: First-line: continuous nebs + ipratropium x3 + oral prednisolone
Second-line: IV magnesium 50 mg/kg over 20 min, max 2 g
Third-line: IV salbutamol or aminophylline infusion (PICU)
Watch for salbutamol lactic acidosis, hypokalaemia, tachyarrhythmia
Intubation is high-risk in asthma; use experienced operator and ketamine
explanation.pearls: A normal or rising pCO2 in a child with severe asthma is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure - it should escalate, not reassure.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Aminophylline is third-line after IV magnesium fails; narrow therapeutic index with arrhythmia and seizure risk. Would be correct in PICU after magnesium and IV salbutamol failure (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma).

Nebulised adrenaline is the croup drug; in asthma it offers no benefit over salbutamol and may cause hypertensive effects. Would be correct in severe croup with stridor at rest (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma; RCH CPG: Croup).

IV salbutamol is reserved for after IV magnesium has failed; using it first risks worsening the existing beta-agonist-driven lactic acidosis and tachyarrhythmia. Would be appropriate after magnesium trial with persistent severe asthma (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma).

Oral prednisolone is equipotent to IV hydrocortisone if absorbed; doubling up adds toxicity (hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia) without benefit. IV hydrocortisone is correct only when oral is not tolerated (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma; National Asthma Handbook).

IV magnesium 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes is the recommended second-line bronchodilator for paediatric asthma not responding to first-line inhaled therapy plus oral steroid, with PICU involvement; aminophylline and IV salbutamol are reserved for further failure (RCH CPG: Asthma acute; National Asthma Council Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: No single feature reliably distinguishes bacterial from viral paediatric pneumonia. The combination of procalcitonin elevation (especially >0.5 microg/L), neutrophilic leucocytosis, lobar consolidation on CXR and high fever is more specific than any single feature. In practice, all children with clinical pneumonia receive empirical antibiotics in Australia, but biomarker stratification informs duration and de-escalation.
key_points: Bacterial features: high fever, focal/lobar consolidation, neutrophilia, elevated PCT
Viral features: diffuse interstitial pattern, lymphocytosis, normal PCT, prominent URTI
Procalcitonin >0.5 microg/L is the best single biomarker for bacterial cause
Treat clinical pneumonia empirically; reserve narrow-spectrum oral amoxicillin first
Common pathogens by age: <2 viral, 2-5 viral plus pneumococcus, >5 add mycoplasma
explanation.pearls: Procalcitonin is more specific than CRP for bacterial infection in children but is not universally available; combined with neutrophilia and focal imaging it best separates bacterial from viral infection.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: Tachypnoea is a severity marker but non-specific; both viral and bacterial pneumonia produce it. Would never alone discriminate aetiology (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Childhood pneumonia).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: Lobar consolidation supports bacterial cause but viral pneumonia (RSV, adenovirus, influenza) can produce lobar pattern, and bacterial can be patchy. Biomarkers are more specific. Would be more discriminating if combined with high procalcitonin (Source: RCH CPG: CAP).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: CRP rises in both viral and bacterial disease; an isolated high CRP without neutrophilia or procalcitonin has poor specificity. Would be more discriminating combined with procalcitonin over 0.5 (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: A procalcitonin above approximately 0.5 microg/L (and especially above 2) combined with neutrophilic leucocytosis is the most specific biomarker pattern for bacterial pneumonia; isolated CRP elevation and lobar appearance both have meaningful overlap with severe viral pneumonia. The combined pattern strengthens the bacterial diagnosis substantially (BMJ Best Practice; Stockmann 2018 J Pediatr).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: Both bacterial and viral pneumonia commonly follow a viral URTI and sibling contact is non-discriminating. Would discriminate only with extrapulmonary atypical features (e.g. rash, haemolysis suggesting Mycoplasma) (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

explanation.summary: Foreign body aspiration classically presents in toddlers with a witnessed choking episode followed by focal monophonic wheeze and reduced breath sounds on the affected side. A normal CXR does not exclude the diagnosis. Inspiratory/expiratory views may show air trapping; rigid bronchoscopy under GA remains both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: Classic triad: choke + cough + focal wheeze / reduced breath sounds
Most common location: right main bronchus (more vertical takeoff)
Normal CXR does NOT rule out FBA
Inspiratory/expiratory or decubitus films may show air trapping
Rigid bronchoscopy is the gold standard
explanation.pearls: If the history is right, take the child to theatre even with a normal CXR. Peanuts and other organic foreign bodies are radiolucent and frequently missed.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Foreign body aspiration

options.rationale: Normal CXR does not exclude a radiolucent foreign body (most peanuts and plastics); a witnessed choking episode plus focal signs mandates bronchoscopy. Discharge risks a missed aspiration, which can lead to chronic lung damage (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Foreign body aspiration

options.rationale: Focal monophonic wheeze after a choking episode is not asthma; salbutamol trial delays diagnosis. Would be appropriate only with diffuse polyphonic wheeze and no choking history (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration).

No fever, no consolidation, no systemic illness; antibiotics and steroids do not dislodge a foreign body. Empirical antibiotics would be appropriate only with established post-obstructive pneumonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

CT is more sensitive than CXR but adds radiation without changing management; rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic. CT is appropriate only in atypical or chronic presentations where diagnosis is unclear (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration).

A witnessed choking episode followed by focal monophonic wheeze and asymmetrical breath sounds is the classic triad of foreign body aspiration. Inspiratory/expiratory or lateral decubitus films may show air trapping on the affected side, but a normal CXR does not exclude FBA; rigid bronchoscopy under GA is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is the standard next step (RCH CPG: Foreign body aspiration; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Foreign body aspiration

explanation.summary: Pre-school wheeze in children under 5 is divided into episodic viral-triggered wheeze (most common, often resolves) and multi-trigger wheeze (more likely to evolve into asthma). Maintenance ICS is indicated when attacks are frequent (more than 2 to 3 per year with severity features), when interval symptoms are present, or when there are strong atopic features. PRN salbutamol via spacer with mask and a written action plan is the cornerstone of episodic management.
key_points: Episodic viral wheeze without interval symptoms: PRN salbutamol
Maintenance ICS only if >2-3 attacks/year, interval symptoms or atopy
Use mask spacer in children under 4-5 unless mouthpiece technique reliable
Provide a written action plan for every wheezy child
Modified Asthma Predictive Index helps identify higher-risk patterns
explanation.pearls: Most viral-triggered pre-school wheeze resolves by school age. Avoid starting ICS in children who do not meet maintenance criteria - growth effects accumulate.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Daily ICS is for the Modified Asthma Predictive Index pattern: frequent symptoms, interval symptoms, or over 2-3 severe attacks/year. Infrequent viral-triggered wheeze without interval symptoms does not meet criteria. Would be correct with mAPI-positive or frequent severe attacks (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Montelukast has only modest benefit in preschool wheeze, is not preferred first-line maintenance, and carries an FDA black-box neuropsychiatric warning. Considered only when ICS not tolerated (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Episodic viral-triggered wheeze in a child under 5 without interval symptoms, without atopy, and with fewer than 3 to 4 severe attacks per year is managed with PRN salbutamol via MDI plus spacer with mask, technique reinforcement and a written action plan. Maintenance ICS is not indicated until episodes are more frequent, more severe or interval symptoms develop (National Asthma Council Handbook; RCH CPG: Asthma).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Pre-emptive high-dose ICS at URTI onset has evidence only in severe preschool wheezers and risks growth velocity reduction. Would be appropriate only with severe recurrent attacks failing other strategies under specialist input (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Specialist referral is for diagnostic uncertainty, severe/frequent attacks, failure of standard therapy, or atypical features; this is textbook preschool viral wheeze and is managed in primary care. Would be correct with poor response to standard step-up (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Moderate croup (Westley 3 to 7; stridor at rest with recession but otherwise alert and pink) is treated with nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000) plus oral dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg standard, up to 0.6 mg/kg) and observed for 3 hours (RCH minimum) after the last adrenaline dose to detect rebound. Severe croup (Westley 8 or above, hypoxia, exhaustion, drowsiness) needs PICU and consideration of intubation.
key_points: Mild (Westley 0-2): dex 0.15 mg/kg PO, observe briefly
Moderate (3-7): nebulised adrenaline + dex, observe 4 hrs post-adrenaline
Severe (8+): adrenaline + dex, ICU, anaesthetics, consider intubation
Adrenaline acts in 10-30 min, effect lasts ~2 hrs; rebound mandates observation
Steroid onset ~1-2 hrs; covers symptom course of 24-48 hrs
explanation.pearls: Drooling, tripod posture, muffled voice and toxic appearance in an unwell unimmunised child should prompt consideration of epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis rather than croup, with airway team activation rather than examination of the throat.

options.rationale: Dexamethasone alone is for mild croup (Westley 0-2); stridor at rest and marked recession is moderate (Westley 3-7) and requires nebulised adrenaline plus 4-hour observation for rebound. Would be correct for mild croup with no stridor at rest (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Moderate croup (Westley 3-7) with stridor at rest is treated with nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg). Adrenaline acts within 30 minutes but lasts about 2 hours; steroid onset is 1-2 hours. The 3-hour (RCH minimum) minimum observation captures any rebound, per RCH CPG: Croup.

Epiglottitis presents with drooling, tripod posture, toxic appearance and muffled (not hoarse) voice, typically in unimmunised children; this presentation is viral croup. Would be correct only with epiglottitis features (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).
Humidified air and heliox have no proven benefit; deferring steroid is harmful as steroid reduces admission and return visits. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Salbutamol/ipratropium addresses bronchospasm not subglottic oedema; treating croup as asthma misses the pathology. Would be correct for acute asthma with audible wheeze and recession (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: For a school-age child with uncontrolled asthma on low-dose ICS despite confirmed correct technique, good adherence and absence of modifiable triggers, the National Asthma Council preferred step-up is combination low-dose ICS-LABA. Doubling the ICS dose is an acceptable alternative. Always recheck adherence, technique, environmental factors and the diagnosis before stepping up.
key_points: Before stepping up: recheck technique, adherence, triggers, diagnosis (the 4 As)
Preferred step-up (age 6+): low-dose ICS-LABA
Alternative: medium-dose ICS, or ICS + LTRA
Step down once control achieved for 3 months
Refer to specialist if uncontrolled on medium-dose ICS-LABA
explanation.pearls: The most common reason for 'uncontrolled asthma' is technique or adherence failure, not severity. Watch every patient use their inhaler at every review.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Montelukast is an alternative add-on but less effective than LABA at this step in children 6 plus; AU guidelines prefer ICS-LABA as primary step-up. Would be considered only if LABA contraindicated or not tolerated (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: She has poor symptom control on low-dose ICS despite correct technique, good adherence and no modifiable factors. The National Asthma Council preferred step-up in children 6 and over is combination low-dose ICS-LABA. Doubling the ICS dose is an alternative but ICS-LABA generally produces better symptom and lung function gains for the same total ICS exposure (National Asthma Council Handbook; GINA 2024).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: MART (as-needed budesonide-formoterol) is the preferred adult/adolescent strategy but not the primary step-up for a 10-year-old already on regular ICS with poor control; combination ICS-LABA is preferred. Would be appropriate from age 12 with structured MART introduction (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab) require failure of high-dose ICS-LABA with optimised adherence; jumping to biologic without intermediate step-up is the over-escalation error. Would be correct only after high-dose ICS-LABA failure (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: LAMA (tiotropium) is add-on for severe asthma uncontrolled on medium-to-high-dose ICS-LABA, not first step-up from low-dose ICS. Would be appropriate at later step after ICS-LABA failure (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Pertussis in unvaccinated young infants presents in three phases (catarrhal, paroxysmal, convalescent) and carries significant morbidity from apnoea, pneumonia and pertussis-related pulmonary hypertension. Infants under 6 months with apnoea or feeding difficulty are admitted. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days is the first-line treatment in young infants (lower pyloric stenosis risk than erythromycin). Pertussis is notifiable on clinical suspicion and close contacts require post-exposure prophylaxis with the same macrolide.
key_points: Three phases: catarrhal (1-2 wk) - paroxysmal (2-6 wk) - convalescent (weeks)
Infants <6 months: admit if apnoea, feeding difficulty, cyanosis
Azithromycin first-line in young infants (10 mg/kg/day x 5 days)
Notifiable disease on clinical suspicion
Post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts including pregnant women and young infants
explanation.pearls: Lymphocytosis (often >20 x10^9/L) is a clinical clue in pertussis. In ex-premature or under-6-month infants, the first sign may be apnoea rather than cough.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin does not cover Bordetella pertussis; macrolides are required. Apnoea in an under-6-month infant warrants admission, and pertussis is notifiable on clinical suspicion. Would be correct only for a different bacterial cause (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG; Therapeutic Guidelines).

Azithromycin and admission are correct but salbutamol does not relieve pertussis spasm, and contact tracing plus household post-exposure prophylaxis is mandatory under CDNA. Would be appropriate without the salbutamol and with the public health step (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG).

Infants under 6 months with pertussis and any apnoeic features should be admitted because of the risk of bradycardia, apnoea and death. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days is the first-line macrolide for infants under 6 months (lower risk of pyloric stenosis than erythromycin). Pertussis is notifiable on clinical suspicion, and close household contacts (especially infants and pregnant women) require post-exposure prophylaxis with the same regimen (Therapeutic Guidelines; CDNA Pertussis SoNG; NCIRS).

Erythromycin is associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in under-1-month infants and has more GI side effects than azithromycin; under-6-months with apnoea must be admitted. Would be acceptable only for older children when azithromycin unavailable (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG).
Ceftriaxone and prednisolone do not treat pertussis; notification on clinical suspicion is required to begin contact tracing immediately. (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG).

explanation.summary: A written asthma action plan uses traffic-light zones: green (well, take preventer), yellow (symptoms worsening - intensify), red (severe - emergency). Yellow zone actions include increased salbutamol (4 to 6 puffs every 4 hours via spacer), continued or temporarily increased preventer, and review within 24 to 48 hours. Red zone triggers emergency response (4 puffs salbutamol, repeat every 4 minutes if no improvement, call 000).
key_points: Green: regular preventer + reliever as needed; recognise triggers
Yellow: salbutamol 4-6 puffs q4h; continue or increase preventer; GP review 24-48 hrs
Red: 4 puffs every 4 min, call 000, oral prednisolone if prescribed
Update plan every 12 months and after every significant exacerbation
Provide a copy to the school and any out-of-school carer
explanation.pearls: Action plans reduce hospitalisations and school absence. The most common reason for repeated exacerbations is delayed family escalation in the yellow zone.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Yellow zone by definition requires intensification; 2 puffs 4-hourly equals background PRN and misses the early deterioration. Would be appropriate only in the green zone (Source: National Asthma Handbook Action Plan).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Home-initiated prednisolone is for selected children with frequent severe exacerbations under specialist tailored plans, not routine yellow-zone primary-care advice. Would be appropriate with a documented specialist plan (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Stopping the preventer during deterioration worsens control by removing anti-inflammatory cover; preventer is continued or intensified. (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: The National Asthma Council yellow zone increases salbutamol to 4-6 puffs via spacer every 4 hours, continues or temporarily steps up preventer, and arranges GP review within 24-48 hours with clear red-flag criteria for ED. Written zone-based plans reduce hospitalisation and time off school.
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Mandating ED for any salbutamol increase produces unnecessary attendances and undermines self-management; the plan needs graded thresholds (home/GP/ED). Would be appropriate only for red-zone criteria (Source: National Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: A CF pulmonary exacerbation is defined by increased cough, sputum volume or purulence, dyspnoea, anorexia, weight loss, and a fall in FEV1 (typically 10% or more from baseline). Admission is indicated for significant FEV1 decline, hypoxia or failure to respond to oral therapy. Standard empirical IV regimen for chronic mucoid Pseudomonas: a beta-lactam (ceftazidime or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus an aminoglycoside (tobramycin once daily) for 10 to 14 days, with intensified physiotherapy and dietetic input. CFTR modulators are continued throughout.
key_points: Exacerbation triggers: fall in FEV1 >=10%, increased sputum/cough, weight loss, hypoxia
Empirical IV: anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam + aminoglycoside x 10-14 days
Once-daily tobramycin with trough monitoring (renal and auditory toxicity)
Continue CFTR modulator and adjust based on culture
Adjuncts: intensified physio, nutrition, treat any DIOS or hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: In a CF patient with chronic Pseudomonas, never treat an exacerbation with a single agent. The double-cover principle reduces emergence of resistance and is the Australian and international standard.

sources.label: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Standards of Care

options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin monotherapy is for early Pseudomonas eradication or mild outpatient exacerbations; FEV1 drop of 17 points with consolidation, weight loss and hypoxia mandates IV dual therapy and admission. Would be correct for mild exacerbation with preserved spirometry (Source: CF Foundation Pulmonary Guidelines).

Ceftriaxone does not reliably cover Pseudomonas; ceftazidime, piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem is required. Azithromycin has anti-inflammatory but not adequate antipseudomonal effect in CF. Would be appropriate for non-CF CAP (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Flucloxacillin covers MSSA, which is supplementary not primary in chronic Pseudomonas exacerbation; rifampicin adds no value and is hepatotoxic. Would be appropriate with confirmed MSSA exacerbation and no Pseudomonas (Source: CF Foundation Pulmonary Guidelines).

Carbapenem monotherapy is reserved for multi-resistant Pseudomonas or beta-lactam allergy; standard is beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside to preserve carbapenems and exploit synergy. Would be appropriate with documented multi-resistant Pseudomonas (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines; CF Australia).
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Standards of Care

options.rationale: A CF pulmonary exacerbation in an adolescent with chronic mucoid Pseudomonas is treated empirically with dual anti-pseudomonal IV therapy combining an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (commonly ceftazidime) with an aminoglycoside (tobramycin once daily, with levels monitored) for 10 to 14 days. Intensified airway clearance physiotherapy and nutritional optimisation are essential adjuncts and her CFTR modulator is continued. MSSA is co-covered or treated separately if persistent (Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory; CF Australia Standards of Care; Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Guidelines).
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Standards of Care

explanation.summary: HEEADSSS begins with separating the parent, framing confidentiality and its limits, and then progressing from low-threat to high-threat domains (Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Self-harm, Safety), as per the RACP GP Resource Kit.
key_points: Always interview adolescent alone for at least part of the consult
Frame confidentiality and its mandatory limits BEFORE questions
Order matters: lower threat domains first, sexuality and suicide later
Every encounter is a HEEADSSS opportunity
Self-report screens supplement, never replace, the interview
explanation.pearls: Maternal 'just school stress' framing in front of a guarded teenager is a cue to politely separate, not to defer.

sources.label: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health
NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework

options.rationale: The standard adolescent consultation structure is parent out, confidentiality and its mandatory-reporting limits explained, then HEEADSSS progressing from least to most sensitive domains, as per RACP GP Resource Kit and NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework.
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health
NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework

options.rationale: Parental presence systematically suppresses disclosure of risk behaviour; HEEADSSS is conducted with the adolescent alone after explicit confidentiality framing. Would be reasonable only as warm-up small talk before the parent leaves (Source: RACP Adolescent Health GP Resource Kit).
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health

options.rationale: HEEADSSS deliberately starts with low-threat domains (Home, Education) and saves Sexuality and Suicide for after rapport. Opening with high-threat domains discourages disclosure (Source: RACP GP Resource Kit).
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health

options.rationale: Every adolescent encounter is a HEEADSSS opportunity; deferral risks missing the disclosure the guarded presentation suggests. Would be acceptable only if the patient refuses, with explicit return-to-it next visit (Source: RACP GP Resource Kit).
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health

options.rationale: Self-administered screens can supplement but never replace structured face-to-face interview; subtle cues and follow-up questions are lost. Would be appropriate only as an adjunct to direct interview (Source: NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework).
source_refs: NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework

explanation.summary: The standard adolescent confidentiality frame names three limits up front: risk of serious harm to self, risk of serious harm to others, and current abuse. This is delivered BEFORE the HEEADSSS interview so the young person can give informed consent to the conversation.
key_points: Confidentiality is conditional, not absolute
Limits = harm to self, harm to others, abuse
Limits are explained BEFORE questions, not after disclosure
Under 16 does not automatically mean parental disclosure
Drug, sex and mental health content alone do not breach confidentiality
explanation.pearls: Adolescents test the boundary first; a clear script buys trust for the rest of the consult.

sources.label: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health
NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework

options.rationale: Unconditional promises misrepresent the legal duty to disclose risk of serious harm and destroy trust when a later break becomes necessary. Would never be correct; framing the limits up-front protects the relationship (Source: RACP GP Resource Kit).
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health

options.rationale: The standard adolescent confidentiality script names the three limits up front (self-harm risk, harm to others, abuse) before the interview begins, as per RACP GP Resource Kit and NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework.
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health
NSW Health Youth Health Better Practice Framework

options.rationale: Parental disclosure is not automatic under 16 in Australia; the Gillick framework permits confidential care if the adolescent is competent. Would be correct only if the adolescent is not Gillick-competent and parental involvement is in their best interest (Source: RACGP; RACP).
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health

options.rationale: Confidentiality limits are tied to risk of serious harm and abuse, not to which topic is discussed; carving out drug use as private misrepresents the duty. (Source: RACP GP Resource Kit).
source_refs: RACP GP Resource Kit Adolescent Health

options.rationale: Confidential adolescent care without a parent present is the recommended model; parental consent is not required to interview a Gillick-competent young person. Would be appropriate only if the adolescent is clearly not Gillick-competent (Source: RACGP Adolescent Confidentiality Guidance).

explanation.summary: Contraception for under-16s in Australia follows the Gillick competence test (also known as the mature minor doctrine): a young person who can demonstrate sufficient understanding can consent to medical treatment without parental involvement. The standard documentation includes the young person's ability to understand the proposed treatment and its risks, alternatives including non-treatment, the implications of declining parental involvement, broader sexual health (consent, contraception, STI screening, safety, exploitation), and the reasons for the request. The clinician encourages parental involvement but does not require it once competence is documented. Reportable concerns include relationships with significant age or power imbalance, evidence of exploitation, coercion, or trafficking - mandatory reporting thresholds vary by state but all jurisdictions mandate report when sexual abuse is suspected. STI screening, hepatitis B status, cervical screening eligibility (now from age 25), and HPV vaccination should be addressed at the same visit. LARC (implant, IUS, copper IUD) are first-line for adolescents because of failure rates an order of magnitude lower than oral methods.
key_points: Gillick competence is decision-specific (this decision, today)
Encourage parental involvement, do not require it
Consensual same-age relationships are not automatically reportable in NSW
Document understanding of method, side effects, risks, alternatives
Screen for coercion and power imbalance
explanation.pearls: Gillick competence assesses the minor's understanding of the contraceptive being prescribed, its risks, alternatives, the implications of refusing parental involvement, and the broader sexual health context. Once documented, parental consent is not required - though parental involvement should be encouraged (Royal Australian College of GP).

options.rationale: AU law follows Gillick: a competent minor may consent to contraception without parental involvement. A blanket parental-consent rule has no legal basis for a competent minor. Would be appropriate only if Gillick competence is not established (Source: Family Planning NSW; RACGP).
