Would be correct only with any red-flag feature (diastolic component, harsh quality, abnormal pulses, failure to thrive) (Source: RCH CPG).

No Jones features and no sore throat history; investigating ARF in an asymptomatic child with classic innocent murmur is inappropriate. Would be correct only in high-risk populations with sore throat history and Jones features (Source: RHDAustralia).
HCM has a harsh systolic murmur that INCREASES with Valsalva (opposite of this), often family history of sudden death. Would be correct only with that profile (Source: RCH CPG).

Small VSD murmur is harsh, pansystolic, often with thrill, and does not soften with Valsalva; the described musical dynamic murmur is innocent. Would be correct only with the pansystolic VSD profile (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: A tet spell is a sudden increase in right-to-left shunt through the VSD due to infundibular spasm or a drop in SVR. The murmur softens because pulmonary flow falls. Stepwise management: calm the child, knee-chest position, 100% oxygen, IV fluid bolus 10 to 20 mL/kg, IV or IM morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then IV propranolol 0.1 mg/kg or phenylephrine if refractory.
key_points: Murmur softens during spell (less pulmonary flow)
Knee-chest raises SVR, reducing right-to-left shunt
Morphine reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm
Avoid agents that drop SVR or preload
Refractory: propranolol, phenylephrine, intubation, ECMO, urgent surgery
explanation.pearls: Beta-blockers are used both acutely and as a bridge to surgery to prevent spells; never give inotropes that increase contractility (worsens infundibular spasm).

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Tetralogy of Fallot

options.rationale: Adenosine treats SVT, not a hypercyanotic spell; rhythm is sinus tachycardia from right-to-left shunting. Would be correct in narrow-complex SVT not responding to vagal manoeuvres (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot).

First-line management of a tet spell is knee-chest positioning to raise systemic vascular resistance plus IV or IM morphine 0.1 mg/kg to abolish hyperpnoea and reduce infundibular spasm, as per RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot and AHA scientific statement.
Furosemide reduces preload and worsens right-to-left shunting in a tet spell; volume expansion not depletion is needed. Would never be correct in a tet spell (Source: RCH CPG: ToF).
PGE1 maintains ductal patency in duct-dependent neonatal lesions; at 8 months the duct is closed. Would be correct in a neonate with duct-dependent cyanotic lesion (Source: BMJ Best Practice: ToF).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Tetralogy of Fallot

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for documented severe acidosis after positioning, oxygen, fluids and morphine have failed. Would be correct only as final step in refractory tet spell with confirmed acidosis (Source: AHA scientific statement).

explanation.summary: Symptomatic large VSD presents at 6 to 12 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls and left-to-right shunt increases. Features include tachypnoea, sweating with feeds, hepatomegaly and failure to thrive. Medical management is loop diuretic plus ACE inhibitor plus high-energy feeds, with surgical closure for ongoing failure to thrive, pulmonary hypertension, or large unrestricted shunt before fixed pulmonary vascular disease develops.
key_points: Murmur is harsh pansystolic LLSE, often with thrill
Furosemide 1 to 2 mg/kg BD plus ACE inhibitor (captopril or enalapril)
Avoid supplemental O2 (drops PVR, worsens shunt)
Surgery before fixed pulmonary vascular disease
Small muscular VSDs often close spontaneously
explanation.pearls: Symptoms typically appear at 4 to 8 weeks because pulmonary vascular resistance must fall before left-to-right shunting becomes haemodynamically significant.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children
BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.rationale: Spontaneous closure is common only for small muscular VSDs; failure to thrive and heart failure demand treatment. Would be correct only for a small muscular VSD without haemodynamic features (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Failure in Children).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children

options.rationale: Beta-blockers are not first-line in infant left-to-right shunt failure; diuretic plus afterload reduction is standard. Would be correct in tet-spell prophylaxis or other specific indications (Source: BMJ Best Practice: VSD).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.rationale: Standard medical therapy of large VSD with heart failure in infancy is loop diuretic plus ACE inhibitor for afterload reduction plus calorie-dense feeds, with surgical closure typically before 6 to 12 months if failure to thrive or pulmonary hypertension persists, per RCH CPG and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children
BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.rationale: PGE1 is for duct-dependent lesions; a VSD with left-to-right shunt does not depend on the duct. Would be correct in duct-dependent cyanotic lesions (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Ventricular septal defect

options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen lowers PVR and worsens pulmonary overcirculation in a VSD; this is the textbook iatrogenic error in left-to-right shunts. Would be correct only for documented hypoxaemia from another cause (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Failure).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Heart failure in children

explanation.summary: Haemodynamically significant PDA in preterm neonates causes pulmonary overcirculation, prolonged ventilation, IVH, NEC and BPD. Echo criteria for significance include diameter > 1.5 mm, LA:Ao > 1.4, reversed diastolic flow in descending aorta. First-line closure is a COX-inhibitor course (ibuprofen or indometacin) or paracetamol if contraindicated, with surgical ligation if pharmacological therapy fails. Term PDA usually closes spontaneously within 72 hours; persistent term PDA is managed by elective device closure beyond infancy.
key_points: Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg then 5 mg/kg at 24 and 48 h is now preferred (less renal toxicity than indometacin)
Contraindications: NEC, IVH, oliguria, thrombocytopenia, sepsis
Surgical ligation if medical fails and PDA remains significant
Term infants: catheter device closure beyond infancy
Echo confirms significance before treatment
explanation.pearls: Indometacin reduces IVH rates but at the cost of more transient oliguria; ibuprofen has become the more widely used agent in Australian NICUs.

sources.label: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus
BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

options.rationale: PGE1 keeps the duct open in duct-dependent lesions; here a haemodynamically significant PDA needs closure, not patency. Would be correct only for duct-dependent neonatal cyanotic lesions (Source: RCH NICU PDA Guideline).
source_refs: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus

options.rationale: Conservative is reasonable for non-haemodynamically significant PDA; this infant has clear significance (escalating ventilation, wide pulse pressure, reversed diastolic flow). Would be correct only for small non-significant PDAs (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

options.rationale: Surgical ligation is reserved for failure or contraindication of medical therapy; pharmacological closure is first-line. Would be correct after failed COX-inhibitor course or contraindication (Source: RCH NICU CPG: PDA).
source_refs: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus

options.rationale: In preterm infants with haemodynamically significant PDA and no contraindication (NEC, active IVH, renal failure, thrombocytopenia), a course of ibuprofen or indometacin is first-line pharmacological closure, per RCH NICU CPG: PDA.
source_refs: RCH NICU CPG: Patent ductus arteriosus
BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

options.rationale: Paracetamol is an emerging second-line as a 3-7 day course when COX inhibitors are contraindicated, not indefinite or first-line. Would be correct as a short course with contraindication to indometacin/ibuprofen (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Patent ductus arteriosus in preterm neonates

explanation.summary: Critical coarctation presents at the end of the first week as the duct closes, producing shock, absent femoral pulses, upper-to-lower limb BP gradient, pre/post-ductal SpO2 differential, and metabolic acidosis. Immediate management is PGE1 infusion (commonly 0.01 to 0.05 microg/kg/min titrated), correction of acidosis, careful fluid resuscitation, and urgent transfer for surgical repair. Side effects of PGE1 include apnoea, fever, hypotension, and flushing; be prepared to intubate.
key_points: Duct-dependent systemic: coarctation, interrupted arch, critical AS, HLHS
PGE1 0.01 to 0.05 microg/kg/min IV
Apnoea is a common side effect; have airway ready
Avoid hyperoxia (constricts duct)
Definitive: surgical or catheter repair
explanation.pearls: If the duct closes before diagnosis, the infant can deteriorate from well to moribund within hours; any unwell neonate in the first 2 weeks needs femoral pulses and 4-limb BPs.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation of the aorta

options.rationale: Diuresis is adjunctive for pulmonary congestion but does not address lethal ductal closure in duct-dependent systemic circulation. Would be correct only as adjunct once PGE1 has restored ductal flow (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cardiology).

Vitamin K does not treat duct closure; PGE1 is required to reopen the duct. Would be correct as routine post-birth, not as immediate management of duct-dependent shock (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation of the aorta

options.rationale: Supplemental O2 further constricts the ductus and accelerates collapse in duct-dependent systemic circulation; target SpO2 is 85-95 percent, not over 95. Would be correct only with confirmed non-cardiac hypoxaemia (Source: RCH CPG).
No narrow-complex tachycardia described; differential pulses and saturation differential are diagnostic of coarctation. Would be correct in SVT (Source: RCH CPG: SVT).

Duct-dependent systemic circulation from coarctation or interrupted aortic arch presents at day 5 to 10 with shock as the duct closes; PGE1 at 0.01 to 0.05 microg/kg/min reopens the duct and is the immediate life-saving therapy, per RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiology and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation of the aorta

explanation.summary: Infant SVT typically presents as poor feeding, pallor and tachypnoea with rates over 220 bpm and a narrow complex on ECG. In the stable infant: vagal manoeuvre (ice to face) then IV adenosine 0.1 mg/kg, repeat 0.2 mg/kg, then 0.3 mg/kg up to a single max of 12 mg, given rapidly into a large vein with saline flush. In the unstable infant proceed straight to synchronised DC cardioversion 0.5 to 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg.
key_points: Stable: ice to face, then adenosine 0.1 then 0.2 mg/kg
Unstable: synchronised cardioversion 0.5 to 1 J/kg
Avoid verapamil under 12 months
Maintenance with propranolol or flecainide guided by cardiology
Check for WPW on sinus ECG after termination
explanation.pearls: Adenosine causes a brief, alarming asystolic pause; counsel the team, have monitor/defib pads on, and use a 3-way tap so the saline flush immediately follows the bolus.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

options.rationale: In a haemodynamically stable infant with SVT, the diving reflex provoked by an ice bag to the face is the recommended vagal manoeuvre and can be attempted first while preparing adenosine, per RCH CPG: SVT and ANZCOR guideline 12.6.
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

options.rationale: Unsynchronised defibrillation is for VF/pulseless VT; unstable SVT needs synchronised cardioversion at 0.5-1 J/kg. Would be correct in pulseless VT or VF (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

options.rationale: Verapamil is contraindicated under 12 months (risk of refractory hypotension and cardiac arrest). Would be correct only in older children with stable SVT and no Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion).
Oral beta-blockade is for chronic prevention, not acute termination in an unwell infant. Would be correct only as maintenance after acute conversion (Source: RCH CPG: SVT).
Carotid sinus massage is not used in infants; ice to the face is the recommended vagal manoeuvre at this age. Would be correct only in older children/adolescents and adults (Source: ANZCOR 12.6).
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.6: Resuscitation in paediatric tachyarrhythmias

explanation.summary: Diagnostic QTc cut-offs: a single resting QTc > 480 ms with unexplained syncope, or > 500 ms without symptoms, supports LQTS (Schwartz score also used). Management includes activity modification (especially swimming/competitive sport in LQT1), avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte derangement, non-selective beta-blockade (propranolol or nadolol), genetic testing, cascade family screening, and ICD for survivors of cardiac arrest or breakthrough events.
key_points: QTc > 480 ms with syncope or > 500 ms asymptomatic suggests LQTS
LQT1: exertion (swimming); LQT2: auditory/emotion; LQT3: rest/sleep
First-line: nadolol or propranolol
Avoid sotalol and other QT-prolonging drugs
Cascade screening of first-degree relatives
explanation.pearls: A sudden death in a young relative while swimming is classic for LQT1; warn the family about both medication and electrolyte triggers and provide a written drug-avoidance list.

sources.label: AHA/HRS expert consensus on inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes
BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

options.rationale: QTc over 480 ms with exertional syncope and family history meets LQTS diagnostic criteria; reassurance misses the diagnosis. Would be correct only with borderline QTc and no syncope/family history (Source: Heart Rhythm Society/AHA expert consensus).
source_refs: AHA/HRS expert consensus on inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes

options.rationale: LQTS with syncope is high-risk; non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol or nadolol) reduce events, exercise restriction is recommended particularly for swimming in LQT1, and first-degree relatives need cascade screening with ECG +/- genetic testing, per AHA/HRS consensus and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: AHA/HRS expert consensus on inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes
BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

options.rationale: Sotalol prolongs QT and is contraindicated in LQTS; non-QT-prolonging beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol) are preferred. Would never be correct in LQTS (Source: AMH; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

options.rationale: ICD is reserved for arrest survivors or breakthrough syncope on beta-blocker; first-line is beta-blocker plus lifestyle modification. Would be correct after beta-blocker failure (Source: AHA/HRS consensus).
source_refs: AHA/HRS expert consensus on inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes

options.rationale: Exertional trigger, family sudden death, and prolonged QTc point to LQTS not epilepsy; hypoxic limb jerking mimics seizure but is not seizure. Would be correct only with confirmed seizure on EEG (Source: BMJ Best Practice: LQTS).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease cause one of the largest health gaps for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians, with incidence rates 100-fold higher than non-Indigenous populations. Diagnosis uses Jones criteria modified for high-risk populations: 2 majors, or 1 major plus 2 minors, plus evidence of preceding group A strep infection (ASOT, anti-DNase B, throat swab or PCR). Majors in high-risk populations include carditis (clinical or subclinical), polyarthritis, monoarthritis or polyarthralgia, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules; minors include fever above 38, ESR above 30 or CRP above 30, prolonged PR interval (age-adjusted), and monoarthralgia. All confirmed cases require notification to the state RHD register, echocardiogram for baseline carditis assessment, and benzathine penicillin G secondary prophylaxis 4-weekly for a minimum of 10 years or until age 21 (longer for those with carditis or valve disease).
key_points: High-risk Australia: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori/Pacific Islander, immigrants from endemic areas
Majors high-risk: carditis (incl. subclinical), polyarthritis OR monoarthritis OR polyarthralgia, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules
Minors high-risk: fever >= 38 deg C, ESR >= 30 mm/h or CRP elevated, prolonged PR for age, monoarthralgia
Recurrence: 2 majors, OR 1 major + 2 minors, OR 3 minors + GAS evidence
Treat: benzathine penicillin G IM and secondary prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: In high-risk populations (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori, Pacific Islander), the 2020 RHDAustralia Jones criteria accept monoarthritis and polyarthralgia as major manifestations and lower the minor thresholds for fever (38) and ESR (30); secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G 4-weekly for 10+ years is the cornerstone (RHDAustralia 2020).

options.rationale: Fever is a minor criterion, not mandatory; diagnosis requires 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor with GAS evidence. Would be correct only if fever were a stated mandatory feature (it is not) (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Jones).
Carditis is one of several majors, not mandatory; absence does not exclude ARF if other criteria met. Would never be correct as a rule-out (Source: RHDAustralia 2020).

Under the 2020 RHDAustralia high-risk criteria, polyarthritis is a major; she has 1 major (polyarthritis) plus 3 minors (prolonged PR for age, raised CRP and ESR) plus serological evidence of recent GAS (raised ASOT and anti-DNase B), satisfying the 1 major + 2 minor + GAS evidence threshold for definite initial ARF, per RHDAustralia 2020.
In high-risk populations monoarthritis/polyarthralgia can also be a major; polyarthritis remains a major giving definite (not probable) ARF when criteria met. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020).
Anti-DNase B is accepted GAS evidence in addition to ASOT; the criteria are met. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020).

explanation.summary: Classic KD requires fever >= 5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features (conjunctival injection, oral changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy > 1.5 cm). Infants under 6 months and over 8 years commonly have incomplete disease with fewer features but a high risk of coronary artery aneurysms. The AHA algorithm allows diagnosis when fever >= 5 days plus 2 to 3 features plus supportive labs are present, or with abnormal echocardiogram. Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion plus aspirin (high-dose anti-inflammatory then low-dose antiplatelet).
key_points: Incomplete KD: think in any infant under 6 months with fever > 7 days
Supportive labs: CRP >= 30, ESR >= 40, plus 3 of (anaemia, plt >= 450 after day 7, albumin <= 30, raised ALT, WCC >= 15, sterile pyuria)
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%
Aspirin (high-dose anti-inflammatory, then low-dose antiplatelet)
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria is a classic and often missed clue; always check a urine in prolonged unexplained fever.

options.rationale: Persistent fever over 5 days with KD features in an infant under 6 months mandates urgent assessment for coronary artery disease, not discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki).

Persistently negative cultures and no antibiotic response shift the differential to Kawasaki; continued empirical antibiotics delay IVIG. Would be correct only with culture-positive infection (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Kawasaki).

Echo is essential and arranged urgently, but treatment with IVIG must not be delayed pending echo in incomplete KD with supportive labs. Would be correct only if echo could be done immediately at no delay to IVIG (Source: AHA Kawasaki).

Infants under 6 months commonly present with incomplete KD. Fever >= 5 days plus 2 to 3 principal features plus supportive labs (CRP >= 30 mg/L or ESR >= 40 mm/h, plus 3 or more of anaemia, platelets >= 450, albumin <= 30, raised ALT, WCC >= 15, sterile pyuria) supports incomplete KD; treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion plus aspirin, with urgent echo to assess coronaries, per AHA statement and RCH CPG.

Steroids are an adjunct (high-risk patients, IVIG-resistant disease), not monotherapy; IVIG remains first-line. Would be correct only as adjunct alongside IVIG in high-risk patients (Source: AHA Kawasaki).

explanation.summary: All newborns with suspected or confirmed T21 require echocardiography within the first month (within days if a duct-dependent lesion is suspected or surgery is planned), karyotype confirmation, audiology, ophthalmology referral, thyroid screening on bloodspot, and FBC. With concurrent duodenal atresia requiring laparotomy and a murmur, urgent pre-operative echo is essential to characterise an AVSD or other lesion.
key_points: Up to 50% have CHD; AVSD is the commonest serious defect
Duodenal atresia in 5% of T21 newborns
TAM in 10%; usually self-resolves but 20% develop AML by age 5
Newborn workup: echo, karyotype, FBC, TSH, audiology, red reflex, hip US at 6 weeks
Lifelong: regular thyroid, coeliac, vision, hearing, OSA screening
explanation.pearls: Before anaesthesia in any T21 infant, you must know the cardiac anatomy and the C1-C2 stability for older children (atlanto-axial instability).

options.rationale: Transient abnormal myelopoiesis usually self-resolves and does not require LP at presentation; cardiac and surgical assessment take priority. Would be correct only with persistent blast cells and CNS signs (Source: RCH CPG: Down Syndrome).
Routine MRI brain is not part of newborn Down syndrome assessment. Would be correct only with focal neuro signs or seizures (Source: RCH CPG).
Hip US is performed at 6 weeks (or earlier with clinical signs); not a 24-hour priority over cardiac/surgical assessment. Would be correct at scheduled 6-week time-point (Source: RCH CPG).

Congenital hypothyroidism is screened on the newborn bloodspot at 48-72 hours; important but lower priority than urgent cardiac assessment with duodenal atresia. Would be correct as planned screen, not the highest priority now (Source: RCH CPG).

Up to 50% of T21 newborns have a structural cardiac defect, commonly AVSD. The infant requires urgent laparotomy for duodenal atresia; defining cardiac anatomy by echo is essential before anaesthesia to anticipate haemodynamic risks and plan management, per RCH CPG: Down syndrome and BMJ Best Practice.

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome (45,X and variants) classically presents at birth with lymphoedema and webbed neck (residual cystic hygroma) or later with short stature and primary ovarian failure. Congenital heart disease occurs in 25 to 45%, predominantly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation, with aortic dissection risk in adulthood. All confirmed or suspected Turner syndrome patients need echo at diagnosis, with periodic surveillance lifelong.
key_points: 30% of Turner neonates have CHD; BAV and coarctation predominate
Newborn signs: lymphoedema, webbed neck, weak femorals
Later: short stature, delayed puberty, primary ovarian failure
Renal anomalies (horseshoe kidney) in 30%
Lifelong cardiac surveillance for aortic dilatation
explanation.pearls: Any female newborn with unexplained pedal lymphoedema should have femoral pulses checked carefully and a karyotype sent.

options.rationale: Approximately 30% of Turner syndrome neonates have congenital heart disease, of which coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve are commonest. Weak femorals and an upper-to-lower limb BP gradient are clinical signs of coarctation that mandate urgent echo to assess for duct-dependent systemic circulation, per RCH CPG: Turner syndrome and BMJ Best Practice.
Lymphoedema is due to congenital lymphatic dysplasia and does not require renal artery imaging; cardiac assessment is the priority. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Turner Syndrome).
Atlanto-axial instability is associated with Down syndrome, not Turner; webbed neck reflects cystic hygroma resolution. Would be correct in Down syndrome with neck signs (Source: RCH CPG).
Widely spaced nipples are a dysmorphic feature without imaging indication in the newborn period. (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
Thyroid disease in Turner is monitored over time via TFTs, not via newborn US based on hairline. (Source: RCH CPG: Turner Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Noonan syndrome is an autosomal dominant RASopathy with variable expression. About 50% have pulmonary valve stenosis (often dysplastic and resistant to balloon valvuloplasty) and 20% have hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Short stature, characteristic facies (hypertelorism with downslanting fissures, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, webbed neck), pectus deformity, mild intellectual disability, cryptorchidism, and bleeding diathesis are typical. Half the cases are due to PTPN11 mutations.
key_points: PTPN11 in approximately 50%; other RAS-MAPK genes (SOS1, RAF1, KRAS) account for most others
Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis is the cardiac hallmark
HCM in 20%; can present as infant heart failure or sudden cardiac death
Growth hormone is approved for short stature
Echo and ECG at diagnosis and periodically
explanation.pearls: A boy with the Turner phenotype is the classic teaching cue for Noonan syndrome (formerly mis-called male Turner).

options.rationale: Williams has supravalvular aortic stenosis with elfin facies; this child has dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis with Noonan facies. Would be correct with elfin facies and supravalvular AS (Source: RCH CPG).
Turner affects phenotypic females with bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation; this patient is male with PS. Would be correct only in a phenotypic female (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis (50 percent of cases) with short stature, hypertelorism with downslanting fissures, webbed neck, pectus carinatum/excavatum and mild developmental delay is the Noonan phenotype. PTPN11 mutations are responsible for about half of cases, but several RASopathy genes can produce the phenotype, so a multi-gene panel (not single-gene PTPN11) is the appropriate first-line genetic test per RCH CPG.

Marfan features tall stature, arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis and aortic root dilatation; short stature with webbed neck and PS does not fit. Would be correct with tall stature and lens dislocation (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Marfan).
T21 features upslanting fissures, single palmar crease and AVSD; downslanting fissures and pulmonary valve dysplasia do not fit. Would be correct with classic T21 features (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: The revised (2010) Ghent nosology diagnoses Marfan syndrome via various combinations of aortic root dilatation, ectopia lentis, FBN1 mutation, family history, and systemic features (systemic score >= 7). This patient meets criteria multiple ways. Management centres on slowing aortic dilatation with beta-blocker or losartan, lifestyle modification, annual echo, ophthalmology review for lens and retinal pathology, and prophylactic root replacement at threshold diameter (commonly >= 5.0 cm, or >= 4.5 cm with adverse features).
key_points: Revised Ghent (2010): aortic root Z >= 2 plus ectopia lentis is sufficient
Beta-blocker (atenolol) or losartan slows root growth
Restrict competitive contact and isometric sport
Annual echo plus ophthalmology
Cascade FBN1 testing of first-degree relatives
explanation.pearls: An aortic root Z-score in childhood is more meaningful than absolute diameter because of body size variability.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement: thoracic aortic disease

options.rationale: Ghent criteria met (ectopia lentis plus aortic root Z-score over 2 with family history); reassurance and high-impact contact sport is unsafe. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Marfan).
Sotalol is not the agent of choice in Marfan; atenolol/propranolol or losartan slow root dilatation, and contact/competitive sport must be avoided. (Source: AHA scientific statement).
source_refs: AHA scientific statement: thoracic aortic disease

options.rationale: Elective root replacement is indicated at >= 5.0 cm in adults, or >= 4.5 cm with family history of dissection/rapid expansion; at 4.4 cm with Z 3.8 medical therapy and surveillance are appropriate. Would be correct at >= 5.0 cm or rapid expansion (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

Marfan syndrome with aortic root dilatation requires medical therapy to slow root growth (beta-blocker or losartan, with evidence supporting both), restriction from competitive contact and isometric sport, annual echo surveillance, ophthalmology review for ectopia lentis and retinal complications, and cascade screening of first-degree relatives with FBN1 testing, per BMJ Best Practice and revised Ghent nosology.
source_refs: AHA scientific statement: thoracic aortic disease

options.rationale: Losartan (ARB), not ramipril (ACEi), is shown to slow root dilatation; competitive isometric/strenuous sport is restricted. Would be correct only if ramipril and competitive swimming were guideline-endorsed (they are not) (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and a leading single-gene cause of autism. It results from CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion (> 200) in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 on Xq27.3, with methylation silencing the gene. Premutation carriers (55 to 200 repeats) can develop FXTAS (older men) or FXPOI (women under 40). Standard microarrays do not detect trinucleotide repeats; targeted FMR1 testing (PCR with methylation analysis or Southern blot) is required.
key_points: FMR1 full expansion > 200 CGG, methylated, silenced
Long face, prominent ears, macroorchidism after puberty, joint hypermobility, autistic features
Premutation 55 to 200: FXTAS in older males, FXPOI in younger females
Microarray does not detect repeat expansions
Cascade testing across maternal line is essential
explanation.pearls: A combination of a boy with intellectual disability, an older male relative with late-onset ataxia/tremor, and a female relative with early menopause is essentially diagnostic of FMR1 pathology until proven otherwise.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Fragile X syndrome

options.rationale: Klinefelter has tall stature, small testes (not macroorchidism) and milder cognitive impact; FXTAS/FXPOI family pattern is not explained. Would be correct with 47,XXY phenotype (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

Williams (7q11.23 deletion) would have shown on prior microarray; elfin facies/supravalvular AS/hypercalcaemia and macroorchidism are inconsistent. Would never be correct given the negative microarray (Source: RCH CPG).
Prader-Willi has neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity and small testes; macroorchidism does not fit. Would be correct with hypotonia and hypogonadism (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
TSC features hypopigmented macules, facial angiofibromas, cardiac rhabdomyomas and epilepsy; none present. Would be correct with seizures and skin findings (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

Moderate ID with autistic features, long face, prominent ears, joint hypermobility, macroorchidism (already enlarged prepubertally), a maternal uncle with FXTAS and a maternal grandmother with FXPOI fits Fragile X (FMR1 CGG expansion over 200 with methylation). Microarrays do not detect CGG trinucleotide expansions, which is why the prior microarray was normal; FMR1 targeted testing with methylation analysis is the correct next investigation, per RCH CPG: Fragile X.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Fragile X syndrome

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in toddlers is most commonly driven by excessive cow's milk intake (>500-600 mL/day), which displaces iron-rich solids and causes occult GI blood loss. Treatment is dietary modification plus oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day for 3 months total (1 month to correct Hb, then continue to refill stores).
key_points: Cow's milk cap 500 mL/day from 12 months
Oral iron 3-6 mg/kg/day elemental, once daily, with vitamin C source
Expect Hb rise of 10 g/L in 4 weeks
Treat for 3 months total to refill stores
Low ferritin + high RDW + microcytosis = iron deficiency until proven otherwise
explanation.pearls: Mild thrombocytosis is common in iron deficiency and is not lymphoproliferative; it resolves with iron repletion.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Iron deficiency
RACGP Red Book - Preventive activities in children

options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia from excess cow's milk: low ferritin, microcytic anaemia with high RDW and mild thrombocytosis. RCH CPG guidance: dietary modification (cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day) PLUS oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day, with a 4-week response check, continuing for 3 months after Hb normalises to replete stores.
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Iron deficiency

options.rationale: Haemodynamically stable and asymptomatic; transfusion reserved for symptomatic anaemia or Hb under 70 with CV compromise. Would be correct with symptomatic anaemia or Hb under 70 (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Iron deficiency

options.rationale: Ferritin unequivocally low and dietary history fits iron deficiency; haemoglobinopathy screening is only considered after iron therapy failure or by ethnic background. Would be correct after failed iron replacement (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Iron deficiency

options.rationale: IV iron in a toddler is reserved for malabsorption, oral intolerance or non-response to oral therapy. Would be correct only after oral trial failure (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion).
Multivitamin iron (5 mg) is inadequate (required 3-6 mg/kg/day, ~36-72 mg for this 12 kg child) and excessive milk perpetuates deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Iron deficiency

explanation.summary: Atopic dermatitis maintenance combines liberal emollients with site-matched topical corticosteroids (mild on face/genitals, moderate on body/limbs, potent only with specialist input on thickened plaques) and proactive twice-weekly application to flare-prone sites once skin is clear.
key_points: Emollient at least twice daily, including soap substitute
Face: hydrocortisone 1% (mild); flexures/body: methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% (moderate)
Apply once daily until clear, then twice weekly proactively
Wet wraps over TCS for severe flares (short course)
Food allergy testing only if reproducible food-triggered flare
explanation.pearls: Aqueous cream contains sodium lauryl sulfate and is no longer recommended as a leave-on emollient; it can drive flares.

options.rationale: Emollients alone do not control established eczema with lichenification; appropriate TCS use is safe and effective. Would be correct only for very mild dry skin without inflammation (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

Site-matched topical corticosteroid potency (mild for face, moderate such as methylprednisolone aceponate for trunk/flexures) plus generous emollient is standard. Once-daily TCS until clear and then twice-weekly proactive application reduces flares (RCH CPG Eczema; TG Dermatology).

Potent TCS should not be used on the face in young children; boom-bust without proactive maintenance leads to repeated flares. Would never be correct in this age group on face (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Systemic immunosuppression is reserved for severe refractory eczema after optimised topical therapy; she has not had adequate site-matched TCS plus emollient. Would be correct only after failed maximised topical regimen (Source: RCH CPG).

Routine oral antibiotics do not improve non-infected eczema and drive resistance; bleach baths may help colonisation but are not maintenance monotherapy. Would be correct only for documented infected eczema (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Eczema herpeticum is disseminated HSV in atopic skin, presenting with monomorphic 2-3 mm umbilicated vesicles, punched-out erosions, systemic features and an HSV contact. Periocular disease threatens the cornea and mandates IV aciclovir plus ophthalmology review.
key_points: Monomorphic umbilicated vesicles = HSV (eczema herpeticum)
Polymorphic pustules with honey-crust = S aureus impetiginised eczema
Periocular HSV = admit, IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h, ophthalmology
Withhold TCS on actively infected sites until controlled
Co-infection with S aureus is common; cover if features suggest
explanation.pearls: If the morphology is monomorphic, think herpetic. If you see punched-out erosions in an atopic child, treat as HSV until proven otherwise.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Eczema herpeticum

options.rationale: Potent TCS on face with concurrent HSV is harmful; bleach baths do not treat HSV. Would never be correct in suspected eczema herpeticum (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Eczema herpeticum

options.rationale: This is HSV not impetigo; mupirocin does not treat the virus, and continuing TCS over HSV can worsen dissemination. Would be correct in confirmed impetigo (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Honey-crusting and polymorphic pustules would suggest S aureus impetigo; monomorphic umbilicated vesicles and HSV contact indicate eczema herpeticum. Would be correct with classic impetigo features (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Eczema herpeticum

options.rationale: Monomorphic umbilicated vesicles, punched-out erosions, fever, an HSV contact and rapid progression in an atopic child are eczema herpeticum. Periorbital involvement risks HSV keratitis, mandating admission, IV aciclovir and ophthalmology review (RCH CPG Eczema herpeticum).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Eczema herpeticum

options.rationale: Periorbital involvement, fever and poor intake in a 3-year-old with eczema herpeticum warrant admission for IV therapy and ophthalmology. Would be correct only for mild non-facial eczema herpeticum with good intake (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Eczema herpeticum

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 95% of paediatric constipation and is diagnosed clinically using the Rome IV criteria (two or more of: 2 or fewer defecations per week, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard bowel movements, faecal mass in the rectum, large stools). Red flags that mandate organic workup include onset under one month of age, delayed meconium passage over 48 hours, ribbon stools, explosive release on rectal exam, faltering growth, bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, abnormal sacrum (dimple, hair tuft, asymmetric gluteal cleft), lower-limb neurology, and severe anal pathology. The leading organic diagnoses are Hirschsprung disease, anorectal malformation, cystic fibrosis (meconium ileus), spinal dysraphism, hypothyroidism and cow's milk protein allergy. Hirschsprung is diagnosed by suction rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells and increased acetylcholinesterase-staining nerve fibres; contrast enema shows a transition zone.
key_points: Delayed meconium >48 hours = think Hirschsprung
Explosive release on PR is a classic clue
Suction rectal biopsy is the diagnostic test
Total colonic Hirschsprung can be associated with Down syndrome
Bilious vomiting in an infant is surgical until proven otherwise
explanation.pearls: Delayed meconium passage beyond 48 hours, ribbon stools, explosive release on rectal exam, and faltering growth are red flags for Hirschsprung disease - suction rectal biopsy is diagnostic, contrast enema supports surgical planning (RCH CPG Constipation).

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Bilious vomiting

options.rationale: Delayed meconium over 48 hours, faltering growth, bilious vomiting and explosive PR are red flags for organic cause; discharge without further investigation is unsafe. Would be correct only without red flags (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).
Anal stenosis has a narrow caudal anus on exam; here the anus is normally sited and obstruction is functional from aganglionic segment. Would be correct with anal stenosis on exam (Source: RCH CPG).
CMPA causes loose stools, blood streaks or eczema, not delayed meconium and obstruction. Would be correct with blood-streaked stools and atopy (Source: RCH CPG).

Delayed meconium >48 hours, abdominal distension, faltering growth, ribbon stool with explosive release on PR and bilious vomiting are classic for Hirschsprung disease. Suction rectal biopsy demonstrating aganglionosis is the diagnostic gold standard (RCH CPG; RACS).
Congenital hypothyroidism is detected on newborn heelprick and causes prolonged jaundice/lethargy, not delayed meconium with explosive PR. Would be correct with positive Guthrie (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Faltering growth is defined by sustained drop across centiles (typically >=2 major centiles on the weight chart). The three buckets are: inadequate intake (commonest), malabsorption, and increased metabolic demand. Always observe a feed and take a 24-hour recall before broad investigation.
key_points: Plot weight, length and head circumference; check for centile crossing
Head sparing in early malnutrition (weight drops, length next, HC last)
Inadequate intake is the commonest cause
Targeted investigations only after history/examination flag a cause
Multidisciplinary management (dietitian, MCHN, paediatrician) for sustained faltering
explanation.pearls: A single low weight is not faltering growth; you need the trajectory. Always plot the chart yourself.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Faltering growth
RACGP Red Book - Preventive activities in children

options.rationale: Pharmacological appetite stimulation is not first-line in young children; address feeding behaviour, energy density and mealtime environment first. Would be correct only as specialist add-on after multidisciplinary first-line (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Faltering growth

options.rationale: Hospital admission is for severe malnutrition, safeguarding concerns or failed community management. Would be correct with severe undernutrition or social concerns (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Faltering growth

options.rationale: Investigations are history/exam-guided; only 1-2 percent of faltering growth is non-nutritional organic. Broad untargeted screen is low-yield. Would be correct only with specific red-flag features (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Faltering growth

options.rationale: Safeguarding is considered if history is inconsistent or other concerns exist; feeding history and dietary advice come first. Would be correct only with specific safeguarding red flags (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Faltering growth

options.rationale: Faltering growth is most commonly due to inadequate intake. The first step is a detailed feeding and dietary history with a feed observation, before targeted investigations are considered. Anthropometry should plot weight, length and head circumference and check for centile crossing (RCH CPG Faltering growth).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Faltering growth
RACGP Red Book - Preventive activities in children

explanation.summary: ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptom counts present for >=6 months, in >=2 settings, causing functional impairment, with onset before age 12. First-line pharmacotherapy is a stimulant (methylphenidate or dexamfetamine) under paediatrician supervision and state authority/TGA authorisation, alongside behavioural and educational supports.
key_points: DSM-5: >=6 inattentive and/or >=6 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (<17 yo)
Two settings, >=6 months, onset <12 years, functional impairment
Pre-stimulant: cardiac history, family SCD history, exam, ECG
Monitor height, weight, BP, HR, mood, sleep, appetite
Stimulants are S8 in Australia and require state authority
explanation.pearls: School-only symptoms suggest a learning disorder or environment problem; home-only symptoms suggest parenting or attachment. ADHD is across settings.

sources.label: AADPA Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline 2022

options.rationale: Restrictive diets are not recommended as primary; behavioural/environmental supports plus stimulants are first-line. Would be correct only with documented food trigger and dietitian oversight (Source: RACGP; Therapeutic Guidelines).

Stimulants are first-line in children without contraindications; atomoxetine is for stimulant intolerance, tics, anxiety or diversion risk. Would be correct with those specific indications (Source: AADPA ADHD).
source_refs: AADPA Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline 2022

options.rationale: He meets DSM-5 ADHD criteria (>=6 months, two settings, functional impairment). Methylphenidate is first-line; in Australia, stimulants require state authority/TGA pathway via a paediatrician. Behavioural interventions run in parallel and monitoring includes growth, BP, HR and mental state (AADPA 2022; RACGP).
source_refs: AADPA Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline 2022

options.rationale: Over 6 months of symptoms with functional impairment in 2 settings warrants treatment; behavioural strategies are necessary but not sufficient. Would be correct only with mild symptoms in one setting (Source: AADPA 2022).
source_refs: AADPA Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline 2022

options.rationale: Routine cardiology review is not required with unremarkable history/exam/ECG; only red flags (family sudden death, exertional syncope, abnormal ECG) mandate review. Would be correct only with red flags (Source: AADPA).
source_refs: AADPA Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline 2022

explanation.summary: ASD diagnostic criteria require persistent deficits in social communication AND restricted/repetitive behaviours, present from early development, causing functional impairment. M-CHAT-R/F is the validated 18-24 month screen. NDIS Early Childhood provides early intervention before formal diagnosis if developmental delay is documented.
key_points: Red flags at 18 mo: no response to name, no joint attention, no pointing to share, language regression
M-CHAT-R/F: low risk 0-2, medium 3-7 (do follow-up), high >=8 (refer)
Always check hearing in any speech delay
Multidisciplinary assessment: paediatrician + speech path + psychology
NDIS Early Childhood is available from before diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Joint attention (sharing interest with another person via gaze or pointing) is the single most predictive early autism feature.

sources.label: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders 2018

options.rationale: Multiple core ASD features plus M-CHAT-R/F at high-risk threshold; reassurance delays access to early intervention. Would be correct only with isolated mild language delay and normal social communication (Source: Autism CRC National Guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders 2018

options.rationale: M-CHAT-R/F >=8 with concerning features warrants referral for a multidisciplinary autism assessment, formal audiology to exclude hearing loss as a contributor, and early access to NDIS Early Childhood early intervention (available before formal diagnosis if developmental delay is documented) (Autism CRC National Guideline; NDIS Early Childhood).
source_refs: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders 2018

options.rationale: Genetic testing (CMA, Fragile X) is arranged by the paediatrician alongside multidisciplinary assessment, not as a standalone first step. Would be correct as part of paediatrician-led workup (Source: Autism CRC).
source_refs: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders 2018

options.rationale: ASD pharmacotherapy is reserved for specific severe behavioural symptoms after specialist assessment; not first-line at age 18 months. Would be correct only after specialist review for severe behaviour (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders 2018

options.rationale: Speech pathology alone misses multidimensional ASD; multidisciplinary assessment with audiology and NDIS early intervention is needed. Would be correct only as adjunct, not sole referral (Source: Autism CRC).
source_refs: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders 2018

explanation.summary: Adolescent depression with self-harm requires a HEEADSSS-based assessment, structured suicide risk assessment, a written safety plan, family involvement with consent, and tiered referral (GP -> headspace -> CAMHS). Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescents with moderate-severe depression, started low with early review for activation.
key_points: HEEADSSS: Home, Education/Employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/self-harm, Safety
Safety plan: warning signs, coping, distractions, social supports, professional contacts, means restriction
Fluoxetine is the SSRI with the best evidence in adolescent depression
Black-box: monitor closely for activation/suicidality first 4 weeks of SSRI
headspace is the national youth mental health service (12-25 yo)
explanation.pearls: Means restriction (lock medicines, remove blades) is the single highest-impact element of a safety plan.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood disorders

options.rationale: Confidentiality has limits with risk of harm; involving a supportive parent with consent improves outcomes. Would be correct only if there were no immediate safety concern (Source: RACGP Adolescent Confidentiality).
Psychological therapy is first-line for mild-moderate adolescent depression; fluoxetine starts at 10 mg with close monitoring alongside therapy. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood disorders

options.rationale: Involuntary admission is for acute risk with intent/plan or inability to maintain safety. Passive ideation without plan, with family support, and willingness to engage warrants community management. Would be correct only with imminent risk and refusal to engage (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood disorders

options.rationale: Adolescent depression with self-harm and passive suicidal ideation requires a documented safety plan with means restriction, family involvement (with consent where possible), early review, and specialist mental health referral. headspace and CAMHS provide tiered care. Pharmacotherapy is considered when psychological therapy is insufficient or symptoms are moderate-severe and persistent (RANZCP; headspace).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood disorders

options.rationale: Self-harm with persistent low mood and passive suicidal ideation is a mental illness marker and elevated future suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP; headspace).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood disorders

explanation.summary: MARSIPAN-AU high-risk indicators for anorexia nervosa admission include BMI <14 (or <13 in adolescents), HR <45, postural BP fall >20/10 with HR rise >30, T <35.5 degC, QTc >450 ms, hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypoglycaemia and acute medical instability. Refeeding starts low (5-10 kcal/kg/day) with daily electrolytes, prophylactic phosphate and thiamine, cardiac monitoring.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome: low PO4, K, Mg; fluid shifts; arrhythmia; Wernicke
Start refeeding cautiously - 'start low, go slow' especially in severe AN
Prophylactic thiamine 100 mg before any glucose-containing fluids
Family-Based Treatment (FBT/Maudsley) is first-line psychotherapy for adolescent AN
Monitor QTc daily during refeeding
explanation.pearls: The first 72 hours of refeeding kill people, not the starvation. Phosphate is the canary.

sources.label: MARSIPAN-AU - Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline - Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Multiple MARSIPAN-AU high-risk criteria mandate inpatient admission. Would be correct only with low-risk vitals and electrolytes (Source: RANZCP; ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline - Eating Disorders
MARSIPAN-AU - Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive in eating disorders, not a substitute for medical stabilisation and family-based treatment. Would be correct as adjunct after stabilisation (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline - Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Aggressive refeeding precipitates refeeding syndrome (fluid overload, hypophosphataemia, arrhythmia, Wernicke encephalopathy). Would never be correct in high-risk patient (Source: MARSIPAN-AU).
source_refs: MARSIPAN-AU - Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa

options.rationale: She is medically unstable; medical stabilisation precedes or runs alongside psychiatric admission. (Source: MARSIPAN-AU; RANZCP).
source_refs: MARSIPAN-AU - Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline - Eating Disorders

options.rationale: She has severe anorexia nervosa with refeeding syndrome risk (low PO4, low Mg, low K, low glucose). MARSIPAN-AU mandates medical admission with cautious refeeding, electrolyte and glucose monitoring, prophylactic phosphate and thiamine, cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia, and FBT engagement (MARSIPAN-AU; RANZCP).
source_refs: MARSIPAN-AU - Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline - Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: After recurrent febrile UTI in a young child, the RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral. The NICE NG224 algorithm includes DMSA at 4 to 6 months; the RCH CPG has not adopted DMSA in its routine cascade. MCUG is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound. Constipation contributes substantially to recurrence and must be optimised.
key_points: RCH Melbourne recurrent UTI: non-urgent renal tract ultrasound plus paediatric referral
DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE construct, not part of the RCH cascade
MCUG reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound
Optimise constipation - reduces UTI recurrence
Prophylaxis individualised: high-grade VUR, severe scarring, breakthrough UTI
explanation.pearls: If you can fix the constipation you fix the UTI in many of these children.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral for recurrent febrile UTI in a young child; DMSA is part of the NICE NG224 algorithm and is not included in the RCH cascade. Optimising constipation is essential because it contributes substantially to recurrence. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: MCUG is invasive (catheter, ionising radiation) and is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; it is not first-line in the RCH recurrent-UTI pathway. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Prophylaxis is considered after risk stratification (proven high-grade VUR or significant scarring); empirical prophylaxis without imaging is not first-line in the RCH pathway. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; DMSA is not part of the RCH recurrent-UTI imaging cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Deferred imaging is inadequate after recurrent febrile UTI; the RCH pathway calls for a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound now and specialist referral, not a 12-month deferral. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: Live vaccines are contraindicated IN the immunocompromised person but in general are SAFE for their household contacts (MMR not transmitted; varicella vaccine virus transmission rare and only via vesicular rash). Rotavirus is the practical exception due to faecal shedding - hand hygiene needed for 4-6 weeks. Influenza inactivated is encouraged for household contacts annually.
key_points: Live vaccines contraindicated IN immunocompromised individuals
Household contacts SHOULD be immunised, including MMR and varicella
Manage post-varicella rash with covering/isolation
Rotavirus faecal shedding - hand hygiene precaution for 4-6 weeks
Influenza (inactivated) annually for all household contacts
explanation.pearls: Cocooning protects the immunocompromised; under-immunising the household is the opposite of safe.

options.rationale: Deferring all vaccines leaves the immunocompromised mother more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease in the home; child should be fully immunised, including most live vaccines. Would never be correct as blanket policy (Source: NCIRS).

MMR and varicella vaccine viruses are not transmitted from immunocompetent vaccinees in routine contact (varicella vaccine virus transmission is rare and only from vesicular rash). Immunising household contacts of immunocompromised people is recommended. Rotavirus is the exception (faecal shedding) and would need hand hygiene precautions; he is too old for rotavirus anyway (NCIRS).
No inactivated MMR alternative exists on NIP; MMR vaccine viruses are not transmitted from vaccinees to contacts. (Source: NCIRS).
Oral typhoid is not routinely indicated and not part of NIP catch-up; introduces a live oral vaccine inappropriately. (Source: NCIRS).
MMR and varicella are NOT contraindicated in household contacts of immunocompromised people; he remains at risk if unprotected. (Source: NCIRS; eviQ).

explanation.summary: Vaccine hesitancy is best addressed with a presumptive opening, motivational interviewing, exploration of specific concerns, tailored factual rebuttal, an explicit clinician recommendation, and signposting to evidence-based resources (NCIRS SKAI). Maintain the therapeutic relationship; many hesitant parents accept vaccines over time with continuity.
key_points: Presumptive opening: 'Today we'll do the 6-month vaccines.'
Motivational interviewing: explore, affirm, reflect, summarise
Address specific concerns with specific evidence
Make an explicit recommendation - 'I recommend...'
SKAI website is the Australian go-to resource
explanation.pearls: Don't try to win the argument in one visit; you are building a relationship that often takes 2-3 conversations to land.

options.rationale: Withholding general care is unethical and not supported by RACGP/NCIRS; trusted continuity is a key driver of eventual acceptance. (Source: RACGP; NCIRS SKAI).

NCIRS SKAI and RACGP recommend MI-style engagement: presumptive language, exploration of concerns, tailored factual rebuttal of specific myths, a clear clinician recommendation and signposting to reputable resources, with a planned follow-up. Adversarial debate and alternative schedules are less effective.
Vaccine hesitancy in an otherwise well-cared-for child is not itself medical neglect. Would be correct only with broader documented neglect (Source: NCIRS).
Alternative schedules prolong susceptibility, increase visits/pain, and reinforce immune-overload misconception. (Source: NCIRS SKAI).

Court orders are a last resort after parental deadlock and other approaches have failed; initial step is shared GP-led discussion. Would be correct only after exhausted negotiation and ongoing risk to child (Source: NCIRS).

explanation.summary: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets is treated with colecalciferol (1000-2000 IU/day for toddlers; 600 IU/day prevention) for 3 months, with calcium intake optimisation and sun exposure counselling. Always screen the breastfeeding mother. The 25-OH vitamin D threshold for deficiency is <50 nmol/L (severe <30 nmol/L).
key_points: 25-OH vitamin D: <30 severe deficient, <50 deficient, 50-75 insufficient
Raised ALP and PTH are early biochemical markers
X-ray: cupping and fraying of metaphyses (wrist, knees, ankles)
Treat with colecalciferol (daily) - not calcitriol - for nutritional rickets
Screen the mother; vitamin D-deficient mothers explain vitamin D-deficient infants
explanation.pearls: If ALP is 'unbelievably high' in a toddler, think rickets before liver. ALP is the most sensitive biochemical sign.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency
APEG/ASBMR Australian and New Zealand consensus on vitamin D

options.rationale: Bisphosphonates have no role in nutritional rickets and may impair mineralisation; deformity usually corrects with vitamin D and calcium repletion. Would never be correct in nutritional rickets (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.rationale: Stoss therapy carries hypercalcaemia risk in young children and limits follow-up biochemistry; daily replacement is safer and standard in Australia. Would be correct only in selected older children with adherence concerns under specialist input (Source: APEG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.rationale: IV calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, ECG changes); he is asymptomatic. Would be correct with tetany, seizures or ECG changes (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.rationale: Calcitriol is reserved for vitamin D-dependent rickets, CKD and hypoparathyroidism; nutritional deficiency uses colecalciferol because 1-alpha-hydroxylation is intact. Would be correct in CKD or VDDR (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency

options.rationale: Confirmed nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets (low 25-OH vitamin D <50 nmol/L, raised ALP and PTH, radiographic changes) is treated with colecalciferol 1000-2000 IU daily for 3 months in a toddler, plus 500 mg/day elemental calcium, with sun exposure counselling. Screen the breastfeeding mother because deficient mothers explain the infant's deficiency (RCH CPG Vitamin D; APEG/ASBMR consensus).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline - Vitamin D deficiency
APEG/ASBMR Australian and New Zealand consensus on vitamin D

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis is failure to respond to two or more IM adrenaline doses. Management is an IV adrenaline infusion in a monitored area (PICU/ED resus) alongside ongoing fluid resuscitation, oxygen, and airway preparation. Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts, not next steps. Glucagon is reserved for beta-blocked patients.
key_points: Refractory anaphylaxis = persistent hypotension or airway compromise after >=2 IM adrenaline doses
Start IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microg/kg/min and titrate
Continuous cardiac monitoring is mandatory
Fluid resuscitation 20 mL/kg crystalloid boluses repeated as needed
Tryptase taken acutely and at 1-2 hours and at 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Stridor in anaphylaxis is laryngeal oedema, not bronchospasm; nebulised adrenaline buys time but does not replace IV adrenaline.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Steroids and antihistamines do not treat airway/CV collapse and have no role as the next escalation after adrenaline failure. Would be correct only as adjunct after definitive adrenaline (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: After two or more IM doses without response, refractory anaphylaxis is declared; IV infusion is preferred for sustained titratable effect. Would be correct only if IV access were unavailable (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Refractory anaphylaxis (persistent hypotension or airway compromise after at least two IM doses) is treated with a titrated IV adrenaline infusion starting at 0.1 microg/kg/min in a monitored area, with PICU involvement, as per ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines and RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis.
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Glucagon is for refractory anaphylaxis in beta-blocked patients; this child is not on beta-blockers. Would be correct only with documented beta-blocker use (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Hydroxocobalamin is the cyanide-toxicity antidote (smoke inhalation), no role in anaphylaxis. Would be correct only with smoke inhalation and suspected cyanide toxicity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus algorithm: oxygen, glucose check, two doses of benzodiazepine 5 minutes apart, then second-line antiepileptic at ~25 minutes. Following EcLiPSE/ConSEPT/ESETT, levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg IV is the preferred second-line agent in children outside the neonatal period. If still seizing, proceed to RSI with thiopentone or midazolam infusion.
key_points: Two doses of benzodiazepine max before moving on
Levetiracetam preferred over phenytoin in young children
Phenobarbital is for neonates as second-line
Refractory status -> thiopentone RSI and PICU
Always check glucose, sodium, and consider non-convulsive causes
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine 100 mg IV should be considered in infants under 18 months with refractory seizures of unclear cause.

options.rationale: Phenytoin is acceptable but EcLiPSE and ConSEPT trials and updated APLS prefer levetiracetam, especially under 2 years where phenytoin extravasation risk is higher. Would be correct in older children with appropriate venous access (Source: APLS Australia Status Epilepticus).
Phenobarbital is the preferred second-line agent only in neonates; outside the neonatal period it is third-line. Would be correct in a neonate (Source: APLS Australia).
More than two benzodiazepine doses increases respiratory depression without improving termination; algorithm advances to second-line antiepileptic. (Source: APLS Australia).

After two benzodiazepine doses, the current APLS Australia and RCH algorithm recommends IV levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg as the preferred second-line agent in infants and children, supported by EcLiPSE/ConSEPT/ESETT data, as per APLS Australia Status Epilepticus Algorithm and RCH CPG: Status epilepticus.
Thiopentone induction is for refractory status after second-line agents have failed; jumping straight to RSI skips the algorithm. Would be correct only in refractory status (Source: APLS Australia).

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric asthma is identified by tachypnoea, accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation under 92%, inability to complete sentences, agitation or drowsiness, and a silent chest (impending arrest). Stepwise Australian management is oxygen to maintain SpO2 over 94%, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 micrograms every 20 minutes for the first hour, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg or IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg), then IV magnesium sulfate 25-50 mg/kg over 20 minutes if no improvement. Further escalation is IV salbutamol bolus then infusion, then IV aminophylline (rarely used now), with PICU transfer alongside. Intubation is the last resort: hypoxia and hypercapnia rise quickly post-intubation due to high airway pressures, so ketamine is the induction agent of choice for its bronchodilator effect. Permissive hypercapnia and lung-protective ventilation are the rule.
key_points: IV magnesium dose: 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 min
Silent chest indicates life-threatening asthma
Watch for hypokalaemia and lactic acidosis from salbutamol
Aminophylline is last-line because of arrhythmia risk
Involve PICU early when failing nebs + steroid
explanation.pearls: IV magnesium sulfate 25-50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes is the standard third-line agent in severe paediatric asthma not responding to back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium plus oral corticosteroid - works on bronchial smooth muscle Ca2+ channels (RCH CPG Asthma).

options.rationale: Already failed three back-to-back nebulised doses plus systemic steroid; persisting risks decompensation. Would be correct only at an earlier step before escalation (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma).

Severe acute asthma failing oxygen, back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium and systemic steroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate before IV salbutamol or aminophylline, as per RCH CPG: Asthma acute and Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory.
Aminophylline is reserved for failure of IV magnesium and IV salbutamol due to narrow therapeutic index and arrhythmia risk. Would be correct as third-line in PICU (Source: RCH CPG).
IV salbutamol typically follows IV magnesium; potassium 3.0 and lactate 3.8 will worsen with more beta-agonist. Would be correct after IV magnesium failure (Source: RCH CPG).

Intubation in severe asthma risks bronchospasm, hypotension and barotrauma; reserved for impending arrest after maximal medical therapy. Would be correct only after maximal therapy and impending arrest (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Paediatric septic shock that is fluid-refractory after 40-60 mL/kg of crystalloid requires early inotrope. Cold shock (low cardiac output, narrow pulse pressure, prolonged capillary refill) is treated with adrenaline; warm shock (vasodilated, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses) is treated with noradrenaline. Peripheral or intraosseous infusion is appropriate while central access is being arranged.
key_points: Cold shock -> adrenaline; warm shock -> noradrenaline
Do not delay inotrope for central line if peripherally feasible
Stop fluid boluses once signs of fluid overload appear
Stress-dose hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock
Source control and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
explanation.pearls: Varicella plus septic shock equals invasive group A strep until proven otherwise; clindamycin is added to suppress toxin production.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Cold septic shock in children (low cardiac output, high systemic vascular resistance) is treated with adrenaline as the first-line inotrope; when only peripheral access is available, dilute peripheral adrenaline is recommended over delay for central access, as per ANZICS Paediatric Septic Shock Guideline and Surviving Sepsis Campaign Paediatric Guidelines.
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12 Paediatric Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Noradrenaline is first-line in warm shock (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure); this child has cold shock with vasoconstriction. Would be correct in warm shock (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric).

After 40-60 mL/kg in septic shock without response, further crystalloid risks pulmonary oedema; inotropes should be started. Would be correct only before reaching 40-60 mL/kg threshold (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric; FEAST trial).

Stress-dose hydrocortisone is for catecholamine-resistant shock or suspected adrenal insufficiency; not the next step before any inotrope. Would be correct after inotrope started and shock persists (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric).
Delaying inotrope for central access in fluid-refractory shock increases mortality; dilute peripheral or IO is recommended. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Paediatric).

explanation.summary: DKA-related cerebral oedema presents 4-12 hours into treatment with headache, vomiting, falling GCS, bradycardia and hypertension. Immediate management is hyperosmolar therapy (3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), reduction of fluid rate by one-third, head-up positioning, and urgent imaging only once stabilised. Avoid aggressive hyperventilation.
key_points: Risk factors: new diagnosis, age <5, severe acidosis, high urea, low pCO2, bicarbonate use, rapid fluid
Treat clinically; do not wait for imaging
3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce IV fluid rate; keep glucose falling no faster than ~5 mmol/L/h
Avoid pCO2 below 30 mmHg
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium should rise as glucose falls; a falling corrected sodium is an early warning sign of cerebral oedema.

options.rationale: Adding dextrose/reducing insulin is appropriate when glucose falls below ~14-17 mmol/L but does not address suspected cerebral oedema with bradycardia, hypertension and falling GCS. Would be correct at later glucose phase without cerebral oedema (Source: ISPAD DKA).
Increasing fluid worsens cerebral oedema; PECARN FLUID supports cautious rehydration with hyperosmolar therapy when oedema suspected. Would never be correct in suspected oedema (Source: ISPAD DKA).

Bradycardia, hypertension, falling GCS, headache and vomiting are the Cushing-like triad of DKA-related cerebral oedema; immediate hyperosmolar therapy with 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg (or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg) plus fluid rate reduction and head CT once stable are first-line, as per ISPAD DKA Guidelines and RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis.
Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic oedema (tumour, meningitis) but has no role in DKA-related cytotoxic/osmotic oedema. Would never be correct in DKA cerebral oedema (Source: ISPAD DKA).

Prophylactic hyperventilation below pCO2 30 in DKA cerebral oedema worsens outcomes; intubation may follow but is not the first step before hyperosmolar therapy. Would be correct only after hyperosmolar therapy and clinical deterioration (Source: ISPAD DKA).

explanation.summary: Paediatric SVT with shock = immediate synchronised cardioversion at 1 J/kg, escalating to 2 J/kg. Stable SVT = vagal manoeuvres then adenosine 0.1 mg/kg, then 0.2 mg/kg. Avoid verapamil in young children and avoid unsynchronised shocks on perfusing rhythms.
key_points: Unstable = shock, altered mental state, hypotension; cardiovert immediately
1 J/kg synchronised, then 2 J/kg if unsuccessful
Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg then 0.2 mg/kg in stable SVT
Verapamil contraindicated under 1 year and in shock
Amiodarone is second-line for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: If rate is over 220 bpm in an infant or over 180 bpm in a child with abrupt onset and no P waves, think SVT, not sinus tachycardia.

options.rationale: Adenosine is for stable SVT; this is haemodynamically unstable SVT requiring immediate synchronised cardioversion. Would be correct in stable SVT (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

Unstable SVT in a child with shock requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 J/kg (then 2 J/kg if unsuccessful), with sedation only if it does not delay shock delivery, as per ANZCOR Guideline 12.7 and AHA PALS.
Unsynchronised defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; delivering on a perfusing rhythm risks VF induction. Would be correct only in pulseless VT/VF (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

Amiodarone is for refractory/recurrent SVT in stable patients or post-cardioversion; not before electrical therapy in unstable SVT. Would be correct as adjunct after cardioversion (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).
Verapamil is contraindicated under 1 year and unsafe with poor cardiac output (profound hypotension/arrest). Would never be correct in this patient (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).

explanation.summary: Severe croup unresponsive to nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone with signs of impending respiratory failure (hypoxia, exhaustion, decreasing air entry, paradoxical breathing) requires definitive airway in theatre. Inhalational induction with preserved spontaneous ventilation is preferred over paralysis-based RSI. ENT must be on standby for a potential surgical airway, and a smaller-than-predicted ETT should be selected.
key_points: Repeat nebulised adrenaline every 20-30 minutes as needed as a bridge
Definitive airway in theatre when impending failure
Inhalational induction; avoid paralysis
Use ETT one size smaller than predicted
ENT for emergency surgical airway
explanation.pearls: Quiet stridor with exhaustion is more ominous than loud stridor with vigorous breathing.

options.rationale: Impending respiratory failure (hypoxia, exhaustion, paradoxical breathing); passive waiting is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

Repeat adrenaline is reasonable as a bridge but does not substitute for definitive airway when impending failure is present. Would be correct only as bridge alongside airway team activation (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).
HFNC does not bypass critical subglottic narrowing and must not delay airway team. Would be correct only in milder distress without impending failure (Source: RCH CPG).

Severe croup unresponsive to initial adrenaline plus steroid with signs of impending respiratory failure requires definitive airway management in theatre under inhalational induction (preserving spontaneous ventilation), with ENT standby for surgical airway and a smaller-than-predicted ETT. Repeat adrenaline acts as a bridge during transfer.

RSI with paralysis risks losing the airway when bag-mask ventilation may be difficult; inhalational induction preserving spontaneous ventilation in theatre is standard. Would be correct only in catastrophic airway loss when inhalational induction impossible (Source: ANZCA airway guidance).

explanation.summary: Staggered paracetamol overdose (more than one ingestion within a 24-hour window) renders the Rumack-Matthew nomogram invalid. If the total dose exceeds 200 mg/kg or 10 g, give full-course IV N-acetylcysteine regardless of the level. Charcoal is only useful within 1-2 hours of ingestion. Normal ALT and INR at presentation do not exclude developing toxicity.
key_points: Nomogram applies only to single ingestions with known time
Staggered ingestion >200 mg/kg or >10 g -> immediate NAC
NAC regimen: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h
Repeat paracetamol, ALT, INR at 8 h to decide on extension of NAC
Charcoal only if presentation within 1-2 h of ingestion
explanation.pearls: Massive ingestion (>30 g or paracetamol >1000 micromol/L at 4 h) may need double-dose NAC and dialysis consideration.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand consensus statement: paracetamol poisoning

options.rationale: Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies only to single acute ingestions with known time; in staggered or unknown timing it cannot be used. Would be correct only for single acute ingestion with known time and level under treatment line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
