ALT and INR rise late (24-36 h); waiting in a staggered overdose over 200 mg/kg risks missing the treatment window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Staggered paracetamol ingestion >200 mg/kg (or >10 g in adults) over <24 hours mandates immediate full-course IV N-acetylcysteine regardless of the nomogram level; the nomogram does not apply, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness, RCH CPG: Paracetamol poisoning, and the Australian/New Zealand consensus statement on paracetamol overdose.
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus statement: paracetamol poisoning

options.rationale: Activated charcoal is useful within 1-2 h of ingestion; here ingestions are 18 h and 4 h old, minimal benefit, and NAC must not be delayed. Would be correct within 1-2 h of single ingestion (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Oral methionine is not used in current Australian practice; IV NAC is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Paediatric haemorrhagic shock not responding to a 10-20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, with positive FAST or known source of bleeding, requires MTP activation, balanced product resuscitation (PRBC:FFP:platelets ~1:1:1, initial PRBC 10 mL/kg), and empirical TXA within 3 hours of injury. Avoid further crystalloid where blood is available.
key_points: MTP activation: shock unresponsive to 10-20 mL/kg crystalloid or known major haemorrhage
TXA 15 mg/kg (max 1 g) over 10 min, then 2 mg/kg/h for 8 h
Aim ionised calcium >1.1 mmol/L; give calcium with each unit
Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy = lethal triad
Surgical or radiological source control as soon as possible
explanation.pearls: Children compensate longer then decompensate suddenly; do not be falsely reassured by a normal blood pressure early.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Paediatric trauma with shock, positive FAST and lactic acidosis after 10 mL/kg crystalloid meets MTP activation criteria; TXA is indicated when given within 3 hours of injury at 15 mg/kg (max 1 g) followed by an infusion, and initial PRBC bolus is 10 mL/kg, as per CRASH-3/CRASH-2 paediatric data and RCH CPG: Trauma resuscitation.
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Large-volume crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy and acidosis in haemorrhagic shock; blood products are the next resuscitation fluid. (Source: RCH CPG: Trauma).

TXA should be given empirically within 3 h of injury with significant bleeding; waiting for viscoelastic testing delays a time-critical intervention. Would be correct only outside the 3-h window (Source: ANZ Paediatric MTP).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: TXA is not contraindicated in paediatric trauma; recommended within 3 h. Cryoprecipitate is used for fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L but is not the first product in MTP. (Source: ANZ Paediatric MTP).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Trauma Society Paediatric Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Vasopressors as primary treatment of haemorrhagic shock mask ongoing bleeding and worsen tissue perfusion; volume with blood products is the priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Trauma).

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries in pre-mobile infants (TEN-4 FACESp: Torso, Ear, Neck bruising; Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Sclera, plus any patterned injury; under 4 months any bruising) require admission, mandatory child protection notification, skeletal survey, fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages, and CT head to assess for occult abusive head trauma.
key_points: Bruising/frenulum injury in a pre-mobile infant is NAI until proven otherwise
Mandatory reporting is statutory in all Australian states/territories
Skeletal survey + fundoscopy + CT head are minimum imaging
Coagulation screen to exclude bleeding diathesis is adjunctive
Involve paediatric child protection team and social work
explanation.pearls: Those who don't cruise don't bruise: any bruise in a non-mobile infant warrants child protection assessment.

sources.label: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

options.rationale: Frenulum tear in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury for NAI; never warrants outpatient reassurance. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).
source_refs: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

options.rationale: Coagulation studies are part of workup but a normal screen does not exclude inflicted injury; discharge without protective action is unsafe. Would never be sufficient (Source: RCH CPG).
Mandatory reporting is required at the time of clinical suspicion, not deferred. (Source: RCH CPG; state child protection legislation).
source_refs: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

options.rationale: Discharging a pre-mobile infant with sentinel injury without statutory notification does not meet duty of care. (Source: RCH CPG).

A frenulum tear or bruise in a pre-mobile infant (TEN-4 FACESp rule) is a high-risk sentinel injury for inflicted injury; the standard response is admission, mandatory notification, skeletal survey (NAI series), fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages, and CT head, with paediatric protection team involvement, as per RCH CPG: Child abuse and the RACGP child protection resource.
source_refs: RACGP: Identifying and responding to child abuse and neglect

explanation.summary: Acute upper airway obstruction in a child requires rapid differentiation between croup, epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, and retropharyngeal abscess. Epiglottitis features rapid onset, high fever, drooling, muffled voice, tripoding, no barking cough. In an unimmunised child Hib is the leading pathogen.
key_points: Epiglottitis: 4 Ds (drooling, dysphagia, distress, dysphonia), tripoding, no cough
Croup: preceding URTI, barking cough, hoarseness, stridor
Bacterial tracheitis: croup-like prodrome then toxic decline
Foreign body: sudden choking event, unilateral signs
Retropharyngeal abscess: neck stiffness, dysphagia, preceding URTI or dental
explanation.pearls: Keep the child calm on the parent's lap, do not examine the throat, call anaesthetics and ENT, and plan inhalational induction in theatre.

options.rationale: Rapid onset of fever, drooling, muffled voice and tripoding without barking cough in an unimmunised child is classic for Hib epiglottitis. Definitive airway management in theatre by anaesthetics with ENT standby precedes investigations; cannulation, bloods and imaging are deferred until the airway is secured because distress can precipitate complete obstruction, per RCH CPG.
Croup has coryzal prodrome with barking cough and hoarseness, not drooling, muffled voice or toxic appearance. Would be correct in barking cough without drooling (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

FB aspiration follows witnessed choking with focal asymmetry; no choking history plus high fever and toxic appearance make this unlikely. Would be correct with witnessed choking and focal signs (Source: RCH CPG).

Bacterial tracheitis usually follows several days of croup-like illness; rapid single-afternoon onset and tripoding favour epiglottitis. Would be correct with preceding croup-like illness over days (Source: RCH CPG).

Retropharyngeal abscess usually presents with neck stiffness/torticollis and preceding URTI or dental focus; CT-before-airway in a tripoding child with impending obstruction is unsafe. Would be correct with neck stiffness, no impending obstruction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome (high urate, high phosphate, high potassium, low calcium, AKI) is a classic emergency in high-risk haematological malignancies. Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated in three steps: stabilise the myocardium (IV calcium gluconate), shift potassium (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate selectively), and remove potassium (dialysis when AKI is established, oliguric, or refractory).
key_points: Calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 mL/kg IV over 5-10 min for ECG changes
Insulin 0.1 unit/kg with dextrose 0.5 g/kg
Salbutamol nebulised 5 mg as adjunct
Dialysis criteria in TLS: oliguric AKI, K >7 refractory, severe hyperphosphataemia, fluid overload
Avoid potassium-containing fluids; rasburicase for high urate
explanation.pearls: Hypocalcaemia in TLS is precipitation as calcium phosphate; correct calcium cautiously only if symptomatic because raising it worsens calcium phosphate deposition.

options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium but acts more slowly than calcium and does not protect the myocardium; calcium membrane stabilisation is the first step with ECG changes. Would be correct as second step after calcium (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia).

Bicarbonate has limited variable effect on potassium and worsens hypocalcaemia (already 1.78), risking tetany/arrhythmia. Would be correct only with severe metabolic acidosis and normocalcaemia (Source: APLS Australia).

Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, prolonged PR) requires immediate myocardial protection with IV calcium gluconate, followed by potassium-shifting therapy (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol) and definitive removal via dialysis given the rising creatinine, oliguria and hyperphosphataemia of TLS, as per RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia, RCH CPG: Tumour lysis syndrome, and APLS Australia.
Resin binders are slow-acting and unsuitable for immediate intervention with ECG changes; carry GI necrosis risk. Would be correct only as adjunct for chronic hyperkalaemia (Source: RCH CPG).

Loop diuretics need functional kidneys and are ineffective in oliguric AKI from TLS; cardiac protection and dialysis are needed. Would be correct only in non-oliguric AKI with preserved function (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Neonatal collapse between days 3-14 with shock, pre/post-ductal saturation differential and weak femoral pulses should be assumed to be duct-dependent congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Treatment is IV prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen the duct. Avoid high FiO2 and indometacin. Be ready for apnoea, fever, and hypotension as PGE1 side effects.
key_points: Duct-dependent systemic: coarctation, IAA, HLHS, critical AS
PGE1 0.01-0.05 microg/kg/min titrated to effect
Apnoea risk: anticipate intubation
Target SpO2 ~85-92%; avoid 100% oxygen
Retrieve early to cardiac centre
explanation.pearls: Differential SpO2 with lower foot than hand is highly suggestive of a duct-dependent systemic or mixing lesion; check four-limb BPs.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Closing the duct in duct-dependent systemic circulation precipitates cardiovascular collapse; the goal is to keep the duct OPEN. Would never be correct in duct-dependent lesion (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Coarctation).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: No narrow-complex tachycardia over 220 bpm with absent P waves; picture is duct-dependent systemic shock not SVT. Would be correct only in SVT (Source: ANZCOR 12.7).
Sildenafil is used in persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn, not duct-dependent systemic lesions; does not maintain ductal patency. Would never be correct here (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Duct-dependent systemic circulation with a closing PDA is reopened with prostaglandin E1 at 0.01-0.05 microgram/kg/min titrated to effect, with airway readiness for PGE-induced apnoea. High FiO2 is avoided because oxygen promotes ductal closure; target pre-ductal SpO2 about 85-92 percent.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: High FiO2 promotes ductal closure and worsens systemic perfusion in duct-dependent systemic lesions. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cardiology).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Duct dependent congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant reversal in life-threatening bleeding is agent-specific: warfarin = vitamin K + prothrombinex (or FFP if PCC unavailable); dabigatran = idarucizumab 5 g IV; factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) = andexanet alfa where available, otherwise prothrombinex 50 IU/kg. A markedly prolonged thrombin time confirms dabigatran activity.
key_points: Warfarin -> vitamin K + prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg
Dabigatran -> idarucizumab 5 g IV (2 x 2.5 g)
Apixaban/rivaroxaban -> andexanet alfa; alternative prothrombinex
FFP is volume-heavy and slow; not first choice when PCC/antidote available
Thrombin time is sensitive to dabigatran effect
explanation.pearls: Always check the last dose time and renal function for DOACs; dabigatran is renally cleared and may persist longer in AKI.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Vitamin K and prothrombinex reverse warfarin; dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor not reversed by vitamin K. Would be correct in warfarin-treated patient (Source: ANZSBT Guidelines).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban), not dabigatran. Would be correct in apixaban/rivaroxaban-treated patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
FFP does not reliably reverse direct thrombin inhibitors and volume-loads the patient. Would be correct only as bridge when idarucizumab unavailable (Source: ANZSBT).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Recombinant FVIIa is off-label, carries thrombotic risk especially with mechanical valve, and is not a specific reversal agent. Would never be correct as first-line (Source: ANZSBT).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a specific monoclonal antibody fragment that immediately neutralises dabigatran and is indicated for life-threatening bleeding (including intracranial haemorrhage) or urgent surgery in patients on dabigatran, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular and ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines.
source_refs: ANZ Society of Blood Transfusion Guidelines

explanation.summary: New-onset T1DM in a clinically well child without DKA (pH >=7.30, HCO3 >=15) is admitted for subcutaneous insulin commencement, glucose monitoring training and structured family education. DKA biochemical criteria are pH <7.30 or HCO3 <15 mmol/L with ketonaemia.
key_points: DKA criteria (ISPAD): hyperglycaemia >11 mmol/L + ketonaemia + pH <7.30 or HCO3 <15
Without DKA, use subcutaneous insulin and oral hydration
Outpatient initiation is not appropriate in Australian paediatric practice
Education covers carbohydrate counting, hypoglycaemia recognition, sick day rules
explanation.pearls: A pH of exactly 7.35 with bicarbonate 19 is not DKA. Do not start a DKA protocol on a child who does not need one.

options.rationale: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia with ketonaemia mandates same-day specialist paediatric review for insulin initiation and education. (Source: ISPAD; RCH CPG: T1DM).

DKA-protocol fluid plus insulin is reserved for pH under 7.30 or HCO3 under 15; this child's pH 7.35 and HCO3 are above threshold. Would be correct with pH under 7.30 or HCO3 under 15 (Source: ISPAD).

New-onset T1DM without DKA (pH 7.30 or more, HCO3 15 or more, ketones present but child clinically well) is admitted for subcutaneous insulin initiation, education and family training, per RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus and the APEG handbook.
Metformin is not first-line in suspected paediatric T1DM; insulin is required. Would be correct only in confirmed T2DM (Source: RCH CPG).
Glucose will not self-correct without exogenous insulin in T1DM. (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA: assume 5-8% dehydration; give one or two 10 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% saline only if shocked; replace remaining deficit over 48 hours; start insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h 1-2 hours after fluid resuscitation begins; switch fluid to 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose once glucose falls below 14-17 mmol/L; monitor neuro hourly.
key_points: Cerebral oedema risk factors: young age, new-onset DM, severe acidosis, low pCO2, high urea, bicarbonate therapy, rapid fluid, early insulin
Do not give insulin bolus
Replace K early once urine output established
Watch for headache, GCS drop, bradycardia, hypertension (Cushing response)
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema typically occurs 4-12 hours into therapy. The temptation to fix the numbers fast is the danger.

options.rationale: Insulin should not start until at least 1 h after fluid resuscitation has begun, because early insulin increases cerebral oedema risk and rapid osmolar shifts. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA).
IV insulin boluses are contraindicated in paediatric DKA (cerebral oedema risk); rapid deficit replacement under 48 h increases osmolar shifts. (Source: ISPAD 2022).
Dextrose addition before glucose falls below 14-17 mmol/L is inappropriate; 0.15 units/kg/h exceeds the 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h ceiling. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA).

ISPAD and the RCH DKA pathway use 0.9% saline (transitioned to 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose once glucose <14-17 mmol/L), with the calculated deficit replaced over 48 hours and insulin starting 1-2 hours after fluid resuscitation at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h to reduce cerebral oedema risk.
Rapid 6-h deficit replacement and simultaneous insulin commencement substantially increase cerebral oedema risk; deficit is replaced over 48 h. (Source: ISPAD 2022).

explanation.summary: DKA-associated cerebral oedema occurs in approximately 0.5-1% of paediatric DKA episodes, typically 4-12 hours into therapy, and has a 20-25% mortality. Treatment is immediate hypertonic saline 3% (2.5-5 mL/kg over 10-15 min) or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 15-20 min, head up 30 degrees, reduction of fluid rate by one third, and urgent intensivist input. CT is only after stabilisation.
key_points: Clinical diagnostic criteria (Muir): abnormal motor/verbal response, decorticate or decerebrate posturing, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal respiratory pattern
Hypertonic saline 3% 2.5-5 mL/kg OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce maintenance fluid rate by one third
Avoid hyperventilation below pCO2 35 mmHg unless herniating
explanation.pearls: A bradycardia in a child who was just tachycardic in DKA is cerebral oedema until proven otherwise. Treat first, image after.

options.rationale: Bradycardia with hypertension and falling GCS is Cushing response indicating raised ICP from cerebral oedema; fluid expansion worsens oedema and rate must be REDUCED. (Source: ISPAD 2022).

Glucose 14 is not the cause of declining GCS; stopping insulin worsens ketosis; picture points to cerebral oedema not hypoglycaemia. Would be correct only in confirmed hypoglycaemia (Source: ISPAD 2022).

Suspected DKA-associated cerebral oedema (declining GCS, headache, Cushing response, vomiting) is treated immediately with hypertonic saline 2.7-3% at 2.5-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes (or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), reduction of IV fluid rate by one third, head-up 30 degrees, and neuroimaging only after stabilisation per RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis and ISPAD 2022.
Bicarbonate is an independent risk factor for DKA-associated cerebral oedema and is not indicated; pH already improving to 7.18. (Source: ISPAD 2022).
LP in raised ICP risks coning and delays osmotherapy; the picture is cerebral oedema not meningitis. Would never be correct in suspected DKA cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: DKA).

explanation.summary: Severe hypoglycaemia (BSL <4 mmol/L with reduced consciousness or seizure) in a child with T1DM is treated outside hospital with IM glucagon: 0.5 mg if <25 kg or <8 years, 1 mg if >=25 kg. In hospital, 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV is preferred. Mild hypoglycaemia (conscious, able to swallow) is treated with 10-15 g rapid-acting oral carbohydrate, then complex carbohydrate.
key_points: Treatment threshold BSL <4 mmol/L
Glucagon 0.5 mg <25 kg, 1 mg >=25 kg
Repeat BSL 15 minutes after treatment
Investigate cause: missed meal, exercise, insulin dose error, illness
explanation.pearls: Glucagon does not work well in glycogen-depleted states (alcohol, prolonged starvation, repeated hypoglycaemia). Give IV dextrose if available.

options.rationale: Oral glucose is contraindicated with reduced consciousness or active seizure (aspiration risk); parenteral glucagon is indicated. Would be correct only with alert child able to swallow (Source: APEG hypoglycaemia).
1 mg glucagon is the dose for 25 kg or more; she is 22 kg. Insulin is contraindicated in hypoglycaemia. Would be correct in over-25-kg child without insulin error (Source: APEG; Hypokit dosing).
Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure needs immediate treatment; delay risks hypoxic injury and prolonged seizure. (Source: APEG).
Severe hypoglycaemia (unconscious or seizing) in a child UNDER 25 kg is treated with IM glucagon 0.5 mg; 1 mg is for at least 25 kg. Recovery position and ambulance attendance complete the response.

Hypoglycaemic seizure terminates with glucose, not benzodiazepine; midazolam first risks airway compromise without correcting cause. Would never be correct in hypoglycaemic seizure (Source: APLS Australia).

explanation.summary: Classical salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents at day 7-14 with vomiting, lethargy, weight loss, dehydration and the characteristic electrolyte triad of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis. Females are usually identified earlier from virilised genitalia; males present in crisis. Diagnosis is by markedly elevated 17-OH progesterone. Treatment is IV fluids, hydrocortisone, dextrose, and long-term hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.
key_points: Newborn screen (when returned) shows raised 17-OH progesterone
Salt-wasting crisis day 7-14 is the classic timing
Initial bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline, then hydrocortisone 50-100 mg/m^2 IV
Long-term: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone + salt supplementation in infancy
explanation.pearls: Any unwell second-week-of-life infant with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia is CAH until proven otherwise. The genitalia look normal in boys.

options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis gives hypochloraemic hypokalaemic ALKALOSIS; this infant has HYPERkalaemia and ACIDOSIS (opposite). Would be correct with classic pyloric biochemistry (Source: RCH CPG).

GBS can present with shock but does not characteristically produce the specific Na-low, K-high, glucose-low pattern; that electrolyte pattern points to adrenal insufficiency. Would be correct only with positive cultures and no electrolyte signature (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis).
Urea cycle defects produce respiratory ALKALOSIS with hyperammonaemia, not hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis. Would be correct with high ammonia and respiratory alkalosis (Source: HMSANZ).

PHA1 shares the biochemistry but is much rarer; distinguished by elevated aldosterone with normal 17-OHP (opposite of CAH). Would be correct with normal 17-OHP and elevated aldosterone (Source: APEG).

Day 7-14 presentation with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and shock in either sex is salt-wasting CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency; males have normal external genitalia and so are missed clinically until biochemical crisis, per RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis and ESPE 2018.

explanation.summary: Stress-dose hydrocortisone for paediatric adrenal crisis is 50-100 mg/m^2 IV (or 2 mg/kg if BSA unknown), followed by 50-100 mg/m^2/day in divided doses. Resuscitation is 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline, with 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid effect.
key_points: Bolus: 50 mg/m^2 IV or 2 mg/kg
Maintenance: 50-100 mg/m^2/day divided 4-6 hourly
Fluids: 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline; 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg if BSL <3.0
Dexamethasone is for diagnostic testing only, not crisis management
explanation.pearls: Every CAH family should carry an in-date IM hydrocortisone ampoule and have been trained in its use. Sick day rules: double or triple oral dose, switch to IM if vomiting.

options.rationale: She is shocked, hypoglycaemic and vomiting; oral therapy is inappropriate, parenteral hydrocortisone with IV resuscitation is required. Would never be correct in adrenal crisis (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is unsuitable for adrenal crisis; high-dose hydrocortisone provides both effects. Would be correct only in cerebral oedema (which is not the issue) (Source: RCH CPG).

Adrenal crisis management is stress-dose IV hydrocortisone 50-100 mg/m^2 bolus (approximately 50 mg for a BSA of 0.7 m^2, or 2 mg/kg if BSA unknown), 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, and 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for documented hypoglycaemia per RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology.

IM is acceptable if no IV access, but IV is preferred when access available; oral fludrocortisone does not address acute crisis and is not stress-dosed. Would be correct only without IV access (Source: APEG).
Methylprednisolone is not preferred; hypertonic saline is not indicated as she has only mild hyponatraemia not cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: First-line workup of short stature in a girl: FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH/free T4, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA), IGF-1 with IGFBP-3, vitamin D, bone age, and karyotype for any girl with unexplained short stature (Turner can present without classical features). Specialist GH testing and pituitary MRI are reserved for after this panel narrows the differential.
key_points: Growth velocity <5 cm/year between ages 4 and puberty is abnormal
Bone age delay >2 years suggests constitutional delay, hypothyroidism, GH deficiency or chronic illness
Karyotype mandatory in all unexplained short girls to exclude Turner
Mid-parental height = (mother + father)/2, minus 6.5 cm for girls
explanation.pearls: Turner syndrome can have a completely normal phenotype apart from short stature. Karyotype any girl who deserves a workup.

options.rationale: GH provocation testing is second-line after exclusion of systemic disease, hypothyroidism, coeliac and Turner; first-line is broad screening. Would be correct after first-line normal (Source: RCH CPG; APEG).

The standard first-line short-stature workup includes FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH/T4, coeliac serology, IGF-1, bone age and karyotype (in girls) to exclude systemic illness, hypothyroidism, coeliac, GH deficiency and Turner syndrome before specialist provocation testing per RCH CPG: Short Stature and ESPE consensus.
Pituitary MRI is indicated after biochemical confirmation of GHD or with neurological features, not as first-line screen. Would be correct after confirmed GHD (Source: RCH CPG).
Addison's is not a typical cause of isolated short stature with normal weight; targeted adrenal testing is not first-line. Would be correct only with hyperpigmentation or salt-craving (Source: APEG).
IBD workup is targeted to GI symptoms or abnormal first-line bloods; endoscopy is invasive not screening. Would be correct with GI symptoms or anaemia/raised CRP (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty in girls is breast development before age 8 (or pubic hair/menarche before age 8/9). Central PP is gonadotropin-dependent (HPG axis activation); peripheral PP is gonadotropin-independent (ovarian, adrenal, exogenous). GnRH stimulation distinguishes the two: peak LH >=5 IU/L indicates central. Central PP in girls <6 years mandates MRI brain.
key_points: Random LH alone has poor sensitivity; stimulation is the test
Pubertal pelvic ultrasound: uterus >3.5-4 cm, endometrial echo, multifollicular ovaries
Bone age advancement >2 years suggests significant oestrogen exposure
Treatment for confirmed central PP is GnRH analogue to preserve adult height
explanation.pearls: Isolated premature thelarche (no growth spurt, no bone age advance, prepubertal LH response) does not need treatment, just surveillance.

options.rationale: Pelvic US already shows pubertal pattern without ovarian mass; pelvic MRI is reserved for US abnormality or suspected peripheral cause. Would be correct only with US abnormality (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

GnRH (or GnRH analogue) stimulation testing with peak LH >=5 IU/L (or LH:FSH ratio >0.66) confirms central precocious puberty, while a suppressed LH response with elevated oestradiol points to a peripheral cause per RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty and ESPE consensus.

Non-classical CAH causes premature adrenarche (pubic/axillary hair, body odour) without breast development; this child has Tanner B3 breast indicating gonadarche. Would be correct with isolated adrenarche features (Source: ESPE).
Treatment should not precede confirmation of diagnosis and underlying cause (including MRI in girls under 6-8 with central PP). Would never be correct without confirmation (Source: APEG).
MRI is done after central PP is biochemically confirmed (or in girls under 6 with central features), not as the first test. Would be correct after biochemical confirmation (Source: ESPE).

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects approximately 1 in 2000 newborns in Australia. Treatment with levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day started within 2 weeks of birth (ideally day 7-10) normalises IQ outcomes. Crushed tablets given with water or breast milk are preferred to liquid suspensions. Target free T4 in the upper half of reference range; aim TSH <5 mIU/L within 4 weeks.
key_points: Dose: levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day oral
Aetiology: thyroid dysgenesis (~80%) > dyshormonogenesis > transient
Imaging: Tc-99m or I-123 scan + ultrasound to characterise
Re-evaluation off treatment at age 3 if dyshormonogenesis suspected
explanation.pearls: Avoid giving levothyroxine with soy-based formula, iron or calcium, which markedly reduce absorption.

options.rationale: Confirmed venous TSH 88 with fT4 5 is unequivocal CH; delaying treatment 3 weeks significantly worsens neurodevelopmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

Confirmed congenital hypothyroidism requires levothyroxine 10-15 microg/kg/day commenced as soon as possible and ideally within 2 weeks of birth to optimise neurodevelopmental outcome, with TFT review at 2 weeks aiming for free T4 in the upper half of the reference range per RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism and ESPE-ATA consensus.

2 microg/kg/day is the adult-equivalent maintenance dose, markedly inadequate for neonatal CH (10-15 mcg/kg/day required). Would be correct only as adult maintenance, not neonatal initiation (Source: ESPE-ATA).
Treatment must not be delayed for imaging; scan can be done concurrently or after stabilisation. (Source: RCH CPG).
Oral levothyroxine is the standard; T3 is reserved for myxoedema coma. Would never be correct in neonatal CH (Source: ESPE-ATA).

explanation.summary: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the commonest cause of acquired hypothyroidism in Australian adolescents, with a female predominance and associations with type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease and Turner syndrome. Treatment is levothyroxine titrated to TSH in the lower half of reference range, with biochemical monitoring at 6-8 weeks then every 6-12 months when stable.
key_points: Dose: 1.2-1.7 microg/kg/day in adolescents
Anti-TPO positive in approximately 90% of Hashimoto's
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (T1DM, coeliac)
Recheck after illness, weight change, pregnancy or new interacting medication
explanation.pearls: TSH may take 4-6 weeks to normalise even with adequate dosing; don't escalate too quickly on a 2-week recheck.

options.rationale: Full adult replacement risks angina-like symptoms, tachyarrhythmia and behavioural symptoms in adolescents; titrate from lower dose. Would be correct only in severe hypothyroidism with myxoedema features (Source: RCH CPG: Hypothyroidism).
Carbimazole/propranolol treat hyperthyroidism; this is hypothyroidism (high TSH, low fT4). Would be correct in hyperthyroidism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Smooth diffuse goitre with anti-TPO is Hashimoto's; FNA is for discrete nodules or rapidly growing goitre. Would be correct with palpable discrete nodule (Source: RCH CPG).
This is overt hypothyroidism (TSH 78, low fT4), not subclinical, requiring treatment. Would be correct only with subclinical (mildly raised TSH, normal fT4) (Source: ESPE).

Adolescent autoimmune (Hashimoto's) hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine 1.2-1.7 microg/kg/day (approximately 50 microg daily for a typical 14-year-old), titrating to TSH in the lower half of the reference range with TFTs at 6-8 week intervals per RCH CPG: Hypothyroidism and ESPE guidance.

explanation.summary: Paediatric Graves' disease accounts for approximately 95% of paediatric hyperthyroidism, with a strong female predominance. Initial therapy is carbimazole (preferred over PTU due to hepatotoxicity) for at least 18-24 months, with propranolol for adrenergic symptoms. Remission rate after a course is approximately 25-30%; relapse warrants discussion of definitive therapy (radioiodine or thyroidectomy).
key_points: Carbimazole 0.5-1 mg/kg/day, max 30 mg/day (titration regimen) or block-and-replace
PTU avoided in children except in thyroid storm or first trimester pregnancy
Monitor for agranulocytosis (FBC if sore throat or fever) and hepatotoxicity
Anti-TSHR Ab titre at end of treatment predicts relapse risk
explanation.pearls: Counsel families about agranulocytosis: any sore throat or fever on carbimazole = stop and check FBC.

options.rationale: PTU has a black-box warning for severe hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure; not first-line in paediatric Graves. Would be correct only with carbimazole intolerance, or first trimester pregnancy (Source: ESPE).

Initial therapy is medical with thionamide for 18-24 months; radioiodine offered after relapse or in older adolescents with persistent disease. Would be correct after relapse (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperthyroidism).
Surgery is for thionamide failure/intolerance, very large goitre, or Graves ophthalmopathy where radioiodine unsuitable. Would be correct in those specific situations (Source: ESPE).

Australian and ESPE-recommended first-line therapy for paediatric Graves' disease is a thionamide (carbimazole preferred to propylthiouracil because of PTU hepatotoxicity in children) at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day with a beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms, baseline and serial neutrophil and LFT monitoring per RCH CPG: Hyperthyroidism and Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology.
Inorganic iodine is used pre-operatively or in thyroid storm, not as chronic monotherapy. Would be correct only as pre-op or thyroid storm adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Diabetes insipidus is suggested by hypotonic polyuria with hypernatraemia and hyperosmolar plasma (>295) with inappropriately dilute urine (<300). Once biochemically confirmed without need for water deprivation, a desmopressin trial distinguishes central (urine concentrates) from nephrogenic (no response). MRI brain is mandatory in confirmed central DI to exclude tumour, infiltration (LCH, germ cell tumour) or malformation.
key_points: Hypernatraemia should be corrected slowly (<10-12 mmol/L per 24 hours) to avoid cerebral oedema
Causes of central DI: idiopathic, tumour (craniopharyngioma, germinoma), LCH, trauma, infection
Nephrogenic DI: X-linked AVPR2 mutation, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, lithium, sickle cell
Treatment of central DI: oral or intranasal desmopressin titrated to symptoms
explanation.pearls: LCH commonly involves the pituitary stalk and presents as central DI before any imaging-visible lesion. Repeat MRI 6-monthly if initial scan is normal.

sources.label: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

options.rationale: Water deprivation test risks dangerous dehydration when there is already biochemical evidence of inappropriate dilute urine in hypernatraemia; diagnosis is already established. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: DI).
source_refs: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

options.rationale: When plasma is already hyperosmolar (>295 mOsm/kg) with hypernatraemia and inappropriately dilute urine (<300 mOsm/kg), DI is biochemically confirmed and a desmopressin trial (urine concentrates >50% = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI) with MRI brain (looking for loss of posterior pituitary bright spot, infiltrative disease) is appropriate, particularly with this child's LCH history per RCH CPG: Diabetes Insipidus.
source_refs: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

options.rationale: Renal imaging is reasonable later if nephrogenic DI is confirmed by no desmopressin response; it is not the first-line test. Would be correct after confirmed nephrogenic DI (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
Random glucose 4.8 and urine SG 1.002 exclude osmotic diuresis; this is hypotonic polyuria not DM. Would be correct only with hyperglycaemia and glycosuria (Source: RCH CPG).
Calcium normal at 2.4; chronic hypercalcaemia is unlikely primary cause here; LCH-related central DI is most likely given history. Would be correct only with hypercalcaemia (Source: ESPE).
source_refs: ESPE Consensus on Central Diabetes Insipidus

explanation.summary: SIADH is a common complication of CNS infection in children. Diagnostic criteria require euvolaemia, hypoosmolar plasma (<275), inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg, usually >plasma), urine Na >40 mmol/L, normal renal/adrenal/thyroid function. First-line treatment is fluid restriction to two-thirds maintenance. Symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, severely altered mental state) is treated with 3% saline 3-5 mL/kg bolus aiming to raise sodium by 4-6 mmol/L. Correction rate should not exceed 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: Fluid restriction is first-line if asymptomatic
3% saline 3-5 mL/kg only if symptomatic (seizures, GCS drop)
Differentiate from cerebral salt wasting (CSW is hypovolaemic with high urine output)
Correction rate max 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Iso-osmolar hyponatraemia in a meningitis admission is more often hospital-acquired from hypotonic IV fluids than true SIADH; always check what's running.

options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality > plasma osmolality and urine sodium >40 mmol/L in a non-seizing asymptomatic child meets criteria for SIADH, treated initially with fluid restriction (typically two-thirds maintenance) and serial monitoring per RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia and Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology.

Hypertonic saline is for symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, severe altered mental state) at Na under 125; she has mild headache only and is alert. Would be correct with seizures or altered mental state at Na under 125 (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia).
Increasing fluid worsens dilutional hyponatraemia in SIADH; this is not cerebral salt wasting (which is hypovolaemic). Would be correct in CSW with hypovolaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Tolvaptan is rarely used in paediatrics, requires inpatient initiation, and is not first-line for transient post-meningitis SIADH. Would be correct only in chronic refractory SIADH (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
Furosemide is sometimes adjunctive in chronic SIADH refractory to restriction; first-line is fluid restriction. Would be correct as adjunct after restriction fails (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Australian management of adolescent obesity is structured family-based intensive lifestyle intervention (diet, activity, behaviour, sleep, screen time) with treatment of comorbidities (OSA, NAFLD, mental health). Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive: metformin is the most evidence-based oral agent for insulin resistance, prediabetes and NAFLD. Bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy) is considered in selected adolescents with BMI >40 (or >35 with comorbidities) after multidisciplinary review. Always exclude secondary causes (hypothyroidism, Cushing, Prader-Willi, MC4R) before labelling primary obesity.
key_points: Metformin 500 mg BD, titrate to max 1000 mg BD if tolerated
Address OSA, NAFLD, mental health and joint pain in parallel
Bariatric criteria (AU): BMI >40 or >35 with comorbidity, age >=15-16, failed intensive therapy
Edmonton Obesity Staging System for Paediatrics (EOSS-P) for risk stratification
explanation.pearls: Acanthosis nigricans + prediabetic HbA1c in an adolescent is a strong indication for metformin; do not wait for overt T2DM to act.

sources.label: APEG Position Statement: Metformin in Adolescents
NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity
ANZMOSS Position Statement on Adolescent Bariatric Surgery

options.rationale: Metformin is the only oral agent approved for use in paediatric obesity-related insulin resistance with prediabetes/NAFLD as an adjunct to intensive lifestyle change in adolescents from age 10, particularly with HbA1c in the prediabetic range, hepatic steatosis and acanthosis nigricans per APEG position on adolescent metformin use and NHMRC obesity guidance.
source_refs: APEG Position Statement: Metformin in Adolescents
NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity

options.rationale: Orlistat has limited efficacy and significant GI side effects in adolescents; not first-line in AU paediatric practice. Would be correct only after metformin failure with high-fat diet (Source: NHMRC Obesity Guidance).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity

options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after intensive medical/lifestyle therapy failure at BMI over 40 (or over 35 with comorbidities) with MDT assessment. Would be correct only with established intensive treatment failure (Source: NHMRC).
source_refs: ANZMOSS Position Statement on Adolescent Bariatric Surgery

options.rationale: GLP-1 agonists are emerging but TGA paediatric approval and PBS subsidy are limited; metformin remains first-line. Would be correct in selected cases with T2DM under specialist input (Source: NHMRC; TGA).
source_refs: APEG Position Statement: Metformin in Adolescents

options.rationale: Thyroid hormone in a euthyroid child is contraindicated and causes iatrogenic hyperthyroidism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Children with trisomy 21 have a markedly increased lifetime risk of both congenital and acquired hypothyroidism, much of it subclinical. Routine annual TSH surveillance from age 1 onwards is recommended in Australian and international guidance (RCH CPG: Down syndrome; AAP Down syndrome health supervision).
key_points: Congenital hypothyroidism is screened on the newborn screen; thereafter, T21 children need ongoing periodic testing
Standard schedule: at birth (newborn screen), at 6 and 12 months, then annually for life
Annual surveillance even in asymptomatic, biochemically normal patients (RCH CPG: Down syndrome)
explanation.pearls: Symptoms of hypothyroidism are easily missed in T21 because hypotonia, constipation, and dry skin overlap with the syndromic baseline - biochemistry, not symptoms, drives detection.

options.rationale: Symptom-based screening misses subclinical hypothyroidism (common and frequently asymptomatic in T21); biochemical surveillance is recommended. Would never be correct in T21 (Source: RCH CPG: Down Syndrome).
Six-monthly testing is recommended only in the first year (CH risk highest); from 12 months annual screening is sufficient. Would be correct only in the first year of life (Source: RCH CPG).

Australian and international Down syndrome guidance recommends annual thyroid screening from age 1 onwards, lifelong, because of the high cumulative incidence of acquired hypothyroidism and frequent subclinical disease in this population (RCH CPG: Down syndrome - health surveillance; AAP clinical report: Down syndrome).
Three-yearly testing is too infrequent given high background incidence; routine autoantibodies are not standard. Would never be correct in T21 (Source: RCH CPG).
Endocrinology referral is for abnormal results or clinical concerns; uncomplicated annual screening is primary/general paediatric care. Would be correct only with abnormal TSH/fT4 (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Routine cervical spine radiography for asymptomatic children with Down syndrome has been abandoned in current Australian and AAP guidance because of poor predictive value. Sports clearance relies on a focused symptom-and-examination screen plus counselling about avoiding activities with forced cervical flexion or head-first impact, such as trampolining and gymnastics (RCH CPG: Down syndrome).
key_points: Screen by history (neck pain, torticollis, gait change, new incontinence, weakness) and examination (tone, reflexes, clonus, plantars, gait)
Trampolining, gymnastics, diving, boxing and certain contact codes are discouraged regardless of imaging
Image only when symptoms or signs raise concern, then with MRI for cord assessment
explanation.pearls: Atlantoaxial instability in T21 presents with subtle changes: torticollis, decline in handwriting or gait, new toe-walking, or new incontinence - all warrant urgent neurosurgical and imaging review.

options.rationale: Routine flex-ext films in asymptomatic T21 children are no longer recommended (poor predictive value). Would be correct only with symptoms/signs of cord compression (Source: RCH CPG: Down Syndrome).

Current guidance is symptom and examination based: ask about neck pain, torticollis, gait change, weakness, sphincter changes; examine for myelopathic signs. Sports involving forced cervical flexion or risk of head-first impact (trampolining, gymnastics, diving, rugby contact, boxing) are specifically discouraged in T21 because of the elevated background risk of atlantoaxial instability (RCH CPG: Down syndrome; AAP Down syndrome health supervision).

MRI is reserved for symptoms/signs of cord compression (neck pain, torticollis, gait deterioration, incontinence, hyperreflexia); not routine pre-sport. Would be correct with neuro signs (Source: RCH CPG).
Normal exam does not exclude AAI and does not negate elevated T21 risk; trampolining/gymnastics/diving/contact rugby remain discouraged. Would never be correct as blanket clearance (Source: RCH CPG).

Blanket sport restriction is not recommended and deprives developmental/social benefit; many sports are encouraged with appropriate selection. Would never be correct as blanket restriction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Trisomy 21 confers a substantially increased risk of acute leukaemia: ALL across childhood and a unique predisposition to acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (AMKL) under age 4. Pancytopenia with circulating blasts demands urgent tertiary referral for marrow examination (RCH CPG: Suspected leukaemia).
key_points: Approximately 10-20-fold increased risk of leukaemia in trisomy 21 compared with the general paediatric population
AMKL predominates under age 4, ALL throughout childhood
Pancytopenia + blasts + organomegaly = same-day tertiary referral
explanation.pearls: Transient abnormal myelopoiesis in T21 neonates resolves spontaneously in most cases but predisposes to AMKL in the first 4 years - prior TAM is a flag for vigilance.

options.rationale: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts plus hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy is leukaemia until proven otherwise; delay is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG; ANZCHOG).
Empirical oral antibiotics without focus and without addressing marrow failure delays diagnosis. Would be correct only with documented infective focus and normal bloods (Source: ANZCHOG).

Pancytopenia with circulating blasts, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy in a child with trisomy 21 is leukaemia until proven otherwise; T21 carries an approximately 10-20-fold increased risk of both ALL and AMKL (and a distinct ML-DS pathway). Same-day tertiary transfer for bone marrow biopsy, supportive care (transfusion as needed, neutropenic precautions) and oncology input is mandatory.
Nutritional workup does not explain thrombocytopenia, blasts, splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Would be correct only in pure microcytic anaemia without these features (Source: RCH CPG).
Outpatient referral risks dangerous delay; needs same-day tertiary oncology assessment. (Source: ANZCHOG).

explanation.summary: Women with Turner syndrome have a substantially elevated lifetime risk of bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, aortic root dilatation, and dissection. Australian and international guidance recommends serial echocardiography through childhood, with a baseline cardiac MRI at adolescent transition and lifelong adult surveillance (International Turner Syndrome Guideline 2017).
key_points: Bicuspid aortic valve in 15-30%, coarctation in 7-12% of Turner syndrome cases
Aortic dissection risk is markedly elevated, particularly with bicuspid valve, coarctation, hypertension or pregnancy
Childhood echocardiography with transition MRI sets the baseline for adult surveillance
explanation.pearls: Indexed aortic size to body surface area (z-score) is used in children; in adults, ascending aortic size index >2.5 cm/m^2 flags very high dissection risk.

options.rationale: Symptom-based surveillance misses progressive aortic dilatation (frequently silent in Turner and a major mortality cause). (Source: Australasian Turner Syndrome Clinical Guideline).

5-yearly imaging is insufficient given lifetime aortic root dilatation/dissection risk; more frequent imaging through childhood plus transition MRI is recommended. (Source: International Turner Syndrome Consensus).

BP and ECG do not exclude aortic root dilatation or evolving coarctation; imaging surveillance is required. Would never be correct as sole surveillance (Source: International Turner Syndrome Consensus).

Current guidance recommends serial childhood echocardiography (typically every 3 to 5 years if the heart and aorta are normal, sooner if abnormal), with a transition cardiac MRI in adolescence to establish a baseline of the aortic dimensions for ongoing adult surveillance; this woman will need lifelong imaging because of the aortopathy risk associated with 45,X and bicuspid aortic valve (International Turner Syndrome Guideline 2017; Australian paediatric endocrine practice).

Annual MRI in a young child often requires sedation and is not warranted in asymptomatic patient with normal recent echo. Would be correct only with abnormal echo or symptoms (Source: International Turner Syndrome Consensus).

explanation.summary: Williams syndrome is a contiguous gene deletion at 7q11.23 - the deleted segment includes the elastin gene (ELN), which produces the syndrome-defining vasculopathy: deficient elastin in arterial walls drives supravalvular aortic stenosis and diffuse arteriopathy. The same deletion encompasses other genes regulating calcium homeostasis and vitamin D sensitivity, which is why children with Williams syndrome are predisposed to idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia (mechanism not fully characterised but reproducible across the cohort). The first-line approach for mild-to-moderate hypercalcaemia is dietary calcium restriction and vitamin D withdrawal with paediatric endocrine guidance; pharmacological escalation (steroids, bisphosphonates, loop diuretics) is reserved for refractory or severe cases (AAP Williams syndrome health supervision).
key_points: Annual calcium and urinary calcium:creatinine screening is recommended in Williams syndrome
Renal ultrasound assesses for nephrocalcinosis when hypercalcaemia is detected
Use low-calcium specialty formula and avoid vitamin D supplementation as first-line management
explanation.pearls: Suppressed PTH plus hypercalcaemia + nephrocalcinosis + elfin facies + supravalvular AS is a syndrome-defining cluster - send microarray for 7q11.23 deletion.

options.rationale: Hydration alone without removing vitamin D and limiting dietary calcium will not address the underlying problem and risks progressive nephrocalcinosis. Would never be correct in Williams hypercalcaemia (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome Health Supervision).

Steroids are for refractory hypercalcaemia after dietary/supplement adjustment; first-line is removing vitamin D and calcium restriction. Would be correct only after first-line failure (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome).

Bisphosphonates are for severe/symptomatic/refractory hypercalcaemia with long-lasting bone effects in young children; not first-line in mild-to-moderate disease. Would be correct only with severe refractory hypercalcaemia (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome).

Loop diuretics promote calciuria but are reserved for severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with adequate hydration; not first-line in mild outpatient disease. Would be correct in severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia (Source: AAP Williams Syndrome).

Idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia is a recognised feature of Williams syndrome and the first-line intervention is to remove exogenous vitamin D, switch to a low-calcium specialty formula, and limit dietary calcium under specialist endocrine and dietetic guidance; this approach typically normalises calcium without bisphosphonate or steroid escalation (Williams Syndrome Association clinical care recommendations; AAP Health care supervision for children with Williams syndrome).

explanation.summary: Noonan syndrome management is multidisciplinary, with feeding difficulties and growth failure dominating infancy in a substantial minority of children. Coordinated speech-pathology-led feeding assessment with dietetic input is the immediate priority once cardiac disease is stable below intervention thresholds (Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines).
key_points: Pulmonary stenosis is the most common cardiac lesion (around 50%) and is often dysplastic, frequently requiring surgical rather than balloon intervention if severe
Bleeding diathesis is common - check FBC, coagulation, and consider von Willebrand and platelet function before any surgery
Growth hormone consideration is later in childhood, after feeding and growth optimisation
explanation.pearls: Noonan syndrome is autosomal dominant - examine parents for subtle phenotype and consider parental molecular testing once the proband variant is known.

sources.label: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.rationale: Feeding difficulties are extremely common in Noonan syndrome and a leading cause of failure to thrive in infancy. A coordinated feeding assessment (speech pathology for swallow safety, dietetics for caloric optimisation, occupational therapy for sensory feeding behaviours) addresses the dominant clinical problem in this child (Noonan Syndrome Clinical Management Guidelines; RCH CPG: Failure to thrive).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.rationale: Valvuloplasty in Noonan is for severe PS (peak gradient over 60 mmHg) or symptomatic disease, with reduced efficacy given dysplastic valve. Would be correct with severe PS gradient (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.rationale: GH in Noonan is considered later in childhood after endocrinology assessment; not appropriate at 8 months with active feeding difficulties. Would be correct in older child after feeding stabilised (Source: APEG).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.rationale: Routine prophylactic platelet transfusions are not indicated in asymptomatic infants; baseline coagulation/platelet function assessment is appropriate. Would be correct only with active bleeding (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

options.rationale: Counselling alone does not address failure to thrive; immediate growth/feeding intervention is needed. Would be correct as part of broader plan, not alone (Source: Noonan Syndrome Consensus).
source_refs: Noonan syndrome clinical management guidelines (van der Burgt)

explanation.summary: When a familial pathogenic FBN1 variant is known, first-degree relatives undergo cascade targeted genetic testing combined with baseline aortic imaging and ophthalmology assessment. The revised Ghent criteria explicitly incorporate genetic findings to confirm or exclude Marfan syndrome in relatives (Revised Ghent criteria 2010).
key_points: Cascade testing of a known familial variant is the most efficient genetic strategy
Echocardiogram measures aortic root Z-score and screens for mitral valve prolapse
Ophthalmology slit-lamp examination is essential to detect ectopia lentis
explanation.pearls: A negative cascade test for a known familial pathogenic FBN1 variant effectively excludes Marfan syndrome in that relative and ends ongoing surveillance.

options.rationale: Whole-exome sequencing is not appropriate as first-line when a specific familial variant is known; cascade testing is more efficient and definitive. Would be correct only without known familial variant (Source: Marfan Foundation).

Multi-gene panels are first-line when no familial variant is known; with a confirmed variant, cascade is faster, cheaper and definitive. Would be correct only without known familial variant (Source: Marfan Foundation).
Symptom-based screening in a first-degree relative of confirmed FBN1 variant carrier is unsafe; root dilatation is usually asymptomatic until dissection. (Source: Marfan Foundation).

Medical therapy starts after diagnosis is made and aortic dimensions documented; empirical beta-blockade before confirming is premature. Would be correct after confirmed diagnosis (Source: Marfan Foundation).

When a familial pathogenic FBN1 variant is known, targeted (cascade) genetic testing for that single variant is the most efficient confirmatory test in at-risk first-degree relatives, alongside baseline imaging of the aorta (echocardiogram +/- subsequent MRI/CT) and an ophthalmology assessment for ectopia lentis; the revised Ghent criteria include both genetic and clinical pathways to diagnosis (Revised Ghent criteria 2010; Marfan Foundation clinical care guidelines).

explanation.summary: Aortic protection in Marfan syndrome combines pharmacotherapy (beta-blockade or angiotensin receptor blockade), activity modification (avoid competitive contact, isometric and burst-Valsalva sport, continue moderate aerobic activity), and serial imaging. Surgical thresholds are 5.0 cm aortic root, or smaller with rapid progression, family history of early dissection, planned pregnancy, or significant aortic regurgitation (Marfan Foundation clinical care recommendations).
key_points: Beta-blockade and angiotensin receptor blockade slow aortic root growth in Marfan syndrome
Family history of early dissection lowers the surgical threshold
Restrict competitive isometric/contact sports; encourage moderate aerobic exercise
explanation.pearls: Indexed aortic Z-score and rate of change matter more than a single absolute diameter when deciding to start or escalate therapy in a growing adolescent.

options.rationale: Z-score increase from 2.5 to 3.2 over 12 months warrants both pharmacological aortic protection and high-intensity isometric/burst-Valsalva sport modification. (Source: Marfan Foundation; Bethesda).

An aortic root Z-score of 3.2 with rapid progression warrants commencement of beta-blockade (or angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan if intolerant), avoidance of competitive contact, isometric and burst-Valsalva sports, and intensified imaging surveillance every 6 months. Moderate aerobic exercise is encouraged (Marfan Foundation clinical care recommendations; AHA / Bethesda Conference guidance).

Elective root replacement is at ~5.0 cm in adults (or smaller with rapid progression/family dissection); current diameter does not meet threshold. Would be correct at >=5.0 cm or rapid progression (Source: AHA).
Pharmacotherapy does not substitute for activity modification; competitive contact/isometric/burst-Valsalva sport is restricted regardless of medication. (Source: AHA exercise guidance).
Complete cessation is not recommended; moderate aerobic non-isometric exercise is encouraged for cardiovascular/psychosocial benefit. (Source: Bethesda/AHA).

explanation.summary: Vascular EDS is a COL3A1 disease: pathogenic variants disrupt the type III collagen homotrimer, the dominant structural collagen of medium-sized arteries, alveolar septa, hollow viscus walls, and the dermal reticular layer. The phenotype follows directly from where type III collagen lives. Fragile arterial media drives spontaneous medium-vessel rupture and dissection (often without preceding aneurysm). Fragile alveolar walls produce spontaneous pneumothorax (a top-decile feature in adolescence). Capillary and venular fragility produces easy bruising in unusual locations. Depletion of dermal type III collagen thins the skin and exposes the subdermal venous network (translucent skin, prominent veins). Reduced subcutaneous fat over the face combined with thin nose, thin lips and prominent eyes gives the recognisable facies. The same defect underlies intestinal (sigmoid) and uterine (third-trimester) rupture and the substantially elevated pregnancy mortality. With a known familial pathogenic variant, management is cascade testing, non-invasive vascular imaging (MRA/CTA, NOT catheter arteriography because instrumentation tears the same vessels), celiprolol where available (BBEST trial reduced arterial events), avoidance of elective surgery and central venous access where possible, and pre-conception multidisciplinary counselling (International EDS classification 2017; EDS Society care recommendations).
key_points: Mechanism: COL3A1 variant -> defective type III collagen -> fragile medium arteries, alveolar walls, hollow viscera, dermis
Major diagnostic features of vEDS: arterial/intestinal/uterine rupture, family history of vEDS, characteristic facies, easy bruising
Celiprolol reduced arterial events in the BBEST trial; not yet routinely PBS-listed but used internationally
Pregnancy in vEDS carries substantially elevated mortality risk and warrants pre-conception multidisciplinary counselling
explanation.pearls: Avoid arteriography, central venous access where possible, and elective surgery in vEDS - tissue fragility makes surgical complications common and severe.

options.rationale: Hypermobile EDS does not explain translucent skin, prominent venous pattern, spontaneous pneumothorax, easy bruising, or familial COL3A1 variant. Would be correct only in isolated hypermobility (Source: EDS Society Care Recommendations).

The combination of translucent skin, characteristic facies, easy bruising in unusual locations, spontaneous pneumothorax, and a first-degree relative with a confirmed pathogenic COL3A1 variant strongly suggests vascular EDS. Cascade targeted testing for her sister's variant is the next step; if confirmed, baseline non-invasive vascular imaging, celiprolol (where available - the BBEST trial showed reduction in arterial events), avoidance of routine arteriography, and detailed pregnancy counselling are recommended (International EDS classification 2017; EDS Society care recommendations).
No marfanoid habitus, no aortic root dilatation, no ectopia lentis, no high-arched palate; known familial COL3A1 not FBN1. (Source: Marfan Foundation).

Classical EDS features atrophic scarring and marked skin hyperextensibility; familial COL3A1 directs cascade not COL5A1/A2. Would be correct only with classical EDS features and family history (Source: EDS Society).
Catheter arteriography in vascular EDS carries high arterial dissection risk; non-invasive MRA/CTA is preferred. (Source: EDS Society).

explanation.summary: Fragile X is X-linked with CGG expansion of the FMR1 gene. Premutation (~55-200 repeats) carriers risk female-line expansion to full mutation (>200 repeats) and direct premutation-associated disease (FXPOI in females, FXTAS in older males). Counselling addresses transmission, expansion risk, reproductive options, and broader family cascade testing (National Fragile X Foundation; RANZCOG).
key_points: Premutation: ~55-200 CGG repeats; full mutation: >200 CGG repeats with FMR1 hypermethylation
Expansion to full mutation occurs only with female-line transmission; risk rises with premutation size
Reproductive options: prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis), preimplantation genetic testing, gamete donation
explanation.pearls: Female premutation carriers are at risk of fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency - relevant when counselling about timing of family planning.

options.rationale: Heterozygous females with full mutation often have variable milder phenotype from X-inactivation; premutation inheritance does not cause full Fragile X. (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).
Fragile X is X-linked, not autosomal recessive; this fundamentally changes carrier risk and reproductive counselling. (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).
Premutation alleles can expand on female-line transmission and cause clinical disease (FXPOI in ~20% of female carriers, FXTAS). (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).
Male premutation carriers transmit only stable premutation to daughters, never the full mutation directly; her father almost certainly carries a premutation. (Source: National Fragile X Foundation).

Fragile X is X-linked. A female premutation carrier transmits the affected X with a 50% probability to each child; only female-line transmission carries the risk of CGG repeat expansion to the full mutation, with the expansion risk rising sharply once maternal premutation length exceeds approximately 90 to 100 repeats. A son who inherits the expanded full mutation will manifest the syndrome (RANZCOG carrier screening; National Fragile X Foundation clinical guidance).

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of NF1 is clinical, based on the 2021 revised NIH/NF1 criteria requiring two or more defined features. Cafe-au-lait macule threshold is 6 or more, >5 mm prepubertally or >15 mm postpubertally, and skin-fold freckling counts as a separate diagnostic feature (Revised NF1 diagnostic criteria 2021).
key_points: 6 or more cafe-au-lait macules with appropriate size threshold
Skin-fold freckling (axillary or inguinal) is a separate diagnostic feature
Other criteria: neurofibromas, optic glioma, Lisch nodules or choroidal abnormalities, distinctive bone lesion, pathogenic NF1 variant, affected first-degree relative
explanation.pearls: Even with diagnostic certainty by clinical criteria, NF1 children need structured surveillance for optic pathway glioma (under age 7), neurofibroma growth, scoliosis, and learning issues.

options.rationale: 2021 revised criteria allow diagnosis on two features and explicitly include 6+ CALMs plus skin-fold freckling without family history. (Source: 2021 Revised NIH/NF1 Criteria).
Molecular confirmation is one criterion but not required when two clinical criteria are present. Would be correct only with one clinical feature plus molecular variant (Source: 2021 NIH).
Threshold is 6+ CALMs over 5 mm pre-pubertally (or over 15 mm post-pubertally), not 10. (Source: 2021 NIH).

Under the 2021 revised criteria she meets two features (macule count/size and skin-fold freckling). AU practice (RCH CPG: NF1) is then to refer for genetics, formal paediatric ophthalmology slit-lamp (Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma screening), blood pressure monitoring annually (phaeochromocytoma/renovascular risk) and structured developmental and learning surveillance.

Affected first-degree relative is one of several alternative features, not required when two clinical features are present. Would be correct only with one clinical feature plus first-degree relative (Source: 2021 NIH).

explanation.summary: Optic pathway glioma is the commonest CNS tumour in childhood NF1 and presents almost exclusively before age 7. Surveillance is by annual paediatric ophthalmology through early childhood, with MRI reserved for clinical or examination concern. Routine screening MRI is not recommended (RCH CPG: NF1).
key_points: Annual paediatric ophthalmology surveillance until approximately age 7 to 8, then less frequent
MRI when clinical concern arises (new strabismus, proptosis, precocious puberty, visual change)
Most NF1 OPGs are indolent and do not need treatment - surveillance triggers intervention only for clinical or imaging progression
explanation.pearls: Precocious puberty in NF1 should trigger MRI of the hypothalamic/optic chiasm region - it can be the first sign of an optic chiasm glioma.

options.rationale: Routine screening MRI is not recommended in asymptomatic NF1 children (most OPGs are indolent); MRI is for clinical/ophthalmic abnormality. Would be correct only with visual change or ophthalmic abnormality (Source: AAP NF1 Health Supervision).
Pre-verbal/young children cannot reliably report visual loss; scheduled ophthalmology detects OPG when intervention may preserve vision. (Source: AAP NF1).

Symptomatic optic pathway glioma in NF1 almost always presents under age 7. The standard surveillance approach is annual paediatric ophthalmology with formal visual acuity, colour vision, visual fields (when age-appropriate), and dilated fundus examination through early childhood; MRI is reserved for concerning ophthalmology findings (RCH CPG: NF1; AAP NF1 health supervision).
Standard primary-care vision checks are not adequately sensitive for OPG in NF1; formal paediatric ophthalmology is required. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: RCH CPG: NF1).
CT delivers ionising radiation compounding NF1-associated second-tumour risk and is less sensitive than MRI for OPG. (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia in TSC are treated first with vigabatrin, which has superior efficacy in this subgroup compared with hormonal therapy. Visual field monitoring is essential because of the recognised risk of peripheral visual field constriction (International TSC Consensus 2021).
key_points: Vigabatrin first-line for TSC-related infantile spasms
Hormonal therapy (prednisolone or ACTH) first-line in non-TSC infantile spasms
Early recognition and treatment improves developmental outcome
explanation.pearls: An antenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma is a strong predictor of tuberous sclerosis - early genetic confirmation enables proactive surveillance for spasms, autism, and TAND.

options.rationale: Levetiracetam is not first-line for infantile spasms; RCT evidence supports vigabatrin (in TSC) and hormonal therapy otherwise. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Spasms).

Hormonal therapy is first-line for infantile spasms without identified cause; in TSC-related spasms vigabatrin is preferred (RCT-superior). Would be correct in non-TSC infantile spasms (Source: International TSC Consensus 2021).
Valproate is not first-line and is avoided in young female infants due to teratogenicity; lower efficacy than hormonal/vigabatrin. Would never be correct as first-line (Source: RCH CPG).

In infantile spasms occurring in the context of tuberous sclerosis complex, vigabatrin is the first-line agent and is preferred over ACTH or prednisolone because of superior efficacy in this specific subgroup; visual field monitoring is required because of the recognised risk of peripheral visual field loss (RCH CPG: Infantile spasms; International TSC Consensus Recommendations 2021).
Ketogenic diet is recognised for refractory infantile spasms but not first-line; trial vigabatrin first in TSC. Would be correct after vigabatrin failure (Source: International TSC Consensus).

explanation.summary: Multiple antenatal cardiac rhabdomyomas should trigger evaluation for tuberous sclerosis complex with fetal brain MRI and postnatal molecular testing of TSC1/TSC2. The cardiac lesions themselves usually regress, but the syndromic implications drive longitudinal surveillance for spasms, TAND, renal and pulmonary disease (International TSC Consensus 2021).
key_points: Multiple fetal rhabdomyomas: about 75-80% are associated with TSC
Single rhabdomyoma: TSC association lower but still warrants assessment
Cardiac lesions typically regress; surveillance is for syndromic, not cardiac, indications
explanation.pearls: Postnatal mTOR inhibitor therapy (sirolimus or everolimus) can shrink TSC-related tumours including SEGAs, renal angiomyolipomas, and rhabdomyomas in selected cases.

options.rationale: International TSC consensus: multiple fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas confer about 75-80 percent risk of TSC. Antenatal workup includes fetal MRI for CNS lesions; postnatal: clinical genetics, TSC1/TSC2 sequencing, dermatologic, ophthalmologic, neurology, renal and cardiac surveillance per RCH CPG.
Although lesions regress, multiple rhabdomyomas are strongly associated with TSC and require workup. (Source: International TSC Consensus).
Williams causes supravalvular AS and elfin facies, not cardiac rhabdomyomas. (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
Noonan cardiac involvement is pulmonary valve stenosis and HCM, not rhabdomyomas. (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

Rhabdomyomas typically peak in the third trimester and regress after birth; surgery is reserved for haemodynamic obstruction or refractory arrhythmia. Would be correct only with obstruction or arrhythmia (Source: International TSC Consensus).

explanation.summary: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is a microdeletion disrupting development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and related neural crest derivatives. The features cluster because they share embryological origin: conotruncal cardiac anomalies (interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot) arise from failed neural crest migration into the cardiac outflow tract; hypoparathyroid hypocalcaemia from failed parathyroid development (third/fourth pouch); thymic hypoplasia with T-cell lymphopenia from failed thymic development (third pouch); palatal anomalies and velopharyngeal insufficiency from disrupted pharyngeal arch derivatives; characteristic facies from neural crest contributions to facial mesenchyme. Chromosomal microarray is the first-line genetic test; immunology (T-cell subsets) should run in parallel, and live vaccines are deferred until immune competence is confirmed (RCH CPG: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome).
key_points: Cardiac anomalies: interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot are typical
Defer live attenuated vaccines (e.g. rotavirus, BCG, MMR, varicella) until immune competence confirmed
Calcium, T-cell subset and immunoglobulin assessment guide ongoing care
explanation.pearls: Velopharyngeal insufficiency, hypernasal speech, and learning difficulties often dominate the phenotype in older children with 22q11.2 deletion.

options.rationale: The combination of conotruncal cardiac anomaly (IAA-B), hypocalcaemia with inappropriately low PTH, suspected thymic hypoplasia and characteristic facies is the classic 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) phenotype. CMA is first-line and detects atypical deletion sizes that FISH may miss. Live vaccines must be withheld until cellular immunity is confirmed by T-cell subsets, per Australian Immunisation Handbook and RCH CPG.
22q11.2 deletion is sub-microscopic and is not detected by standard karyotype; CMA or targeted FISH is required. (Source: HGSA).
CH screening does not address the syndromic combination of cardiac anomaly, hypocalcaemia and thymic hypoplasia. Would be correct only with isolated CH (Source: RCH CPG).
Maternal vitamin D deficiency can cause neonatal hypocalcaemia but does not explain cardiac/thymic/facies. Would be correct only with isolated hypocalcaemia (Source: APEG).
Cranial US does not investigate the unifying syndromic diagnosis. Would be correct only with intracranial concern (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis (3-6 weeks, male predominant 4:1, first-born) produces hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, gastric outlet obstruction, and loss of HCl in vomit. The resulting hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis must be corrected before pyloromyotomy.
key_points: Classic age 3-6 weeks, M:F 4:1, first-born predominance
Non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry vomiter, weight loss
VBG: low Cl, low K, high HCO3, alkalotic pH
USS criteria: muscle thickness greater than 3 mm AND channel length greater than 14 mm
Correct fluids and electrolytes BEFORE theatre to avoid post-op apnoea
explanation.pearls: If the infant is alkalotic, do not let them go to theatre. The anaesthetist will hand them back.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Paediatric Fluid and Electrolyte

options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is never a surgical emergency; operating on an alkalotic, hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic infant risks post-anaesthetic apnoea (compensatory CSF alkalosis). (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis

options.rationale: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. AU-recommended targets are Cl over 100, HCO3 under 30, K over 3.5 mmol/L. Ultrasound (muscle thickness over 3 mm, channel length over 14 mm) confirms diagnosis, per RCH CPG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Paediatric Fluid and Electrolyte.
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Paediatric Fluid and Electrolyte

options.rationale: Projectile non-bilious vomiting with palpable olive and hypochloraemic alkalosis is pyloric stenosis, not GORD. Would be correct in mild reflux without electrolyte disturbance (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis

options.rationale: Vomiting is non-bilious; upper GI contrast is for suspected malrotation with bilious vomiting. Would be correct with bilious vomiting (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis

options.rationale: CMPA does not produce hypochloraemic alkalosis or palpable olive. Would be correct with blood-streaked stools and dermatitis (Source: ASCIA).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Pyloric Stenosis

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception (6 months to 2 years, peak 5-9 months) typically follows a viral illness with Peyer patch hypertrophy as the lead point. Triad of colicky pain, vomiting and red-currant stool is the late presentation. Diagnosis is by USS (target/donut sign on cross-section, pseudokidney sign longitudinally) and reduction is by pneumatic (air) enema.
key_points: Peak age 5-9 months; consider pathological lead point if outside 3 months to 5 years (e.g. Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, HSP)
Triad (pain, vomiting, blood per rectum) present in less than 50%
USS first-line; air enema first-line treatment
Air enema success 75-90% in Australia; perforation rate less than 1%
Surgery if peritonism, perforation, failed enema or pathological lead point
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after successful enema reduction occurs in approximately 10% and is usually within 24-48 hours. Discharge planning includes return-precaution counselling.

options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception with red-currant stool requires immediate reduction; delay risks ischaemia and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

Pneumatic (air) enema is the first-line treatment in haemodynamically stable children without peritonism, with success rates of 75-90% in Australian centres. Resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, NG decompression and surgical standby for the 1% risk of perforation during reduction are mandatory (RCH CPG; RANZCR Paediatric Imaging).
