Surgery is for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point; no peritonism here and air enema has higher success/lower morbidity. Would be correct with peritonism or failed enema (Source: RCH CPG).
US is gold-standard; CT adds radiation and delay without changing management. Would be correct only with diagnostic uncertainty on US (Source: RANZCR; RCH CPG).
Conservative observation of confirmed ileocolic intussusception causes progressive ischaemia; reduction within 24 h has best success. Would never be correct in confirmed cases (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. The midgut twists around a narrow mesenteric pedicle and can necrose within hours. Upper GI contrast is the gold-standard investigation. The corrective operation is a Ladd procedure: counter-clockwise detorsion, division of Ladd bands, broadening of the mesentery, appendicectomy, and placement of small bowel on the right.
key_points: Any green vomit in the first month is malrotation/volvulus until excluded
Upper GI contrast = gold standard (DJ flexure should be left of midline at the level of pylorus)
USS whirlpool sign is supportive but not definitive
Operation = Ladd procedure
Time from established volvulus to midgut loss may be as short as 4-6 hours
explanation.pearls: If you are ever the most senior person at the bedside of a green-vomiting neonate, your job is to phone the paediatric surgical centre before you have all the answers.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Upper GI contrast is the gold-standard investigation, showing an abnormal duodeno-jejunal junction position and a corkscrew or beak appearance if volvulus is present. This must occur with surgical standby because volvulus requires laparotomy within minutes to hours to prevent loss of the midgut (RCH CPG; ANZNN).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Watch-and-wait for bilious neonatal vomiting can result in complete midgut loss within 4-6 h of established volvulus. (Source: RCH CPG: Malrotation).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: USS whirlpool sign is supportive but absence does not exclude malrotation; upper GI contrast is definitive. Would be correct only as adjunct, not gold-standard (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Plain AXR may show double-bubble or paucity of distal gas but is insufficient to confirm/exclude malrotation. Would be correct only as initial screen with upper GI to follow (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Meconium ileus is a differential but in a term infant with meconium passed at 18 h, malrotation is more likely. Would be correct only with strong meconium ileus features (CF family history, microcolon suspicion) (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Paediatric appendicitis diagnosis is clinical plus imaging. The Paediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS) stratifies: 1-3 low (discharge with safety net), 4-6 intermediate (USS, observe), 7-10 high (surgical review, USS if needed, appendicectomy). USS is first-line imaging; CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty after non-diagnostic USS.
key_points: PAS components: anorexia, nausea/vomiting, migration, RIF tenderness, cough/percussion/heel-tap tenderness, fever greater than or equal to 38, WCC greater than 10, neutrophils greater than 7.5
USS first-line: appendix diameter greater than 6 mm, non-compressible, hyperaemic, periappendiceal fluid
Laparoscopic appendicectomy with preoperative IV antibiotics (e.g. cefazolin + metronidazole per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Non-visualising USS does not exclude appendicitis; serial exam by paediatric surgical team
CT reserved for diagnostic uncertainty after USS
explanation.pearls: A child who refuses to climb onto the bed or who walks bent over is telling you the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Appendicitis

options.rationale: PAS 7, WCC 14.8, CRP 38 and migratory pain is high-probability appendicitis; discharge is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Appendicitis).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Appendicitis

options.rationale: CT is for diagnostic uncertainty after US or when US is non-visualising in larger children; US is first-line to minimise paediatric radiation. Would be correct only after non-visualising US (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Appendicitis

options.rationale: Ultrasound is first-line paediatric imaging in Australia. A visualised appendix over 6 mm non-compressible with hyperaemia triggers laparoscopic appendicectomy with preoperative ceftriaxone plus metronidazole. Non-visualisation occurs in 20-40 percent and does not exclude appendicitis; serial examination (with or without CT escalation) is the correct next step rather than discharge, per RCH CPG and RANZCR.
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Appendicitis

options.rationale: Antibiotic-only management is a research approach in selected uncomplicated cases, not standard AU practice; confirmation must precede non-operative trial. Would be correct only in research protocols (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Appendicitis

options.rationale: MRI is not routinely available out-of-hours and is not first-line; US gives best speed-to-diagnosis. Would be correct only with CT contraindication and US non-visualising (Source: RANZCR).

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis treated by immediate scrotal exploration. Salvage rates depend on duration of ischaemia: greater than 90% within 6 hours, approximately 50% at 12 hours, less than 10% beyond 24 hours. Bilateral orchidopexy is performed because the bell-clapper deformity is bilateral in approximately 80%.
key_points: Hallmarks: sudden onset pain (often wakes from sleep), high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn
Differentials: epididymo-orchitis (usually febrile, dysuria, gradual onset), torsion of appendix testis (blue dot sign, less severe), incarcerated hernia
Imaging should not delay exploration when the clinical picture is clear
Bilateral orchidopexy at exploration
Salvage rate greater than 90% within 6 hours
explanation.pearls: When the question gives you a 6-hour window and an obvious clinical diagnosis, the wrong answers are usually 'order an imaging test' or 'transfer'.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.rationale: Torsion is clinical; US must not delay exploration. Salvage falls from over 90 percent within 6 h to under 10 percent beyond 24 h. Would never be correct in classic torsion presentation (Source: RCH CPG; USANZ).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.rationale: Picture (high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn, sudden onset, no urinary symptoms) is torsion not epididymo-orchitis. Antibiotics waste ischaemic time. Would be correct only with epididymo-orchitis features (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum

options.rationale: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis warranting immediate surgical exploration. The salvage window is 4-6 hours from onset of pain (currently 4 hours in this scenario). In regional Australia the on-call general surgeon performs exploration rather than transferring; bilateral orchidopexy is standard because the bell-clapper anatomy is bilateral in approximately 80% (RCH CPG; USANZ Position Statement).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Scrotum
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.rationale: Manual detorsion may be attempted while preparing theatre but does not replace surgical exploration and fixation. Discharge without fixation risks re-torsion. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: USANZ).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

options.rationale: Adding 90 min of transfer when local capability exists pushes total ischaemic time over 6 h. Would be correct only when local paediatric surgical capability is unavailable (Source: USANZ).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) Position Statement on Testicular Torsion

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in the neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. The framework of differentials includes malrotation/volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunal/ileal atresia, meconium ileus (CF), Hirschsprung disease, NEC, sepsis-related ileus, and incarcerated inguinal hernia. Plain radiograph plus upper GI contrast distinguish these.
key_points: Double bubble + no distal gas = duodenal atresia (30% trisomy 21)
Double bubble + distal gas = malrotation with partial obstruction
Multiple dilated loops + soap-bubble = meconium ileus (suspect CF)
Pneumatosis = NEC
Free gas / football sign = perforation
explanation.pearls: If the lower abdomen is scaphoid in a vomiting neonate, suspect a high obstruction; if it is distended, suspect a low obstruction.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Soap-bubble (Neuhauser) is meconium ileus, not duodenal atresia or volvulus. Would be correct in meconium ileus (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Pneumatosis and portal venous gas are NEC findings, clinically and radiographically distinct. Would be correct in NEC (Source: RCH CPG: NEC).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Duodenal atresia produces a classic double bubble (dilated stomach and proximal duodenum) with NO distal bowel gas. In contrast, malrotation with volvulus typically shows some distal gas with a paucity, and the diagnostic test is an URGENT upper GI contrast study showing corkscrew or duodenojejunal junction to the right of midline. Recognising the no-distal-gas double bubble as duodenal atresia therefore obviates upper GI contrast and allows direct fluid resuscitation and surgical referral, whereas any uncertainty mandates urgent contrast study, per RCH CPG.
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Free gas indicates perforation, not uncomplicated atresia or volvulus. Would be correct in perforation (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.rationale: Corkscrew is a fluoroscopic finding on upper GI contrast in malrotation with volvulus, not a plain-film sign. Would be correct on upper GI contrast, not on plain film (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease is congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel due to failed migration of neural crest cells. Suspect in any infant with delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, chronic constipation from birth, or failure-to-thrive. Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is the life-threatening complication.
key_points: Meconium passed greater than 48 hours after birth in approximately 90%
Rectal biopsy is gold standard: absent ganglion cells, hypertrophied nerves, positive acetylcholinesterase
Contrast enema: transition zone, reversed recto-sigmoid ratio
Definitive treatment: pull-through procedure (Soave, Swenson, Duhamel)
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis: fever, distension, foul diarrhoea; mortality up to 30% if missed
explanation.pearls: An infant who needs digital stimulation to pass meconium is telling you the diagnosis; do not wait for failure-to-thrive.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.rationale: CF can cause meconium ileus but does not explain chronic explosive PR decompression or current enterocolitis. Would be correct as adjunct workup in suspected CF (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.rationale: Anorectal manometry shows absent RAIR but is technically difficult in young children and supportive only; biopsy is gold-standard. Would be correct as supportive test in older children (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.rationale: Contrast enema may show transition zone and reversed recto-sigmoid ratio but is supportive only; biopsy is required. Empirical laxatives miss the disease. Would be correct as initial radiological assessment, not definitive (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.rationale: Rectal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung disease, demonstrating absent ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses with hypertrophied nerve trunks staining positive for acetylcholinesterase. The current presentation is Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, which carries up to 30% mortality if untreated (RCH CPG; ANZ Paediatric Surgery).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

options.rationale: Calprotectin is for suspected IBD, not Hirschsprung; stool MCS may identify enterocolitis pathogens but does not diagnose aganglionosis. Would be correct in suspected IBD (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hirschsprung Disease

explanation.summary: Necrotising enterocolitis is a multifactorial inflammatory/ischaemic injury to immature gut, peaking at 28-32 weeks corrected age in the second to third postnatal week. Bell staging: I suspected (non-specific), II definite (IIA pneumatosis, IIB pneumatosis + portal gas), III advanced (IIIA critically ill no perforation, IIIB perforation).
key_points: Peak: 28-32 weeks corrected, day 7-14 of life
Risk factors: prematurity, formula feeding, rapid feed advance, hypoxia, sepsis
Pneumatosis intestinalis is pathognomonic
Management: NBM, OG decompression, triple antibiotics, TPN, serial AXR
Surgery for perforation, fixed dilated loop, abdominal wall erythema/discolouration, or deterioration
explanation.pearls: A shiny abdomen with bluish discolouration is a late sign of full-thickness bowel wall ischaemia and is a call to the operating room.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.rationale: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes must commence immediately on NEC suspicion. Waiting for cultures delays critical therapy. (Source: RCH CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.rationale: Established NEC mandates immediate NBM; continuing feeds worsens ischaemic injury. Probiotics are prophylactic in some units but no role in established NEC. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.rationale: Surgery is for perforation (free gas, fixed loop, deterioration despite medical management). Bell IIB without perforation is medical with surgical standby. Would be correct only with perforation or clinical deterioration (Source: RCH CPG NEC).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.rationale: This is Bell stage IIB NEC (pneumatosis with portal venous gas, no perforation). Management is medical: NBM, OG decompression, triple antibiotics (penicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole per Therapeutic Guidelines), TPN, serial AXR every 6 hours for 48-72 hours to detect perforation. Surgery is indicated for perforation (Bell IIIB) or clinical deterioration (RCH CPG NEC; ANZNN).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Necrotising Enterocolitis

options.rationale: Peritoneal drainage is a salvage technique for unstable ELBW with perforation; not a substitute for antibiotics or definitive laparotomy. Would be correct only as salvage in unstable ELBW (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Button battery in the oesophagus causes alkaline electrolysis injury within 15-30 minutes and can perforate within 2 hours. Australian guidelines (RCH, Poisons Information Centre, ACCC) recommend immediate endoscopic removal, honey every 10 minutes in children over 12 months while awaiting endoscopy, and notification of PIC on 13 11 26.
key_points: Double-rim (halo) sign on AP radiograph distinguishes battery from coin
Step-off sign on lateral
Oesophageal lodgement = endoscopic removal within 2 hours
Honey 10 mL every 10 minutes (children over 12 months) reduces injury severity
Avoid in infants under 12 months (botulism); avoid if airway compromised
explanation.pearls: Coins are smooth and round and easy to ignore. The double rim on the AP film and step-off on the lateral are how you do not miss the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion
ACCC Product Safety Australia - Button Batteries

options.rationale: Honey contraindication is for under-12 months (botulism risk); this child is 22 months. Helicopter is faster than 2-h road transfer for an oesophageal battery. Would be correct only under 12 months (Source: RCH CPG; NHMRC Infant Feeding).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

options.rationale: Any oesophageal button battery is a surgical emergency regardless of current symptoms; delay risks perforation, TOF and aorto-oesophageal fistula. (Source: RCH CPG; ACCC).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

options.rationale: Induced emesis is contraindicated (aspiration, further oesophageal injury); ipecac is no longer recommended by PIC for any ingestion. (Source: PIC).
Watchful waiting is unsafe for oesophageal battery; 4-h delay pushes beyond 2-h necrosis threshold. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

options.rationale: Button battery in the oesophagus is a time-critical emergency: tissue injury begins within 15-30 minutes and full-thickness necrosis can occur within 2 hours. The Australian Resuscitation Council and RCH CPG recommend honey (or sucralfate) every 10 minutes in children over 12 months with no airway compromise to coat the battery and reduce alkaline injury, while urgent endoscopic removal is arranged. Helicopter retrieval is faster than road (RCH CPG; Poisons Information Centre).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Button Battery Ingestion

explanation.summary: Distinguishing GORD from CMPA in a vomiting infant requires assessment for red flags: blood/mucus in stool, eczema, atopic family history, perianal excoriation, and weight faltering favour CMPA. Uncomplicated GORD without red flags is managed with feed positioning, thickeners and reassurance.
key_points: Non-IgE CMPA: bloody/mucousy stool, eczema, faltering growth, no anaphylactic features; skin-prick/IgE negative
IgE CMPA: urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis within 2 hours of ingestion; skin-prick/IgE positive
First-line formula: extensively hydrolysed (eHF) for 2-4 weeks
Amino-acid formula for severe disease or eHF non-response
Re-challenge to confirm diagnosis; most resolve by 3-5 years
explanation.pearls: Bloody mucus + eczema + crossed centiles in a vomiting infant is CMPA until proven otherwise. PPIs do not fix that.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Cow's Milk Protein Allergy

options.rationale: Blood/mucus in stool, eczema, atopic family history and faltering growth are red flags for CMPA, not GORD. PPI trials should not delay elimination diet. Would be correct in uncomplicated GORD without atopy or blood (Source: ASCIA).

Suspected non-IgE-mediated CMPA in a formula-fed infant is managed by a trial of extensively hydrolysed formula (eHF) for 2-4 weeks, with reassessment of symptoms and growth, and a re-challenge to confirm. Amino-acid formula is reserved for severe or eHF-non-responsive cases. Diagnosis is by elimination and re-challenge, not allergy testing (ASCIA; RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Cow's Milk Protein Allergy

options.rationale: Soy is not first-line under 6 months (phytoestrogens) and 10-15 percent CMPA cross-reacts. Extensively hydrolysed formula is first-line. Would be correct in older infants after EHF failure (Source: ASCIA; NHMRC).

Non-IgE-mediated CMPA (the likely subtype) is not detected by IgE/SPT. Diagnosis is by elimination and re-challenge. Would be correct only in suspected IgE-mediated (immediate reactions) (Source: ASCIA).
Diluting formula reduces caloric/electrolyte intake and worsens faltering growth; gripe water has no role in CMPA. (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: The TEN-4 FACES rule (Pierce 2010, validated 2021) identifies sentinel bruising patterns: bruising on Torso, Ear, or Neck in any child 4 years or younger, OR any bruising in an infant 4 months or younger, OR bruising in the FACES regions (Frenulum, Auricular, Cheek, Eye, Sclera). Workup: skeletal survey, CT head, fundoscopy, FBC, coagulation, LFTs, lipase, urine drug screen, social/safety assessment.
key_points: Any bruise in a pre-mobile infant requires NAI workup
TEN-4 FACES: T (torso) E (ear) N (neck) under 4 yr; any bruise under 4 months; FACES regions
Frenular tear in pre-mobile infant is classic NAI sentinel
Mandatory notification to statutory child protection service (DCJ NSW or jurisdictional equivalent)
Mandatory reporters have legal immunity for good-faith reports
explanation.pearls: If a baby cannot roll, they cannot bruise themselves. Document the absence of a developmental match between mechanism and injury.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Child Abuse
Australian Institute of Family Studies - Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect

options.rationale: Mandatory reporting requires notification to statutory child protection service (DCJ in NSW, DFFH in VIC, etc); police notification is additional not substitute. (Source: AIFS).
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies - Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect

options.rationale: Any bruise in a pre-mobile infant is a red flag; TEN-4 FACES mandates investigation. Discharge without workup misses ~30 percent of subsequent severe abuse. (Source: RCH CPG; AIFS).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Child Abuse
Australian Institute of Family Studies - Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect

options.rationale: Coagulation studies are part of workup but cannot replace skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy and notification. Bleeding disorders and NAI are not mutually exclusive. Would never be correct alone (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Child Abuse

options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury for non-accidental injury (TEN-4 FACES rule: bruising on Torso, Ears, Neck, or any bruising in a child 4 months or younger). Multiple bruises plus a frenular tear plus an unwitnessed mechanism plus a sibling with a suspicious historic fracture meet threshold for mandatory reporting and a full medical workup including skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy and coagulation panel (RCH CPG Child Abuse; AIFS; DCJ NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Child Abuse
Australian Institute of Family Studies - Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect

options.rationale: Mandatory reporting acts on reasonable belief, not certainty; waiting risks further injury and breaches legal threshold. (Source: AIFS).
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies - Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect

explanation.summary: Gillick competence (or mature minor doctrine, as applied in Australia after Marion's Case) allows a young person to consent to treatment without parental involvement if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully appreciate what is proposed. Confidentiality is the default; it is breached only when risk of significant harm cannot be otherwise managed.
key_points: Mature minor doctrine: capacity-based, not age-based
HEEADSSS screen: Home, Education/Employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Mood, Safety
Confidentiality is the default; explain limits at the start of every adolescent consultation
Limits: risk of significant harm to self or others, including coercion, grooming, or significant age gap
Document the competence assessment in detail
explanation.pearls: Explain confidentiality and its limits at the start of every adolescent consultation. That sentence does more for engagement than anything else you say.

sources.label: RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus: Adolescent and Young Adult Health
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: GPs are appropriately trained to prescribe contraception to competent adolescents; delay exposes the patient to unintended pregnancy. (Source: RACGP; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus: Adolescent and Young Adult Health
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Mandating parental involvement breaches the right to confidential health care and drives patients away. Gillick competence allows confidential prescribing. Would be correct only if competence not established (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus: Adolescent and Young Adult Health

options.rationale: NSW age of consent is 16, but consensual sex between two 15-year-olds of similar maturity without exploitation/coercion does not automatically meet mandatory reporting threshold. Would be correct with significant age gap or exploitation (Source: NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide).
source_refs: RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus: Adolescent and Young Adult Health

options.rationale: Disclosure to parents without consent breaches confidentiality; reserved for risk-of-significant-harm scenarios the patient cannot/will not address. Would never be correct as routine (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus: Adolescent and Young Adult Health

options.rationale: Under the High Court of Australia decision in Marion's Case (1992), adapting the UK Gillick principle, a mature minor with sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully comprehend a proposed treatment may consent without parental involvement. Contraception in a 15-year-old in a non-coercive relationship of similar age, with no safety concerns, meets the standard for confidential prescribing (RACGP; AMA Code of Ethics).
source_refs: RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus: Adolescent and Young Adult Health

explanation.summary: Paediatric IBD diagnosis follows the ESPGHAN revised Porto criteria: ileocolonoscopy + upper GI endoscopy + small bowel imaging (MR enterography preferred). Faecal calprotectin greater than 250 microg/g has high sensitivity for mucosal inflammation and is used to triage who needs endoscopy. Induction in Crohn is exclusive enteral nutrition or corticosteroids; biologics (infliximab/adalimumab) for severe or fistulising disease per eviQ.
key_points: Faecal calprotectin greater than 250 microg/g = likely organic inflammation
Porto criteria: ileocolonoscopy + OGD + small bowel imaging
MR enterography preferred over CT in children
Crohn induction: exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) 6-8 weeks, mucosal healing in approx 80%
Biologics per eviQ for moderate-severe Crohn, fistulising disease, or steroid-dependent disease
explanation.pearls: Perianal disease in an adolescent + mouth ulcers + growth faltering is Crohn until proven otherwise. Look in the mouth and look at the perianal skin.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
eviQ Paediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease Protocols
ESPGHAN Revised Porto Criteria for Paediatric IBD

options.rationale: Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction for Crohn's, but is started AFTER endoscopic confirmation, not as substitute. Would be correct after diagnosis confirmed (Source: RCH CPG IBD; ESPGHAN).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
eviQ Paediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease Protocols

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics without endoscopy delay diagnosis and risk masking activity; stool studies are already negative. (Source: RCH CPG IBD).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Inflammatory Bowel Disease

options.rationale: Capsule endoscopy is for suspected isolated small bowel disease after negative ileocolonoscopy plus small bowel imaging; contraindicated where stricture risk exists. Would be correct only after negative initial endoscopy and imaging (Source: ESPGHAN).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
ESPGHAN Revised Porto Criteria for Paediatric IBD

options.rationale: MR enterography is preferred over CT in paediatric IBD to minimise lifetime radiation. Would be correct only if MR unavailable and urgent imaging needed (Source: RANZCR; eviQ).
source_refs: eviQ Paediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease Protocols

options.rationale: The clinical picture (perianal fistula, mouth ulcers, growth failure, raised inflammatory markers, faecal calprotectin greater than 250 microg/g, family history) is highly suggestive of paediatric Crohn disease. The Porto criteria recommend ileocolonoscopy plus upper GI endoscopy with biopsies plus small-bowel imaging (MR enterography preferred over CT for radiation reduction) for diagnosis and disease mapping (RCH CPG IBD; eviQ Paediatric IBD; ESPGHAN Porto criteria).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
eviQ Paediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease Protocols
ESPGHAN Revised Porto Criteria for Paediatric IBD

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease in children: screen with anti-tTG IgA plus total IgA (false negative if IgA deficient). Positive serology in a symptomatic child warrants duodenal biopsy via paediatric gastroenterology to confirm Marsh-Oberhuber 2 or higher histology. The ESPGHAN no-biopsy pathway requires anti-tTG IgA greater than 10x upper limit on one sample, positive EMA on a separate sample, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positive, and a specialist setting. Do not start a gluten-free diet before diagnosis is secured.
key_points: Screen: anti-tTG IgA + total IgA; if IgA deficient use IgG-based serology
Positive serology + symptoms = paediatric gastroenterology referral for biopsy
ESPGHAN no-biopsy pathway: anti-tTG IgA greater than 10x ULN + EMA positive on second sample + HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positive
Maintain gluten in diet until diagnosis confirmed
Screen first-degree relatives; monitor growth, iron, vitamin D, calcium, thyroid function and bone density
explanation.pearls: The most common reason a coeliac diagnosis becomes uncertain is starting the gluten-free diet too early. Wait for the biopsy or for the full no-biopsy criteria.

sources.label: ESPGHAN Guidelines for Diagnosing Coeliac Disease 2020

options.rationale: Australian and ESPGHAN guidelines require duodenal biopsy in symptomatic children with positive serology before commencing a gluten-free diet, unless the ESPGHAN no-biopsy pathway is fully met (anti-tTG IgA greater than 10x upper limit of normal AND positive EMA on a separate sample AND HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positive) and this is delivered in a specialist paediatric gastroenterology setting with full counselling. Starting a gluten-free diet before biopsy can invalidate the histology if the family later wants definitive diagnosis. First-degree relative screening is recommended (RACGP; Coeliac Australia; ESPGHAN).
source_refs: ESPGHAN Guidelines for Diagnosing Coeliac Disease 2020

options.rationale: Initiating GFD before biopsy in Australia is not recommended outside the ESPGHAN no-biopsy pathway with full criteria met. Would be correct only under specialist no-biopsy pathway with two-sample criteria (Source: ESPGHAN; RACGP).

Withdrawing gluten before biopsy makes diagnostic biopsy unreliable; gluten challenge is for prior inadequate evidence or diagnostic uncertainty. Would be correct only after prior GFD started without diagnosis (Source: ESPGHAN).
source_refs: ESPGHAN Guidelines for Diagnosing Coeliac Disease 2020

options.rationale: Symptomatic child with strongly positive serology, positive EMA and faltering growth must not have diagnosis delayed; treatment drives growth recovery. (Source: RACGP).
IgG anti-gliadin has been superseded by anti-tTG/EMA; faecal fat is rarely used in modern coeliac diagnosis. (Source: RACGP; ESPGHAN).
source_refs: ESPGHAN Guidelines for Diagnosing Coeliac Disease 2020

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated paediatric vaso-occlusive crisis is managed with timely strong opioid analgesia (target within 30 minutes), multimodal paracetamol and NSAID, maintenance IV fluids, and supplemental oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 95% (RCH CPG: Sickle cell disease).
key_points: Strong opioid within 30 minutes for severe sickle pain
Maintenance fluids, not boluses, in uncomplicated VOC
Oxygen only if SpO2 < 95% to avoid masking acute chest syndrome
Reassess every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours
Screen for triggers: dehydration, infection, hypoxia, cold
explanation.pearls: Bolus fluids and high-flow oxygen in a normoxic child with sickle pain can both precipitate acute chest syndrome - give what is needed, not more.

sources.label: BSH guideline: Acute management of sickle cell pain

options.rationale: Oral NSAID monotherapy is inadequate for severe (9/10) sickle pain; strong opioid within 30 min alongside multimodal is required. Would be correct only for mild pain (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease).

Bolus fluids are not first-line in uncomplicated VOC and risk pulmonary oedema/ACS; maintenance fluids do not replace timely opioid. Would be correct only for confirmed hypovolaemia (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: BSH guideline: Acute management of sickle cell pain

options.rationale: Severe vaso-occlusive crisis requires a strong opioid (IV or intranasal) within 30 minutes, combined with paracetamol and an NSAID if no contraindication, plus maintenance (not bolus) fluids. Oxygen is given only if SpO2 falls below 95% (RCH CPG: Sickle cell disease).
He is afebrile with no infective focus; empirical antibiotics are for sickle patients at 38 degC or higher. Would be correct with fever 38 or higher (Source: RCH CPG).
Exchange transfusion is for ACS, stroke, multi-organ failure or refractory priapism, not uncomplicated VOC. Would be correct in those indications (Source: BSH; RCH CPG).
source_refs: BSH guideline: Acute management of sickle cell pain

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is defined by a new radiographic infiltrate plus fever or respiratory signs in a child with sickle cell disease and is the leading cause of sickle mortality. Management runs in parallel: antibiotics with atypical cover, oxygen, incentive spirometry, two-thirds maintenance fluids, and early haematology-led transfusion (RCH CPG: Sickle cell disease).
key_points: New infiltrate plus fever, hypoxia, or new respiratory signs in a sickle child defines ACS
Empirical antibiotics: third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) plus a macrolide for atypicals
Oxygen to keep SpO2 above 94 percent; incentive spirometry hourly while awake to prevent atelectasis
Fluids at two-thirds maintenance - boluses worsen pulmonary oedema
Simple transfusion if Hb under 90 g/L; exchange transfusion if severe hypoxia, multilobar disease, or no improvement within hours
explanation.pearls: Why sickle predisposes to ACS: in the pulmonary microvasculature, low alveolar PO2 (from atelectasis, splinting, or a viral or atypical lower respiratory infection) drives HbS polymerisation, sickled red cells adhere to activated pulmonary endothelium causing local vaso-occlusion, this worsens regional V/Q mismatch and further deoxygenates passing blood, and the cycle accelerates. Two additional triggers stack on top: fat embolism from bone-marrow infarction during a vaso-occlusive crisis releases free fatty acids that injure pulmonary endothelium, and atypicals (particularly Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae) drive cold-agglutinin haemolysis and direct endothelial activation that propagates sickling. Post-admission ACS classically develops 24-72 hours into a vaso-occlusive crisis admission because chest-wall splinting and opioids drive hypoventilation and atelectasis - prevent it with hourly incentive spirometry while awake.

sources.label: BSH guideline: Management of acute chest syndrome

options.rationale: New infiltrate plus fever, hypoxia and respiratory signs in sickle cell disease defines acute chest syndrome. Management is empirical antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin plus macrolide), oxygen to keep SpO2 above 94%, incentive spirometry, judicious fluids, and urgent transfusion (simple or exchange) directed by haematology (RCH CPG: Sickle cell disease; BSH guideline).
source_refs: BSH guideline: Management of acute chest syndrome

options.rationale: Opioid titration alone misses ACS diagnosis; excess sedation worsens hypoventilation and atelectasis. Would never be correct in evolving ACS (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease).
Fluid boluses are contraindicated in ACS (worsen pulmonary oedema); fluids should be cut to 2/3 maintenance and treatment escalated. Would never be correct in evolving ACS (Source: RCH CPG).

No wheeze or known asthma to support salbutamol as primary; ward-level observation without antibiotics or transfusion planning is inappropriate. Would be correct only in confirmed bronchospasm (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: BSH guideline: Management of acute chest syndrome

options.rationale: CTPA is for genuinely suspected PE; new infiltrate, fever and hypoxia after sickle admission is diagnostic of ACS. Would be correct only with suspicion of PE not ACS (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease is a sudden drop in haemoglobin with a suppressed reticulocyte count (typically < 50 x10^9/L), most often triggered by parvovirus B19 which transiently halts erythropoiesis. It is distinguished from sequestration (sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemia, reticulocytosis) by the reticulocyte count and spleen size (RCH CPG: Sickle cell disease).
key_points: Aplastic: suppressed retics + unchanged spleen + parvovirus contact
Sequestration: spleen enlarged 2+ cm + shock + reticulocytosis
Hyperhaemolysis: post-transfusion + jaundice + brisk retics
Manage aplastic crisis with transfusion and parvovirus isolation
Isolate from pregnant staff/family until resolution
explanation.pearls: A fifth-disease rash in a sibling is the classic clue - the index child may never have been febrile.

sources.label: BSH guideline: Transfusion in sickle cell disease

options.rationale: Splenic sequestration has sudden spleen enlargement over 2 cm from baseline, brisk reticulocyte response and hypovolaemia signs; this child has unchanged spleen and SUPPRESSED reticulocytes. Would be correct with rising spleen and reticulocytosis (Source: RCH CPG).

Hyperhaemolysis has jaundice, dark urine, raised LDH/bilirubin and brisk reticulocytosis 1-3 weeks post-transfusion; last transfusion was 4 months ago and retics suppressed. Would be correct only within 1-3 weeks of transfusion (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: BSH guideline: Transfusion in sickle cell disease

options.rationale: Iron deficiency develops over weeks/months and would not drop Hb by half in 24 h; retics in chronic IDA are typically normal not profoundly suppressed. Would be correct only in chronic gradual anaemia (Source: RCH CPG).

A rapid fall in haemoglobin with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count (here 12 against a baseline of approximately 300 x10^9/L) in a child with chronic haemolysis is diagnostic of an aplastic crisis. Parvovirus B19, the cause of fifth disease (the brother's malar rash), suppresses erythroid precursors for 7-10 days and is the typical precipitant (RCH CPG: Sickle cell disease; eviQ).
Marrow infarction causes severe pain not asymptomatic anaemia, with leucocytosis and appropriate reticulocyte response. Would be correct only with bone pain and leucocytosis (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Acute childhood ITP with cutaneous-only bleeding is managed expectantly because around 80% of children remit within 6 months. Pharmacotherapy (IVIG or steroids) is for moderate mucosal bleeding; platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage (RCH CPG: ITP).
key_points: Skin-only bleeding + platelets > 10 = watchful waiting
Wet purpura / mucosal bleeding = consider IVIG or steroids
Life-threatening bleed = IVIG + methylprednisolone + platelet transfusion + surgical input
Bone marrow before steroids (to exclude ALL) if treating
Safety advice: avoid contact sports, NSAIDs and IM injections
explanation.pearls: The platelet count predicts bleeding poorly - the wet vs dry purpura distinction is the better guide to therapy.

options.rationale: IVIG is for ITP with significant mucosal bleeding or pre-procedure; cutaneous-only does not meet threshold. Would be correct with wet purpura or active mucosal bleeding (Source: RCH CPG: ITP).

Typical acute childhood ITP with platelets above 10 x10^9/L, only cutaneous bleeding (petechiae and skin bruising) and no mucosal or internal bleeding is managed with watchful waiting, written advice on activity restriction and bleeding red flags, and outpatient paediatric follow-up with a repeat FBC at 7-10 days (RCH CPG: ITP).

Corticosteroids require bone marrow exam to exclude leukaemia and are for moderate bleeding, not skin-only. Would be correct after BMA excludes leukaemia and bleeding is moderate (Source: ASH 2019 ITP).
Platelet transfusion in ITP is rapidly consumed by autoantibodies; reserved for life-threatening bleeding such as ICH. Would be correct only in life-threatening bleeding (Source: RCH CPG).

BMA is only needed if atypical features (HSM, lymphadenopathy, multi-line cytopenias, abnormal film) or before steroids; classic ITP picture does not need it. Would be correct only with atypical features (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Children with ITP who have wet purpura (mucosal bleeding such as epistaxis lasting > 15 minutes, oral bullae, haematuria or GI bleed) warrant pharmacotherapy. IVIG produces the most rapid platelet rise and is preferred over corticosteroids when bone marrow examination has not been done, because steroids can partially treat ALL and mask the diagnosis (RCH CPG: ITP).
key_points: Wet purpura = treat; dry purpura = observe
IVIG 0.8 g/kg raises platelets within 24-48 hours
Steroids work but require marrow first to exclude ALL
Tranexamic acid useful as mucosal adjunct, not monotherapy
Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: If the bone marrow looks normal you can use either - but the marrow has to come first for steroids.

options.rationale: Wet purpura with prolonged active epistaxis crosses threshold for inpatient pharmacotherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP).

Significant mucosal (wet) bleeding warrants treatment. IVIG raises the platelet count fastest (within 24-48 hours) and avoids the need for marrow examination before steroids in typical ITP, and is the preferred first-line option in Australian paediatric guidance for moderate non-life-threatening bleeding (RCH CPG: ITP; ASH 2019 ITP guideline).
Transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed by anti-platelet antibodies; reserved for life-threatening bleeding (ICH, major GI). Would be correct only in life-threatening bleeding (Source: RCH CPG).
TXA is a useful adjunct for mucosal bleeding but does not raise platelets; inadequate as monotherapy at this severity. Would be correct as adjunct to IVIG (Source: RCH CPG).
Splenectomy is for chronic refractory ITP after 12+ months of failed medical therapy. Would be correct only in refractory chronic ITP (Source: ASH 2019).

explanation.summary: Life-threatening bleeding in ITP, especially intracranial haemorrhage, is treated with combined platelet transfusion, IV methylprednisolone and IVIG, alongside specialty (neurosurgical / surgical) input. Each component addresses a different mechanism: rapid (transfusion), reticuloendothelial blockade (IVIG) and immunosuppression (steroid) (RCH CPG: ITP).
key_points: Triple therapy: platelets + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG
Add tranexamic acid as adjunct if no contraindication
PICU / HDU admission and urgent neurosurgical review
Repeat imaging and FBC at 6-12 hours
Reverse any antiplatelet or anticoagulant exposure
explanation.pearls: ICH is rare (< 1%) in childhood ITP but the case fatality is high - do not wait for the platelet count to rise on IVIG alone.

options.rationale: IVIG monotherapy is inadequate in life-threatening ICH (24-48 h to raise platelets); concurrent platelet transfusion and high-dose corticosteroid are needed. Would never be correct in ICH (Source: RCH CPG: ITP).
Platelet transfusion alone is rapidly consumed; IVIG and methylprednisolone are required adjuncts. Would never be correct alone in ICH (Source: RCH CPG).
TXA may be cautious adjunct but is not first-line for ICH in ITP and does not raise platelets. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: ASH 2019).

Life-threatening bleeding (including intracranial haemorrhage) in ITP is treated with triple therapy: platelet transfusion (transient but immediate rise), IVIG 1 g/kg to block reticuloendothelial clearance, and high-dose IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg, max 1 g), with urgent neurosurgical review and PICU/HDU admission (RCH CPG: ITP; ASH 2019 ITP guideline).
Emergency splenectomy is not first-line response to ITP-related ICH; reserved for chronic refractory disease. Would never be correct as emergency intervention (Source: ASH 2019).

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia in paediatric oncology is a single temperature 38.0 degC or higher with neutrophils below 0.5 x10^9/L (or expected to fall below). It is a medical emergency requiring empirical IV antibiotics within 60 minutes of arrival (RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia).
key_points: Single T >=38.0 degC + ANC < 0.5 x10^9/L = febrile neutropenia
Door-to-antibiotic target: 60 minutes
Central line bundle: peripheral + line cultures
Antipyretic at home does not exclude the diagnosis
Some protocols also accept sustained 38.0 degC for 1 hour
explanation.pearls: If the child is on chemotherapy and warm to touch, start the FN pathway - do not wait for confirmation.

options.rationale: Australian paediatric oncology guidance (RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia, eviQ) recommends empirical anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime) within 60 minutes of arrival for low-risk well-appearing febrile neutropenia. Empirical vancomycin is reserved for shock, suspected central-line infection, severe mucositis or skin/soft tissue infection, or known resistant Gram-positive colonisation, per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia and eviQ Paediatric Fever and neutropenia.

Ceftriaxone has inadequate anti-pseudomonal activity for empirical paediatric febrile neutropenia; an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or meropenem) is required, per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia.

Empirical vancomycin and dual Gram-negative cover are not routine; the line is uninflamed and the patient is haemodynamically stable. Routine triple cover increases adverse effects without outcome benefit, per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia and eviQ.
Empirical antibiotics within 60 minutes are mandatory; waiting for repeat FBC or culture results delays treatment of a potentially life-threatening sepsis, per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia.

Oral outpatient regimens for low-risk febrile neutropenia are an option only after a period of inpatient observation, stratification, and confirmed culture-negative trajectory in selected protocols; discharge from the ED on oral antibiotics at first contact is unsafe, per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia.

explanation.summary: Septic shock in febrile neutropenia mandates a parallel bundle: paired peripheral and central line cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics (escalated to meropenem plus vancomycin when there is line involvement, recent piperacillin-tazobactam exposure, or shock) and 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, all delivered within the first hour (RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia; ANZICS).
key_points: Door-to-antibiotic 60 minutes regardless of culture results
Paired peripheral + line cultures before first dose
Add vancomycin for line involvement, shock, mucositis or MRSA
Escalate to meropenem if recent pip-tazo or instability
Line removal decided later, after stabilisation and culture data
explanation.pearls: If they look septic and have a line, peripheral access is more important than removing the line in the first 60 minutes.

options.rationale: Antibiotic delivery within 60 min takes priority over line removal; removal is decided later with oncology. Would never be correct as first step (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia).

She has septic shock (hypotension, prolonged capillary refill, lactate 3.6) with suspected central line infection, recent piperacillin-tazobactam exposure and profound neutropenia. The bundle is paired peripheral and line cultures, broad escalation to meropenem with vancomycin to cover line-associated Gram-positives, and a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, within 60 minutes (RCH CPG; ANZICS).
Empirical antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging; CT for typhlitis is after stabilisation only with abdominal signs. (Source: RCH CPG).

Pip-taz was given 8 days ago for similar episode and child is in shock with line erythema; cover should be broadened to meropenem plus vancomycin. Would be correct only on first presentation without prior exposure or line concern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
G-CSF is not part of the acute septic resuscitation bundle and has no role in the first hour. Would be correct only as later adjunct (Source: eviQ).

explanation.summary: Laboratory tumour lysis syndrome in high-risk leukaemia (high WCC, bulky disease, raised LDH) is managed with hyperhydration without potassium, rasburicase when urate is elevated or risk is high, frequent biochemistry and urine output monitoring, and early PICU and nephrology involvement. Induction is delayed until biochemistry is controlled (eviQ Tumour lysis syndrome).
key_points: TLS labs: urate, K, phosphate up; Ca down; LDH high
High risk: WCC > 100, bulky disease, LDH > 2x ULN
Rasburicase replaces allopurinol when urate already elevated
Hyperhydration without K; avoid bicarbonate
G6PD screen before rasburicase (haemolysis risk)
explanation.pearls: Once urate, K and phosphate move together, you are behind - treat the next hour, not the next day.

options.rationale: Allopurinol blocks new urate but does not lower existing urate; adding potassium to fluids in established TLS is dangerous. Would be correct for prophylaxis pre-induction, not for established TLS (Source: eviQ TLS).

Laboratory tumour lysis syndrome is established (urate, potassium, phosphate all elevated with corrected calcium low) at high risk (WCC 180, bulky disease, LDH > 2x normal). Australian guidance recommends rasburicase rather than allopurinol when urate is already elevated or risk is high, continued hyperhydration without potassium, frequent monitoring and early PICU/nephrology involvement (eviQ; Coiffier consensus).

Calcium is for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or ECG instability; routine calcium can precipitate calcium phosphate crystals with high phosphate. Would be correct only with hypocalcaemic tetany/arrhythmia (Source: eviQ).
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended (calcium phosphate precipitation, xanthine deposition); rasburicase superseded this. (Source: eviQ; Coiffier consensus).
Fluid restriction worsens TLS nephropathy; high-risk TLS needs aggressive hyperhydration with strict UO monitoring. (Source: eviQ).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency that fails an adequate oral iron trial of 3 months in a child with falling growth, loose stools or bloating should prompt coeliac screening with anti-tTG IgA and total IgA. Other reasons to investigate include suspected occult bleeding, malabsorption symptoms, or high-risk ethnicity for haemoglobinopathy (RCH CPG: Iron deficiency; RCH CPG: Coeliac disease).
key_points: Investigate iron deficiency if: failed oral trial, faltering growth, GI symptoms, atypical features
First-line for coeliac: anti-tTG IgA + total IgA, on gluten
Confirm coeliac with biopsy (or no-biopsy pathway if criteria met)
Consider H. pylori, occult blood, electrophoresis as situation dictates
Reassess adherence and dose before labelling as treatment-failure
explanation.pearls: Falling centiles plus persistent iron deficiency is coeliac disease until disproven.

sources.label: RCH CPG: GI bleeding in children

options.rationale: Failed 3-month oral iron trial with persistently low ferritin, falling centiles and intermittent loose stools; continuing without investigation misses underlying coeliac. (Source: RCH CPG).
Endoscopy is the test if serology positive or per no-biopsy pathway; not first investigation. Would be correct after positive serology (Source: ESPGHAN).

Iron deficiency that does not respond to an adequate oral iron trial in the setting of falling growth centiles, intermittent loose stools and bloating is a red flag for coeliac disease; coeliac antibody testing (anti-tTG IgA with total IgA to exclude IgA deficiency) is the recommended first-line investigation while the child remains on a gluten-containing diet (RCH CPG: Coeliac disease; RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).
Electrophoresis is for unexplained microcytosis once iron is normal; her ferritin remains low. Would be correct only after iron repletion fails (Source: RCH CPG).
Meckel scan is for painless overt GI bleed; absent here. Would be correct with painless overt bleed (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: GI bleeding in children

explanation.summary: Red flags for malignant lymphadenopathy in children and adolescents are: node > 2 cm, supraclavicular location, persistence > 4-6 weeks, rubbery non-tender consistency, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss > 10%), hepatosplenomegaly, mediastinal mass, elevated LDH or ESR. Any combination warrants urgent referral for excisional biopsy (RCH CPG: Lymphadenopathy).
key_points: Supraclavicular node = biopsy regardless of other features
Size > 2 cm + > 4-6 weeks duration = biopsy
B symptoms: fever > 38, night sweats, unintentional weight loss > 10%
Excisional biopsy, not FNA, for suspected lymphoma
Send LDH, ESR, CXR for mediastinal mass while awaiting biopsy
explanation.pearls: An adolescent supraclavicular node is malignant until proven otherwise - do not start antibiotics and wait.

sources.label: Cancer Council Optimal Care Pathway: Hodgkin lymphoma

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are for tender/fluctuant/rapidly enlarging nodes with bacterial features; none here, and a trial delays biopsy. Would be correct with bacterial features (Source: RCH CPG: Lymphadenopathy).

US may help characterise but does not diagnose lymphoma; 6-week observation with red flags (size, supraclavicular, B symptoms, raised LDH) is unsafe. Would never be correct with red flags (Source: RCH CPG).
FNA cannot reliably diagnose/subtype lymphoma (architecture required); excisional biopsy is standard. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: eviQ).
source_refs: Cancer Council Optimal Care Pathway: Hodgkin lymphoma

options.rationale: Infective serology is reasonable for atypical reactive lymphadenopathy but does not justify deferring biopsy when red flags are present. Would be correct in parallel only (Source: RCH CPG).

She has multiple red flags for lymphoma: supraclavicular location, node larger than 2 cm, persistent for more than 4-6 weeks, non-tender, plus B symptoms (night sweats, unintentional weight loss) and elevated LDH and ESR. Australian and international guidance recommend urgent referral for excisional biopsy rather than FNA, plus staging (CT/PET) coordinated by oncology (RCH CPG: Lymphadenopathy; eviQ; Cancer Council OCP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Optimal Care Pathway: Hodgkin lymphoma

explanation.summary: SCID is a paediatric emergency. Red flags include severe lymphopenia (ALC under age-specific lower limit, often below 2.5 x10^9/L), failure to thrive, opportunistic infection (PCP, CMV, persistent candidiasis), absent thymic shadow, and family history of early unexplained infant death. Urgent immunology referral, reverse isolation, withholding live vaccines, and irradiated CMV-negative leucodepleted blood products are time-critical; haematopoietic stem cell transplant in the first 3.5 months of life carries a markedly better prognosis (ASCIA: SCID).
key_points: Severe lymphopenia at any age: think SCID and check subsets
Withhold live vaccines: rotavirus, BCG, MMR, varicella
Use irradiated CMV-negative leucodepleted blood products
Early HSCT before 3.5 months improves survival markedly
Family history of unexplained infant infectious death is a red flag
explanation.pearls: If a 4-month-old has had Pneumocystis pneumonia, the diagnosis is SCID until immunology proves otherwise.

options.rationale: Persistent candidiasis is the surface feature of likely SCID; fluconazole alone misses the underlying immunodeficiency and time-critical transplant pathway. (Source: ASCIA Primary Immunodeficiency).

The presentation is highly suspicious for severe combined immunodeficiency: failure to thrive, severe lymphopenia (ALC < 2.5-3.0), opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis-like pneumonia, CMV viraemia, persistent candidiasis), maternal family history of unexplained infant death, BCG exposure, and absent thymic shadow. Urgent immunology referral, T/B/NK lymphocyte subsets, reverse isolation, withholding live vaccines and use of irradiated CMV-negative leucodepleted blood products are time-critical (ASCIA: SCID; eviQ).

Pneumocystis-like pneumonia, CMV viraemia, FTT, persistent candidiasis and severe lymphopenia together are not normal at any age; urgent specialist evaluation required. (Source: RCH CPG: Recurrent Infections).
Live vaccines (MMR, rotavirus, BCG, varicella) are contraindicated in suspected SCID and cause disseminated infection. (Source: NCIRS).
Maternal-acquired HIV antibody persists under 18 months regardless of status; HIV PCR is the test of choice. Would be correct only in older children (Source: ASHM).

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis with reduced GCS, focal neurology, recent seizure or cardiorespiratory instability mandates deferring LP, giving dexamethasone just before or with empirical IV ceftriaxone (meningitis dose 100 mg/kg load, max 4 g), and arranging neuroimaging once stable. Vancomycin is added if pneumococcus is suspected.
key_points: LP contraindications: GCS less than 13, focal neurology, recent seizure, cardiorespiratory compromise, coagulopathy, signs of raised ICP, local skin infection
Ceftriaxone meningitis dose 100 mg/kg load (max 4 g), then 50 mg/kg q12h or 100 mg/kg daily (max 4 g)
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h x 4 days, given before or with the first antibiotic dose in children over 3 months
Add vancomycin 15 mg/kg if pneumococcal meningitis suspected (Australian resistance)
Notify public health and consider chemoprophylaxis for contacts if meningococcal or Hib
explanation.pearls: Anisocoria with a falling GCS is uncal herniation until proven otherwise; never put a needle in that back.

options.rationale: Reduced GCS with anisocoria contraindicates immediate LP (herniation risk); CSF is deferred and antibiotics not delayed. Would be correct with normal GCS and no focal signs (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis).

Antibiotics correct but dexamethasone should be given just before or with first antibiotic dose in confirmed bacterial meningitis over 3 months. Would be correct without dexamethasone indication (e.g. neonate) (Source: RCH CPG).

Reduced GCS and focal neurology (anisocoria) are contraindications to immediate LP. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg should be given just before or with the first antibiotic dose in children over 3 months with suspected bacterial meningitis. Ceftriaxone meningitis dose is 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) load, not the standard 50 mg/kg sepsis dose, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and RCH CPG: Meningitis encephalitis.

Benzylpenicillin monotherapy is inadequate in AU paediatric bacterial meningitis (pneumococcal resistance); ceftriaxone with vancomycin if local resistance is required. Would be correct only in confirmed Neisseria meningitidis with susceptible isolate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Delaying antibiotics until after imaging/LP worsens outcomes; empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone must precede imaging when LP is deferred. (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Fever in an infant under 3 months mandates a full septic workup (blood, urine via suprapubic aspiration or catheter, cerebrospinal fluid) and empirical intravenous antibiotics. Australian guidance (RCH Febrile child, Therapeutic Guidelines, AMH Children's Dosing Companion) gives benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin/ampicillin) plus gentamicin in this age group; cefotaxime at meningitic doses is added when meningitis is suspected. Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement and calcium incompatibility.
key_points: Under 3 months: benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin per Australian guidance
Add cefotaxime at meningitic doses when meningitis is suspected
Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates due to bilirubin displacement and calcium incompatibility
Cerebrospinal fluid should be obtained before antibiotics unless contraindicated
Continue antibiotics until cultures are negative at 36-48 hours
explanation.pearls: The US AAP / Boston-criteria cefotaxime plus ampicillin regimen omits gentamicin; Australian practice includes gentamicin in this age band for broader Gram-negative cover.

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates and very young infants because of bilirubin displacement and calcium incompatibility; cefotaxime is preferred in this age group, and combination therapy is required for Listeria and Gram-negative cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Australian practice for the febrile infant under 3 months is intravenous benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin/ampicillin) for Listeria and group B Streptococcus, plus gentamicin for Gram-negative cover; cefotaxime at meningitic doses is added when meningitis is suspected on cerebrospinal fluid, or empirically if lumbar puncture is deferred and meningitis cannot be excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

This is the US AAP / Boston-criteria regimen; Australian practice adds gentamicin in this age group for broader Gram-negative cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Febrile Child)
Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin does not cover Listeria, group B Streptococcus, or many Gram-negative urinary pathogens, and lacks meningeal penetration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Any febrile infant under 3 months requires a full septic workup and parenteral antibiotics until cultures are negative at 36-48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

explanation.summary: Invasive meningococcal disease is an urgent notifiable condition in every Australian state and territory. Close contacts within the 7 days before symptom onset receive single-dose ciprofloxacin (ceftriaxone IM in pregnancy) ideally within 24 hours. Index-case vaccination does not exempt contacts.
key_points: Notify on clinical suspicion (do not wait for PCR or culture)
Close contacts: household, household-like, intimate kissing, childcare under 6 yr, unprotected airway HCW exposure
Ciprofloxacin doses: 500 mg adult, 250 mg child 5 to 12 yr, 30 mg/kg (max 125 mg) under 5 yr
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose if pregnant or ciprofloxacin contraindicated
Offer MenB and MenACWY vaccination to close contacts if not up to date
explanation.pearls: Gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain plus purpura equals meningococcus; Gram-positive diplococci plus older child equals pneumococcus; Gram-negative coccobacilli in unimmunised child equals Hib.

options.rationale: Suspected IMD is notifiable immediately on clinical suspicion in all AU jurisdictions; waiting for PCR delays prophylaxis. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease SoNG).

Chemoprophylaxis is targeted to close contacts within 7 days before symptom onset (household, intimate kissing, childcare under 6, healthcare with significant exposure), not 'all' contacts. Would never be correct as a blanket measure (Source: CDNA).
Vaccination of the index case does not negate prophylaxis for close contacts; IMD is urgently notifiable (hours, not days). (Source: CDNA).

Invasive meningococcal disease is notifiable immediately on clinical suspicion. Chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin 500 mg in adults, 250 mg in children 5 to 12 years, 30 mg/kg up to 125 mg under 5 years; or ceftriaxone IM if pregnant) is given to close contacts within the 7-day exposure window, ideally within 24 hours, as per CDNA Invasive meningococcal disease SoNG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

Rifampicin is second-line (compliance, drug interactions, resistance); ciprofloxacin single-dose is first-line in non-pregnant contacts. Would be correct only with quinolone contraindication (Source: CDNA).

explanation.summary: Suspected viral encephalitis with focal features (especially temporal-lobe localisation, olfactory hallucinations, dysphasia) mandates empirical IV aciclovir while CSF HSV PCR and MRI are pursued. Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDAR) is a key differential, especially in children and young women with prominent psychiatric features, dyskinesias and autonomic instability.
key_points: Aciclovir dose: 500 mg/m^2 (or 20 mg/kg) q8h IV under 12 years; 10 mg/kg q8h adolescents and adults
Maintain hydration and monitor renal function (crystal nephropathy)
MRI: HSV shows temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity; anti-NMDAR often normal MRI
EEG: HSV periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs); anti-NMDAR extreme delta brush
Anti-NMDAR triggers include ovarian teratoma; treat with IVIG/plasmapheresis plus steroids
explanation.pearls: Olfactory hallucinations and dysphasia point to the temporal lobe; assume HSV and start aciclovir while you investigate.

options.rationale: Olfactory hallucinations, dysphasia, temporal-lobe-localising features and a lymphocytic CSF in a child are HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise. Empirical IV aciclovir 500 mg/m^2 (about 20 mg/kg under 12 years) q8h must be started immediately because delay increases mortality and morbidity, per RCH CPG: Meningitis encephalitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

Anti-NMDAR is a differential, but immunotherapy without first excluding/treating HSV is dangerous (steroids worsen untreated HSV). Would be correct only after HSV PCR negative and clinical features pathognomonic for NMDAR (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

CSF is lymphocytic with normal glucose - bacterial meningitis is unlikely; HSV must be empirically covered without waiting for PCR. Would be correct only with neutrophilic CSF and low glucose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
EEG aids diagnosis but is not a reason to delay empirical aciclovir in suspected encephalitis. Would be correct only as adjunct to confirmed treatment (Source: RCH CPG).
No specific antiviral for JEV and no Murray Valley exposure described; JEV is supportive care with vaccination for prevention. (Source: NCIRS).

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in a previously well child over 1 month is treated with oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) q8h for 5 days. Admission and IV antibiotics are reserved for SpO2 under 92%, severe respiratory distress, inability to tolerate oral therapy, dehydration, or complications such as empyema.
key_points: Amoxicillin first-line; covers pneumococcus including penicillin-non-susceptible strains at high dose
Add or substitute macrolide if atypical features (older child, gradual onset, dry cough, headache, extrapulmonary signs)
5-day course non-inferior to longer in mild-moderate CAP
Reassess at 48 to 72 hours if no improvement
CXR not routinely required to diagnose CAP
explanation.pearls: If a well-looking older child gets worse on amoxicillin, think Mycoplasma and add roxithromycin or azithromycin.

options.rationale: Dose too low; Therapeutic Guidelines and AMH Children's specify 25-30 mg/kg eight-hourly for paediatric CAP to cover pneumococci with reduced penicillin susceptibility. Would be correct at higher dose, not lower (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

First-line for uncomplicated CAP in a well child tolerating oral therapy with SpO2 over 92 percent: oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) eight-hourly for 5 days, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and RCH CPG: Pneumonia. Five days is the current AU-recommended duration for uncomplicated CAP.

Macrolides are added for atypical infection (school-age, persistent fever, first-line failure), not monotherapy first-line for typical lobar CAP. Would be correct in atypical pneumonia presentation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Augmentin is reserved for aspiration pneumonia or amoxicillin failure; clavulanate is unnecessary and adds side effects. Would be correct for aspiration pneumonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Cefalexin has poorer activity than amoxicillin against penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus; not first-line for CAP. Would be correct only with confirmed penicillin allergy and non-severe disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Complicated pneumonia in children spans simple parapneumonic effusion, empyema, necrotising pneumonia and lung abscess. Chest ultrasound is the first-line imaging to size and characterise pleural fluid. Effusions with septations or pus on ultrasound, or a thickness over 2 cm with clinical deterioration, are drained, typically with an intercostal catheter plus intrapleural fibrinolytics (alteplase plus dornase) or with primary VATS in selected centres.
key_points: Ultrasound first-line: anechoic equals simple, complex septated equals empyema
Drain if pus, septations, or large effusion with respiratory compromise
Intrapleural fibrinolytics (tPA plus DNase) reduce need for VATS
Necrotising pneumonia and lung abscess seen better on contrast CT
Continue IV antibiotics targeting Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus (including community-acquired MRSA if local prevalence)
explanation.pearls: If a previously responding pneumonia stops responding by day 5, scan with ultrasound before reaching for a new antibiotic.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: CT is for suspected necrotising pneumonia, abscess, or non-diagnostic US or for operative planning; not first-line due to paediatric radiation. Would be correct after non-diagnostic US (Source: RANZCR).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: Lateral decubitus films are largely obsolete; chest US is more accurate at distinguishing simple from complicated effusion. Would never be correct in modern practice (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia).

Diagnostic tap may be performed but in paediatric empyema imaging-guided assessment is first; pleural pH/biochem is not first investigation. Would be correct as adjunct, not first investigation (Source: RCH CPG).

Chest ultrasound is the first-line imaging in paediatric parapneumonic effusion. It is radiation-free, more sensitive than X-ray for septations, and directly guides whether intercostal drain plus intrapleural fibrinolytics or primary VATS is required, as per RCH CPG: Pneumonia and BMJ Best Practice.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Pneumonia in children

options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is for suspected foreign body, atypical organisms in immunocompromised, or persistent atelectasis. Would be correct only in those situations (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Pertussis in an unimmunised young infant is treated with azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days and admission for apnoea and cyanosis monitoring. Public health notification is required. Close-contact post-exposure prophylaxis (azithromycin) is offered to household and high-risk contacts within 21 days of exposure.
key_points: Azithromycin first-line under 1 month and onwards: 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days
Notify public health on clinical suspicion
Marked lymphocytosis (greater than 20 x 10^9/L) is a classic finding
Maternal pertussis vaccination at 20 to 32 weeks protects young infants
Hospitalised infants need negative-pressure or single-room droplet isolation until 5 days of antibiotics complete
explanation.pearls: An afebrile infant with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive emesis and lymphocytosis is pertussis until proven otherwise.

options.rationale: Admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring is appropriate in any infant under 6 months with confirmed or strongly suspected pertussis (apnoea risk), but roxithromycin is not the preferred macrolide in this age group: azithromycin has the stronger paediatric evidence base, a shorter 5-day course and is recommended first-line. Roxithromycin is acceptable only in older children needing a macrolide alternative (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Infants under 6 months with pertussis are admitted for monitoring because of apnoea and pneumonia risk. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is the antibiotic of choice in this age group; it does not alter the established disease course but reduces transmission. Notify public health and offer post-exposure prophylaxis to close contacts, as per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and CDNA Pertussis SoNG.

Admission is appropriate, but TMP-SMX is second-line only when macrolides are contraindicated and is avoided under 2 months (kernicterus risk). It is not first-line for a 9-week-old with macrolide-sensitive pertussis. Would be correct only over 2 months with macrolide contraindication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Ceftriaxone has no role in pertussis (macrolide-sensitive organism) and avoided under 1 month. Would never be correct in pertussis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Antibiotics beyond 21 days of cough don't alter clinical course but are still given within 3 weeks to reduce transmission, especially in infants. Would never be correct in this presentation (Source: CDNA Pertussis SoNG).

explanation.summary: Paediatric TB contact assessment uses Mantoux as the primary test in children under 5 years (IGRA has reduced sensitivity), with cut-offs of 10 mm or more in non-BCG, 5 mm or more in HIV/immunosuppressed, and 15 mm or more in low-risk BCG-vaccinated. Active disease is excluded clinically and with CXR before starting latent TB treatment.
key_points: Mantoux cut-offs: 5 mm (HIV/immunosuppressed/recent contact in some settings), 10 mm (non-BCG migrant/contact), 15 mm (low risk)
IGRA unreliable under 5 years; not first-line in this age group in Australia
Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (max 300 mg) daily for 9 months with pyridoxine for paediatric LTBI
Alternatives: rifampicin 4 months; isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months; weekly isoniazid + rifapentine 3 months (children 2 yr and over)
Notify the state TB control unit; arrange contact tracing of the entire household
explanation.pearls: In any child under 5 with a household TB contact, treat as if infected even with a negative Mantoux until a follow-up test at 8 to 12 weeks confirms otherwise; the window period matters.

options.rationale: Induration 12 mm in a non-BCG child with smear-positive household contact exceeds the 10 mm threshold; treat as LTBI without repeat. (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).
In AU, Mantoux 10 mm+ in non-BCG (or 5 mm+ in HIV/immunosuppression) is positive. (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).
IGRA has reduced sensitivity in under-5s and is not preferred sole test; Mantoux remains test of choice for young children. Would be correct in older children (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).

Rifampicin 4 months monotherapy is alternative but AU default is isoniazid 6-9 months with pyridoxine for paediatric LTBI. Would be correct only with INH intolerance or resistance (Source: CDNA TB SoNG).

A non-BCG child with a household smear-positive contact and Mantoux 10 mm or more, normal CXR and no clinical features of active disease has latent TB infection. The standard Australian paediatric regimen is isoniazid 10 mg/kg (max 300 mg) daily for 9 months with pyridoxine to prevent peripheral neuropathy; isoniazid plus rifampicin for 3 months is an alternative, as per CDNA Tuberculosis SoNG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

explanation.summary: Confidential adolescent sexual health care relies on Gillick competence assessment. PEP (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus a third agent, 28 days) is indicated for significant HIV exposures within 72 hours when the source is HIV positive with detectable or unknown viral load, or unknown HIV status with significant risk. Sustained undetectable viral load on ART (U=U) effectively eliminates transmission risk and PEP is not indicated. Fourth-generation HIV assays are first-line for diagnostic testing.
key_points: Gillick/Fraser competence allows confidential adolescent sexual health care
Fourth-gen HIV assay detects p24 antigen plus antibodies
PEP within 72 h (ideally under 4 h); standard tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir or raltegravir for 28 days
U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable) source equals no PEP indication
Baseline testing: HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, STI screen; follow-up HIV at 6 and 12 weeks (or earlier with fourth-gen)
explanation.pearls: Confidentiality in adolescent care is preserved by bulk-billed sexual health clinics that don't itemise Medicare statements; tell every teenager who is scared of being seen.

options.rationale: The Australian PEP guidelines (ASHM) explicitly state that a known source with a documented sustained undetectable viral load (U=U) is not a recognised indication for PEP because the risk of HIV transmission is effectively zero. Confidential adolescent care under Gillick competence applies, and baseline plus follow-up testing remains appropriate. Confidentiality concerns are addressable via bulk-billed sexual health services that do not generate Medicare statements visible to parents, as per ASHM PEP Guidelines and RACGP Red Book.

Empirical PEP not appropriate when source has sustained undetectable VL (U=U); GP prescribing of PEP is discouraged in favour of specialist. Would be correct only with detectable source VL (Source: ASHM PEP Guidelines).
Gillick-competent adolescent consents to confidential HIV testing/treatment without parental involvement; mandatory disclosure is incorrect. (Source: RACGP).
Antibody-only tests miss the window period; 4th-gen Ag/Ab assay detects p24 earlier. Would never be correct as sole test (Source: ASHM).
PEP remains available across Australia (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus third agent, 28 days, within 72 h), just not indicated in U=U scenarios. (Source: ASHM PEP).

explanation.summary: Measles post-exposure prophylaxis depends on age, gestation and immune status.
