Susceptible contacts 9 months and older receive MMR within 72 hours; under 9 months, pregnant non-immune women, and immunocompromised contacts receive NHIG (or IVIG) within 6 days of exposure. Notify the public health unit immediately on suspicion or confirmed exposure. Long-term complications include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) 7 to 10 years after infection.
key_points: Infectious from 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset
MMR within 72 h of exposure if 9 months or older and no contraindication
NHIG/IVIG within 6 days for: under 9 months, pregnant non-immune, immunocompromised
Notify on clinical suspicion (urgent notification)
Vitamin A reduces complications in severely affected children and in low-vitamin-A settings
explanation.pearls: An MMR dose at 9 to 11 months for outbreak or post-exposure use does not replace the routine 12-month and 18-month doses; document but still give both.

options.rationale: She is over 9 months and MMR within 72 h is preferred PEP; NHIG/IVIG is for under 9 months, pregnant susceptibles, and significantly immunocompromised. Would be correct only under 9 months (Source: CDNA Measles SoNG; NCIRS).

For susceptible contacts aged 9 months and over without contraindications, MMR vaccine within 72 hours of first exposure is the preferred post-exposure prophylaxis. If given to an infant aged 9 to 11 months it counts as a dose but the routine 12-month and 18-month doses are still given. Measles is urgently notifiable, as per CDNA Measles SoNG and NCIRS Measles vaccine.
Susceptible exposed contacts should be offered PEP (MMR within 72 h or NHIG/IVIG within 6 days); waiting for serology delays effective prophylaxis. (Source: CDNA).
No specific antiviral for measles; supportive care plus vitamin A in selected cases. (Source: NCIRS).
She is already 13 months, maternal antibody waned, and she is unvaccinated; she needs PEP. Would be correct only in younger infant with maternal immunity (Source: NCIRS).

explanation.summary: VZIG (or IVIG when VZIG unavailable) is given to susceptible high-risk contacts after significant varicella exposure: significantly immunocompromised patients, non-immune pregnant women, and neonates exposed to peripartum maternal varicella. Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in this group. Maternal varicella before 20 weeks risks congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia, cicatricial scarring, microcephaly, eye defects); peripartum maternal varicella threatens neonatal varicella with high mortality.
key_points: VZIG ideally within 96 h, up to 10 days from exposure
Varicella vaccine contraindicated in significant immunosuppression
Congenital varicella syndrome risk highest with maternal infection 8 to 20 weeks gestation
Neonatal varicella: maternal rash 5 days before to 2 days after birth equals VZIG to neonate plus aciclovir if symptomatic
Treat established varicella in immunocompromised with IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h
explanation.pearls: If you have to think about whether someone is significantly immunocompromised, they probably are; phone for VZIG and don't wait for the rash.

options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in significantly immunocompromised patients on chemo. Would be correct only in immunocompetent contacts within 5 days (Source: NCIRS Varicella Vaccine).

Prophylactic oral aciclovir from day 7 post-exposure is an alternative when VZIG unavailable; VZIG preferred in significantly immunocompromised. Would be correct as alternative when VZIG unavailable (Source: NCIRS).

Immediate aciclovir treats established varicella, not pre-symptomatic prophylaxis; VZIG is preferred PEP in significantly immunocompromised contacts. Would be correct only with established lesions (Source: NCIRS).
Observation alone misses the window for passive immunisation; VZIG within 96 h (up to 10 days) attenuates disease. Would never be correct in significantly immunocompromised contact (Source: NCIRS).

Significantly immunocompromised varicella-susceptible contacts (including children on chemotherapy, transplant recipients, and those on high-dose corticosteroids) should receive VZIG as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within 96 hours but up to 10 days. Other indicated groups include non-immune pregnant women and neonates of mothers with peripartum varicella (5 days before to 2 days after delivery), as per NCIRS Varicella vaccine and the Australian Immunisation Handbook.

explanation.summary: Most AOM in well low-risk Australian children resolves without antibiotics. Indications for immediate antibiotics: under 6 months, under 2 years with bilateral disease, otorrhoea (perforated or grommet), severe systemic symptoms, immunocompromised, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background, cochlear implants, or failure to improve at 48 to 72 hours. First-line amoxicillin 30 mg/kg (max 1 g) q8h for 5 days; amoxicillin-clavulanate for failure or recurrence.
key_points: Analgesia is the priority regardless of antibiotic decision
Antibiotic indications: under 6 mo always; under 2 yr bilateral; otorrhoea; severe; high risk
First-line: amoxicillin 30 mg/kg q8h x 5 days
Topical antibiotics for perforation or grommet discharge
Review at 48 to 72 h; reconsider antibiotics if no improvement
explanation.pearls: In remote and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, AOM is treated more aggressively because of the high burden of chronic suppurative otitis media; the threshold for antibiotics is much lower.

options.rationale: Australian guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, RCH CPG: AOM) reserves antibiotics for children under 6 months always, under 2 years with bilateral disease, otorrhoea, systemically unwell, or high-risk groups (Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background, immunocompromised, cochlear implants). A low-risk, well, over-2 child with unilateral AOM and an intact TM is managed with analgesia and watchful waiting.

AU dose for AOM when antibiotics indicated is amoxicillin 30 mg/kg eight-hourly for 5 days, not 15 mg/kg; and antibiotics are not first-line in low-risk children. Would be correct only at correct dose for high-risk indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Augmentin is for amoxicillin failure, recent amoxicillin use, or recurrent AOM, not first uncomplicated episode. Would be correct only with prior amoxicillin failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Cefaclor has poor activity against penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus and risks serum-sickness-like reactions; not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Topical quinolone drops are for AOM with perforation, otorrhoea through grommet, or chronic suppurative OM; TM intact here. Would be correct only with perforation/grommet/CSOM (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and presents with eyelid swelling and erythema but normal eye movements, vision and pupil response. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis includes proptosis, painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, reduced visual acuity, or RAPD and demands urgent CT sinuses and orbits, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering sinus organisms, anaerobes and Staphylococcus aureus, and joint ophthalmology and ENT input for possible drainage of subperiosteal abscess.
key_points: Preseptal: lid swelling, no proptosis, normal EOM, normal vision
Postseptal: any of proptosis, painful EOM, ophthalmoplegia, reduced VA, RAPD
Imaging: CT sinuses and orbits with contrast (not MRI first-line for speed)
Empirical IV: ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin + metronidazole
Drain subperiosteal abscess if large, vision-threatening or non-responsive to 48 h IV
explanation.pearls: Always test eye movements, visual acuity and the pupil in any swollen eyelid; a missed orbital cellulitis can blind a child in 24 hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Oral and outpatient are for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis without orbital involvement; painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, proptosis or vision change mark orbital cellulitis. Would be correct only in preseptal cellulitis without orbital signs (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy does not cover sinus pathogens (pneumococcus, Strep anginosus, anaerobes) and Haemophilus driving orbital cellulitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Imaging required but antibiotics must not be delayed; CT sinuses/orbits with contrast is the standard urgent imaging, not MRI (more rapidly available, identifies subperiosteal collection). Would be correct as adjunct, not delaying antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: This child has features of orbital (postseptal) cellulitis: painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, reduced visual acuity and RAPD. Urgent CT sinuses and orbits with contrast identifies subperiosteal abscess and sinus disease. Empirical IV therapy must cover sinus pathogens (ceftriaxone), Staphylococcus aureus (flucloxacillin) and anaerobes (metronidazole), with urgent ophthalmology and ENT input for possible surgical drainage, as per RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Allergic eyelid swelling is bilateral, itchy, non-tender, with no vision/movement effect; this is bacterial orbital cellulitis. Would be correct only in allergic angioedema with bilateral involvement (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is fever 38.0 deg C or more (single reading 38.5 deg C or sustained 38.0 deg C) with ANC under 0.5 x 10^9/L (or expected to fall). Empirical antibiotics within 60 minutes (within 30 minutes if septic shock). High-risk or haemodynamically unstable patients: piperacillin-tazobactam plus aminoglycoside; add vancomycin if line infection, MRSA risk, mucositis, or shock. Source control includes line removal if persistent positive cultures.
key_points: ANC under 0.5 x 10^9/L defines neutropenia
Antibiotics within 60 min (30 min if shocked)
First-line high-risk: piperacillin-tazobactam + gentamicin (+/- vancomycin)
Add antifungal cover if persistent fever beyond 96 h
G-CSF for prolonged neutropenia; cannot replace antibiotics in acute phase
explanation.pearls: Time to antibiotics is the single most modifiable predictor of mortality in paediatric febrile neutropenia; the line must be in and antibiotics running before the imaging trolley arrives.

options.rationale: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy with cefepime is a reasonable empirical regimen in stable high-risk febrile neutropenia, but this child is in septic shock with profound prolonged neutropenia and an indwelling central line, where Australian paediatric guidance recommends adding an aminoglycoside for synergistic Gram-negative cover and considering early vancomycin. Monotherapy here under-treats the shock physiology and the line-infection risk (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Ceftriaxone does not cover Pseudomonas; antipseudomonal cover is mandatory in febrile neutropenia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

High-risk febrile neutropenia with septic shock and an indwelling Hickman line in a profoundly neutropenic patient requires antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside for synergy and Gram-negative cover. Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg (piperacillin component) q6h plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily is standard, with vancomycin added if suspected central line infection, mucositis, MRSA risk, or ongoing instability, as per RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

Meropenem is reserved for second-line use in febrile neutropenia: known or suspected ESBL colonisation, severe sepsis not responding to first-line antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside, or significant beta-lactam allergy precluding piperacillin-tazobactam. First-line empirical therapy here is piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Antibiotics must be given within 60 min (ideally 30 min in septic shock); each hour of delay increases mortality. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia).

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria (fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WCC >12) stratify septic arthritis risk in a child with an acutely irritable hip; 4 of 4 predicts approximately 99 percent probability. Definitive management is urgent aspiration / washout plus empirical IV antistaphylococcal therapy, per RCH CPG: Acute limp.
key_points: Kocher 0/4 ~ 2 percent, 1/4 ~ 3 percent, 2/4 ~ 40 percent, 3/4 ~ 93 percent, 4/4 ~ 99 percent
Empirical flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus, the commonest pathogen
Kingella kingae cover (e.g. cefazolin) considered in under 4-year-olds in some centres
Antibiotics after sampling unless the child is septic and aspiration is delayed
explanation.pearls: Transient synovitis classically follows a viral URTI by 1-2 weeks but the child is afebrile and will mobilise with analgesia; fever plus refusal to weight-bear despite analgesia is a major red flag (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: All four Kocher criteria met giving ~99 percent probability of septic arthritis; discharge with analgesia risks irreversible cartilage damage. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).
Withholding antibiotics and aspiration in 4-of-4 Kocher risks irreversible cartilage and femoral head damage; time-to-washout correlates with outcome. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: Oral therapy and outpatient are inappropriate for high-probability septic arthritis of the hip; IV after aspiration is mandated and oral switch is only after cultures known. Would be correct only as step-down after IV course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: With four Kocher criteria positive and a sonographic effusion, the predicted probability of septic arthritis is approximately 99 percent; urgent aspiration (often combined with arthrotomy and washout) confirms the diagnosis and decompresses the joint, with empirical IV flucloxacillin started immediately after sampling to cover Staphylococcus aureus, per RCH CPG: Acute limp and Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: MRI has role with suspected osteomyelitis after equivocal initial assessment but should not delay aspiration and antibiotics in 4-of-4 Kocher patient with confirmed effusion. Would be correct only with equivocal Kocher and effusion uncertainty (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: SUFE typically affects overweight adolescents around puberty and presents with vague hip, thigh or knee pain and an externally rotated, antalgic gait. The key examination sign is obligate external rotation on hip flexion. Management is urgent non-weight-bearing transfer for in-situ pinning, per RCH CPG: SUFE.
key_points: Perthes age 4-8 years, SUFE adolescent (typically 10-15)
Bilateral SUFE in up to 25 percent over time - many centres pin both prophylactically
Stable = able to bear weight (with crutches); unstable = cannot bear weight even with aids
Unstable slips carry up to 50 percent risk of avascular necrosis
explanation.pearls: Any adolescent with knee or thigh pain needs a hip examination; missed SUFE is a leading cause of preventable adolescent hip morbidity (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE).

options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion and widened physis are pathognomonic of SUFE; delay risks stable-to-unstable slip with much higher AVN risk. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE).
Continued weight-bearing risks progression to unstable slip; child must be made non-weight-bearing and referred urgently. (Source: RCH CPG).

Perthes is 4-8 years with femoral head fragmentation, not physeal widening; this 12-year-old with raised BMI and physeal widening has SUFE. Would be correct in 4-8-year-old with classic Perthes XR (Source: RCH CPG).

This is a stable SUFE with classic obligate external rotation and a widened physis on AP view; frog-lateral views improve sensitivity. The child must be made non-weight-bearing immediately and admitted for in-situ percutaneous pinning to prevent progression and avascular necrosis, per RCH CPG: SUFE.
Referred knee pain is classic for hip pathology in adolescents; hip exam and pelvic XR have localised the lesion. Would never be correct as next step (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Osgood-Schlatter is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity at the patellar tendon insertion, typical in adolescents during a growth spurt who do jumping or running sports. Diagnosis is clinical and management is conservative with activity modification, ice and analgesia, with reassurance that symptoms resolve at skeletal maturity, per RCH CPG: Knee pain.
key_points: Bilateral involvement in 25-50 percent
Continue sport within pain tolerance
Imaging only if atypical (unilateral, nocturnal, locking) to exclude tumour or OCD
Symptoms usually self-limit by closure of tibial tuberosity apophysis (~16 years)
explanation.pearls: Persistent unfused ossicle in the patellar tendon after skeletal maturity may need excision but is rare (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain).

options.rationale: Bilateral tibial tuberosity tenderness in an adolescent during a growth spurt with reproducible pain on resisted knee extension and no red flags is diagnostic of Osgood-Schlatter (traction apophysitis); imaging is not required and management is conservative, per RCH CPG: Knee pain.

MRI/orthopaedics are for atypical (unilateral, nocturnal pain, locking, persistent past skeletal maturity); typical bilateral apophysitis does not need them. Would be correct with atypical features (Source: RCH CPG).
Casting is not recommended for Osgood-Schlatter and causes deconditioning; relative rest preserves strength and growth. (Source: RCH CPG).
Intralesional steroid near an open apophysis risks soft tissue atrophy, depigmentation, growth disturbance. (Source: RCH CPG).
Plain films not routine for typical Osgood-Schlatter; tuberosity fragmentation is a normal variant. Would be correct only with atypical features (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is screened with the Adams forward bend test (positive rib prominence) and quantified with the standing Cobb angle. Australian referral cut-offs are: <20 degrees - observe with skeletal maturity assessment; 20-40 degrees in a skeletally immature patient - refer for bracing consideration; >40-50 degrees with progression - surgical referral. Atypical features mandate MRI, per RCH CPG: Scoliosis.
key_points: Right thoracic, painless, neurologically normal AIS is typical
Risser stage 0-2 = high risk of progression
Bracing aims to halt progression, not correct the curve
Red flags for MRI: left thoracic curve, neurology, pain, age <10, cutaneous stigmata
explanation.pearls: A scoliometer reading of 7 degrees or more on the Adams forward bend roughly corresponds to a 20 degree Cobb angle and triggers radiographic assessment (Source: Spine Society of Australia).

options.rationale: Cobb 28 degrees in skeletally immature girl (Risser 2, recent menarche) has significant progression risk and needs specialist follow-up. Would be correct only in skeletally mature patient with stable Cobb under 25 (Source: AAOS Scoliosis Guidelines).

20-40 degree curves in skeletally immature meet threshold for orthopaedic referral and possible bracing; surveillance alone risks missing progression. Would be correct only in skeletally mature with stable Cobb under 25 (Source: AAOS).

Australian guidelines refer skeletally immature adolescents with Cobb angles of 20 degrees or more to a spinal service; bracing is typically considered between 25 and 40 degrees in skeletally immature patients to prevent progression, per RCH CPG: Scoliosis.
Surgery is for Cobb over 45-50 degrees that continues to progress, not 28; bracing is first-line at this Cobb. Would be correct at Cobb over 45-50 with progression (Source: AAOS).

MRI is for atypical features (left thoracic, rapid progression, neuro signs, painful, juvenile under 10, cutaneous stigmata); right thoracic curve in adolescent is typical adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Would be correct with atypical features (Source: AAOS).

explanation.summary: Newborn DDH screening combines clinical examination (Barlow provocative test for dislocatability, Ortolani manoeuvre for reduction of a dislocated hip) with selective ultrasound at 6 weeks for risk factors (female, breech, first-degree family history, oligohydramnios). A positive Ortolani is dislocated hip and warrants immediate paediatric orthopaedic referral and Pavlik harness, per RCH CPG: DDH.
key_points: Ultrasound preferred over XR until femoral head ossifies (~4-6 months)
Pavlik harness from diagnosis, weaned around 6-12 weeks of treatment
Six-week ultrasound for risk factors with normal clinical exam
After ~6 months of age, closed reduction in theatre +/- spica is required
explanation.pearls: Asymmetric skin creases alone are NOT specific for DDH, but limited or asymmetric abduction beyond the neonatal period is the most reliable sign (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

options.rationale: Positive Ortolani is a clinically dislocated reducible hip, not a benign click; same-admission orthopaedic referral is mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).
Plain XR is unreliable before 4-6 months (femoral heads not ossified); US is the neonatal imaging modality. Would be correct in older infant over 4-6 months (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

A frankly positive Ortolani with risk factors (female, breech, family history) mandates urgent paediatric orthopaedic referral, supervised Pavlik harness fitting, and ultrasound (Graf classification, static and dynamic) for morphology, per RCH CPG: DDH and the Australian national hip surveillance guidance.
Double-nappying is not evidence-based and delays definitive Pavlik harness in a frankly dislocated hip. (Source: RCH CPG).
6-week screening is for at-risk infants with normal clinical exam; positive Ortolani requires immediate referral. Would be correct only with risk factors and normal exam (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: DDH that escapes newborn screening may present later with leg-length asymmetry (positive Galeazzi sign), limited hip abduction, asymmetric thigh creases, or an abnormal gait once walking. Imaging choice is age dependent: ultrasound under 4-6 months, plain AP pelvic XR thereafter, per RCH CPG: DDH.
key_points: Late DDH may need closed reduction in theatre +/- spica from approximately 6 months
Older late presentations may require open reduction and femoral or pelvic osteotomy
Galeazzi sign is unreliable in bilateral DDH
Shenton line on AP pelvis is the key radiographic clue
explanation.pearls: All infants who fail to walk by 18 months or who walk with a Trendelenburg gait need a pelvic XR to exclude missed DDH (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).

options.rationale: US is best up to 4-6 months while femoral heads are unossified; by 8 months the ossific nucleus obscures landmarks. Would be correct only under 4-6 months (Source: RCH CPG: DDH).
MRI is for postoperative assessment or atypical/complex cases; not first-line for suspected late-presenting DDH. Would be correct in postop assessment (Source: RCH CPG).

After approximately 4-6 months of age the proximal femoral epiphysis ossifies and plain AP pelvic radiography (assessing acetabular index, Shenton line, Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines) becomes the imaging of choice for DDH, per RCH CPG: DDH.
CT carries unnecessary radiation and is for surgical planning in older children with complex deformity. Would be correct in operative planning (Source: RCH CPG).
Bone scintigraphy has no routine role in DDH; it is for osteomyelitis or occult bone pathology. Would never be correct in suspected DDH (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Limp in the 3-10 year age group is most commonly transient (irritable hip) synovitis following a viral illness, classically Kocher 0-1 of 4. The clinician must actively exclude septic arthritis (Kocher), Perthes (age 4-8, insidious, XR fragmentation), and malignancy (night pain, systemic features), per RCH CPG: Acute limp.
key_points: Under 3: think DDH, septic arthritis, NAI, fracture (toddlers fracture)
3-10: transient synovitis, Perthes, septic arthritis, JIA, ALL
Adolescent: SUFE, sports injury (apophysitis, OCD), JIA
Always include NAI in pre-mobile children with limp
explanation.pearls: Transient synovitis settles within 7-10 days with rest and analgesia; persistent limp beyond 2 weeks should re-prompt imaging and bloods to exclude Perthes or chronic infection (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

options.rationale: Kocher 0/4 gives ~2 percent probability of septic arthritis; clinically very unlikely. Would be correct with elevated Kocher score (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

Mild post-viral limp in a 3-15 year old with low-grade or no fever, normal inflammatory markers, weight-bearing and a small effusion is classic for transient synovitis, the most common cause of atraumatic limp in this age group, per RCH CPG: Acute limp.

Perthes is 4-8 years with insidious painless limp and characteristic XR (subchondral fracture, fragmentation); at age 3 with acute post-URTI onset, it's unlikely. Would be correct in 4-8-year-old with XR changes (Source: RCH CPG).
SUFE is adolescent (10-15 years, often overweight, peripubertal); rare in 3-year-old without endocrine predisposition. Would be correct in adolescent (Source: RCH CPG).
ALL presents with night pain, systemic symptoms, cytopenias and disproportionately raised inflammatory markers; this child has benign profile. Would be correct with red flags (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children warrants antibiotics rather than watchful waiting because of the very high baseline rates of recurrent AOM, perforation and chronic suppurative otitis media. First-line is amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily, typically for 7 days in high-risk children, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual.
key_points: Watchful waiting only for well, non-Indigenous, age >2, unilateral AOM
Always treat: <6 months; <2 years with bilateral disease; severe symptoms; otorrhoea; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander; immunocompromised; cochlear implant
Amoxicillin/clavulanate if no response by 48-72 hours
Topical ciprofloxacin if perforation or grommet discharge
explanation.pearls: Document tympanic membrane appearance carefully; CSOM (discharge >2 weeks through perforation) carries lifelong hearing and language consequences and is a public health priority (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual).

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is for well low-risk non-Indigenous children over 2 years; Aboriginal children have markedly elevated risk of chronic suppurative OM and require antibiotic treatment. Would be correct only in non-Indigenous low-risk child (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Australian guidelines recommend amoxicillin first-line for AOM in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, with a longer duration (typically 7 days) than the 5 day course used for low-risk non-Indigenous children, to reduce risk of progression to chronic suppurative otitis media, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and CARPA Standard Treatment Manual.

Oral cephalosporins are not preferred first-line for AOM in AU; amoxicillin has adequate pneumococcal cover and 3-day course is insufficient for high-risk children. Would be correct as second-line with adequate duration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Topical quinolone drops are for AOM with discharge through perforation/grommet or CSOM, not intact-TM AOM. Would be correct only with perforation/grommet/CSOM (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is for ARF secondary prophylaxis and GAS syndromes, not first-line AOM. Would be correct only in ARF prophylaxis indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Acute mastoiditis is the commonest suppurative complication of AOM and presents with postauricular swelling, protruding pinna and obliteration of the postauricular sulcus, often after failed oral therapy. Management is admission, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone), urgent contrast CT temporal bones and urgent ENT for surgical drainage, per RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis.
key_points: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest pathogen; consider PCV failure
CT temporal bones with contrast identifies subperiosteal abscess and bony erosion
Add metronidazole if intracranial extension; obtain MR venography for sinus thrombosis
ENT may perform cortical mastoidectomy plus myringotomy with grommet insertion
explanation.pearls: Always palpate and inspect behind the ear in any child with persistent fever despite AOM treatment - missing mastoiditis risks intracranial spread, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and facial nerve palsy (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis).

options.rationale: Acute mastoiditis with fluctuant subperiosteal abscess; oral therapy is inadequate, urgent IV antibiotics, imaging and ENT input are mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Mastoiditis).
Flucloxacillin does not adequately cover pneumococcus and other AOM pathogens driving mastoiditis; broader cover and urgent ENT input are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Acute mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess requires admission, IV broad-spectrum cover (e.g. ceftriaxone, with metronidazole added if intracranial extension), contrast CT temporal bones to define abscess and exclude intracranial complications, and urgent ENT for cortical mastoidectomy +/- myringotomy +/- grommet, per RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.
No signs of meningitis (no neck stiffness/photophobia/altered GCS); LP not required. Intracranial complications excluded by CT. Would be correct only with meningitis signs (Source: RCH CPG).

Imaging required but must not delay IV antibiotics and ENT; CT temporal bones with contrast is first-line (rapidly available, characterises bone). Would be correct only as adjunct, not delaying treatment (Source: RANZCR).

explanation.summary: OME (glue ear) is the most common cause of acquired hearing loss in children and is diagnosed by retracted dull TMs with effusion, reduced TM mobility, and type B tympanograms. Referral criteria are bilateral OME for 3 months with hearing loss >=25 dB or language / developmental impact, per RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion.
key_points: Most cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months
No role for routine antibiotics, antihistamines or steroids
Lower threshold for grommets in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children given CSOM risk
Pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry are key diagnostic tools
explanation.pearls: Always check the language and developmental trajectory in recurrent AOM - the indication for grommets is functional impact, not the eardrum appearance alone (Source: NICE NG98).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: OME is not acute infection and routine antibiotics are not recommended; do not change long-term outcomes. Would never be correct in OME (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Intranasal steroids and antihistamines not recommended for OME (no meaningful improvement in hearing/effusion). (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Bilateral OME over 3 months with hearing loss over 25 dB and language/behaviour impact crosses threshold for ENT referral. Would be correct only without hearing loss or language impact (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Australian and international guidance refers children with bilateral OME persisting >=3 months with hearing loss >=25 dB or with developmental, language or behavioural concerns to ENT for tympanostomy tube consideration, per RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion and NICE NG98.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.rationale: Hearing aids are alternative when surgery contraindicated or declined; grommets remain first-line surgical management. Would be correct only with surgical contraindication (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

explanation.summary: Most paediatric epistaxis is anterior from Little area (Kiesselbach plexus) and is provoked by digit trauma and mucosal dryness. Management is reinforced first aid, topical antiseptic ointment and treatment of underlying contributors. Cautery, packing or ENT referral are reserved for ongoing bleeding, atypical features or red flag presentations, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis.
key_points: First aid: pinch soft part of nose, lean forward, 10-15 minutes continuous
Naseptin twice daily for 10-14 days has trial evidence for recurrence reduction
Avoid in peanut/soya allergy - use paraffin alternative
Red flags: unilateral severe bleeds in adolescent boy (JNA), nasal mass, bleeding from other sites
explanation.pearls: Consider non-accidental injury or a coagulation disorder if multiple bruising sites or family history of bleeding are present (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis).

options.rationale: JNA affects adolescent males with unilateral nasal obstruction and severe recurrent epistaxis with mass; digit-trauma anterior bleeding in 6-year-old is not the JNA picture. Would be correct in adolescent male with mass (Source: RCH CPG).

Recurrent anterior epistaxis at Little area in a child is most often due to digit trauma and mucosal dryness. First-line management is topical antiseptic ointment plus reinforced first aid, which reduces recurrence in randomised trials. Silver nitrate cautery is reserved for failure of conservative care, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis.
Bilateral simultaneous septal cautery risks septal perforation; cautery is unilateral and second-line after failed conservative therapy. Would be correct as unilateral second-line (Source: RCH CPG).

Packing is uncomfortable in children and is for ongoing bleeding not controlled by first aid; not appropriate as outpatient management. Would be correct only with active uncontrolled bleeding in ED (Source: RCH CPG).
Oral TXA has no role as first-line for mucosal-trauma epistaxis with normal coagulation. Would be correct only as second-line adjunct (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: A pre-auricular sinus is a common congenital tract anterior to the helical root. Asymptomatic pits do not need treatment, but recurrent infection or abscess formation is an indication for elective complete surgical excision after antibiotic treatment of the acute episode, per RCH CPG: Pre-auricular sinus.
key_points: Most common organism in infection is Staphylococcus aureus
Incomplete excision leads to high recurrence; refer to ENT for full tract excision
Differential: branchial cleft anomaly, sebaceous cyst, infected lymph node
May be associated with syndromal hearing loss in some series - check newborn hearing
explanation.pearls: Bilateral pre-auricular pits warrant renal ultrasound only if there are associated syndromal features or family history; the routine ultrasound for all isolated pits is not supported (Source: RCH CPG: Pre-auricular sinus).

options.rationale: An acutely infected pre-auricular sinus is treated with anti-staphylococcal oral antibiotic and I&D if abscess fails to settle. Definitive excision is delayed until after the acute inflammation resolves because operating on inflamed tissue increases recurrence; the planes are clearer at 4-6 weeks, per RCH CPG: Pre-auricular sinus and Therapeutic Guidelines.

First branchial cleft anomalies are rare with peri-auricular sinus tracts related to facial nerve; typical pre-auricular pit at the helical root is not this. Would be correct only with first branchial cleft anomaly anatomy (Source: RCH CPG).

An infected pre-auricular sinus requires antibiotic treatment and ENT referral for definitive excision; observation alone risks abscess progression. Would be correct only for asymptomatic non-discharging pit (Source: RCH CPG).
Squeezing spreads infection and damages adjacent tissues; systemic antibiotics with surgical drainage if needed is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG).
Operating on acutely inflamed sinus increases recurrence (obscured planes); excision is deferred until acute infection settled. Would be correct after acute infection resolved (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: The Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy require well-documented severe, recurrent bacterial tonsillitis episodes meeting frequency thresholds: 7 in 1 year, OR 5 per year over 2 years, OR 3 per year over 3 years. Each episode must include fever >38.3, exudate or lymphadenopathy or positive throat swab, and have been treated with antibiotics or seen by a clinician, per RCH CPG: Sore throat.
key_points: Episodes must be documented, severe and clinician-confirmed
Other indications: OSA, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), suspected malignancy
Surgical risks: post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage (primary and secondary)
Adenotonsillectomy preferred for OSA
explanation.pearls: Most children with recurrent tonsillitis improve over 1-2 years even without surgery; the Paradise trial showed only a modest absolute reduction in episodes at 2 years and the effect attenuates over time (Source: Paradise et al. NEJM 1984).

options.rationale: Paradise criteria require 7 episodes in 12 months, 5/year for 2 years, or 3/year for 3 years; 4 episodes in 12 months does not meet criteria. Would be correct only when Paradise criteria met (Source: ENT Society Australia).

He has 4 episodes in 12 months and is approaching but does not yet meet Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy; documented surveillance with episode characterisation over the next 1-2 years guides decision-making while avoiding surgery that may not change long-term course, per RCH CPG: Sore throat.
Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is for ARF secondary prevention, not recurrent bacterial tonsillitis without ARF. Would be correct only with ARF indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Asymptomatic GAS carriage is common in children and does not warrant treatment; swabs not indicated in asymptomatic children outside ARF-prevention. Would be correct only in symptomatic episode or ARF prevention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

4 tonsillitis episodes in a well-grown child does not meet criteria for immunodeficiency workup; referral threshold is recurrent serious infections at multiple sites. Would be correct with multi-site recurrent serious infections (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is the cardinal sign of retinoblastoma and other sight-threatening pathology in infants. Red reflex examination should be performed at every newborn, 6 week and 6 month check. Any persistent abnormality requires urgent paediatric ophthalmology referral, per RANZCO Position Statement and RCH CPG.
key_points: Retinoblastoma is the commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood (most cases under 5)
Bilateral disease suggests germline RB1 mutation and trilateral risk (pineal)
Other causes of leukocoria: congenital cataract, PFV, Coats disease, ROP, toxocariasis
Treatment includes focal therapy, systemic / intra-arterial chemotherapy and enucleation
explanation.pearls: Parents often notice leukocoria first in flash photographs; never dismiss the parent who brings a photograph of a white pupil (Source: RANZCO).

options.rationale: Leukocoria is never normal and mandates same-day to next-day paediatric ophthalmology to exclude retinoblastoma. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukocoria).
Optometry deferral risks unacceptable delay; retinoblastoma is curable when caught early but devastating when missed. (Source: RCH CPG).

Persistent unilateral leukocoria in an infant requires urgent paediatric ophthalmology referral. EUA is the diagnostic step; differential includes retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, persistent fetal vasculature, Coats disease and toxocariasis. Imaging is staging not screening, per RANZCO and RCH CPG.
MRI is for staging once retinoblastoma is diagnosed; first step is paediatric ophthalmology EUA, not pre-emptive imaging. Would be correct only after EUA-confirmed diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG).
Patching is for confirmed amblyopia AFTER the underlying lesion has been identified and treated; occluding now could delay diagnosis. Would never be correct as first step (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life. Timing helps differentiate aetiology: chemical 24-48 hours, gonococcal day 2-5 (hyperacute, severe chemosis, corneal risk), chlamydial day 5-14 (mucopurulent, milder), HSV day 6-14 (vesicles, dendritic keratitis, systemic). Suspected gonococcal disease mandates IV third-generation cephalosporin, irrigation and urgent ophthalmology, per RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis.
key_points: Notify chlamydial and gonococcal infection to public health
Treat both mother and partners; arrange contact tracing
Cefotaxime preferred over ceftriaxone in jaundiced neonates (bilirubin displacement)
Chlamydia adds risk of pneumonia (interstitial pattern at 4-12 weeks)
explanation.pearls: Gonococcal ophthalmia can perforate the cornea within 24 hours; treat empirically while awaiting microbiology (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.rationale: Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis with marked chemosis in the first week of life with maternal risk factors must be treated as Neisseria gonorrhoeae until proven otherwise; gonococcal ophthalmia can perforate the cornea within 24 hours. Management is admission, IV third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime preferred in jaundiced neonates over ceftriaxone), copious saline irrigation and urgent ophthalmology, per RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.

Topical chloramphenicol alone is inadequate for gonococcal ophthalmia (corneal penetration, disseminated infection risk); systemic therapy required. Would never be correct in gonococcal ophthalmia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Chlamydial conjunctivitis presents at 5-14 days with mucopurulent discharge and less severe chemosis; this hyperacute first-week purulent presentation is gonococcal. Would be correct in chlamydial pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Chemical conjunctivitis is in first 24-48 h, mild and self-limiting; silver nitrate is not used in Australia. Would never be correct in this presentation (Source: RCH CPG).

Neonatal HSV presents with vesicular skin/keratitis with dendritic ulcer/systemic illness, treated with IV high-dose aciclovir not topical. Would be correct only with HSV-specific findings (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and presents with eyelid swelling and erythema without ocular dysfunction. Postseptal (orbital) cellulitis additionally features painful or restricted eye movements, proptosis, reduced visual acuity, RAPD or chemosis and requires admission, IV antibiotics, contrast CT and urgent ENT / ophthalmology involvement, per RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis.
key_points: Always test acuity, pupil and eye movements in any swollen eye
Postseptal causes - paranasal sinusitis (ethmoid), trauma, dental
Chandler stages: I preseptal, II orbital cellulitis, III subperiosteal abscess, IV orbital abscess, V cavernous sinus thrombosis
Threshold to admit is low in young (<1 yr), immunocompromised, unable to attend review
explanation.pearls: Insect bite, hordeolum (stye) or contiguous skin infection are common preseptal triggers; sinusitis is the commonest postseptal trigger (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Admission, IV broad-spectrum and contrast CT are for orbital (postseptal) cellulitis: pain on eye movement, restricted motility, proptosis, reduced acuity or RAPD; absent here. Would be correct only with orbital signs (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: This is preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis (Chandler stage I): normal acuity, full painless eye movements, no proptosis, no RAPD, no chemosis, child well. Outpatient oral antibiotics with strict safety-netting and 24 hour review is appropriate, per RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Topical and warm compresses do not penetrate the lid soft tissues adequately for cellulitis; systemic antibiotics required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
No fluctuant collection described; preseptal cellulitis without abscess is managed medically. Would be correct only with palpable fluctuant abscess (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.rationale: Systemic steroids not indicated for periorbital cellulitis and may obscure progression to orbital cellulitis. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Pseudoesotropia is the appearance of crossed eyes caused by epicanthic folds, broad nasal bridge or close-set eyes, with normal alignment on Hirschberg and cover-uncover testing. True strabismus is asymmetric Hirschberg or shows movement on cover-uncover. Any true strabismus persisting beyond 4 months of age requires paediatric ophthalmology referral to prevent amblyopia, per RANZCO and RCH CPG: Vision screening.
key_points: Esotropia inwards, exotropia outwards, hypertropia upwards, hypotropia downwards
Persistent strabismus beyond 4 months requires referral
Sudden onset incomitant strabismus needs urgent imaging (cranial nerve palsy, raised ICP)
Routine preschool vision screen catches missed amblyopia
explanation.pearls: Always document the test you used (Hirschberg, cover-uncover, cover-cross-cover) - parental and grandparental concern alone is enough to warrant active testing in any child (Source: RANZCO).

options.rationale: No true strabismus on Hirschberg or cover-uncover; this is pseudoesotropia and surgery is not indicated. Would never be correct in pseudoesotropia (Source: RCH CPG).

Symmetric corneal light reflex and a negative cover-uncover test with epicanthic folds is pseudoesotropia; the apparent squint resolves as facial features mature. Reassurance with routine preschool screen is appropriate, per RANZCO and RCH CPG: Vision screening.
Patching is for confirmed amblyopia after specialist diagnosis; occluding a child without amblyopia is harmful. Would never be correct without confirmed amblyopia (Source: RCH CPG).
Atropine penalisation is for confirmed amblyopia; no role with normal vision and no strabismus. Would be correct only with diagnosed amblyopia (Source: RCH CPG).
6th nerve palsy gives limited abduction and incomitant esotropia; full eye movements and negative cover-uncover exclude this. Would be correct only with limited abduction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: An unwell toddler with hip septic arthritis and shock requires simultaneous resuscitation (10 mL/kg crystalloid boluses with reassessment), early empirical IV antibiotics after blood culture (flucloxacillin plus an agent active against Kingella kingae in under-4s such as cefazolin), and urgent orthopaedic source control. Vancomycin is added when MRSA risk is high or central line associated, per RCH CPG: Sepsis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections.
key_points: A recent oropharyngeal lesion points to Kingella kingae - it enters through breached oral mucosa
Australian paediatric sepsis pathway: 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, reassess, repeat as needed
Source control (washout) is as important as antibiotics in septic arthritis
Add vancomycin for MRSA risk (e.g. remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, line-associated, severe systemic illness)
explanation.pearls: Bacteraemia precedes joint seeding; always draw blood cultures with the first peripheral cannula before antibiotics where it does not delay therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: This child is in compensated septic shock with septic arthritis of the left hip (4 of 4 Kocher, large effusion). Australian paediatric sepsis pathway recommends 10 mL/kg crystalloid boluses with reassessment between, blood culture before antibiotics where possible, and empirical IV anti-staphylococcal cover (flucloxacillin); in under-4s a second-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin is added to cover Kingella kingae. Definitive management requires urgent surgical washout, per RCH CPG: Sepsis, RCH CPG: Acute limp and Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: 20 mL/kg boluses now discouraged in favour of 10 mL/kg with reassessment (fluid overload risk); vancomycin alone misses Gram-negatives in septic arthritis. Would be correct in some adult/older child protocols at 20 mL/kg (Source: APLS Australia).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

options.rationale: No evidence of anaemia or blood loss; crystalloid is first-line. MRI may complement but must not delay antibiotics and source control. (Source: RCH CPG).
Shock and confirmed septic arthritis - observation delays time to antibiotics and source control. (Source: RCH CPG).
Fluid resuscitation must not be deferred; ceftriaxone alone has gaps for severe staphylococcal infection and is not preferred monotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and joint infections

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed by the Australian modified Jones criteria, with a lower threshold for diagnosis in high-risk populations (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori and Pacific peoples). Major manifestations are carditis (subclinical detectable on echo), arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules; minors include fever, raised ESR / CRP, monoarthralgia, prolonged PR. Evidence of preceding GAS (ASOT, anti-DNase B, throat swab) is required, per RHDAustralia 2020 guideline.
key_points: High-risk: 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor + GAS evidence
Standard-risk: same plus more stringent arthritis definitions
Treat acute episode with bed rest, NSAIDs (after diagnosis), eradicate GAS
Secondary prophylaxis with IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21-28 days until at least age 21 and 10 years from last episode
explanation.pearls: Even subclinical mitral regurgitation on echocardiogram now counts as carditis under the 2015 / 2020 Australian modified Jones criteria; always obtain echo when ARF is suspected (Source: RHDAustralia 2020).

options.rationale: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis lacks evidence of carditis and has additive (not migratory) pattern; child has objective carditis on echo. Would be correct only without carditis and additive arthritis (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Jones).

In an Aboriginal child from a remote community (high-risk population) the modified Australian Jones criteria require 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor with evidence of preceding GAS infection. This child has 2 majors (carditis on echo and polyarthritis) plus elevated inflammatory markers and ASOT, fulfilling definite ARF, per RHDAustralia 2020 guideline.
JIA requires 6 weeks of persistent arthritis and is not associated with new pansystolic mitral murmur and elevated strep serology. Would be correct only with 6+ weeks chronic arthritis (Source: ACR).
HSP requires palpable purpura on dependent areas plus arthritis/abdominal pain/renal involvement; absent here. Would be correct with palpable purpura and IgA features (Source: RCH CPG).

Indigenous Lyme disease is not established in Australia; no relevant travel history, migratory polyarthritis plus carditis plus positive strep fits ARF. Would never be correct in Australia (Source: NHMRC Lyme statement).

explanation.summary: Most paediatric epistaxis is anterior and benign, but red flags require ENT referral. The classic triad of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is recurrent severe unilateral epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction and a posterior nasal mass in an adolescent male; clinic biopsy is contraindicated and management requires contrast imaging and specialist surgical (often pre-embolised) resection, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis.
key_points: JNA almost exclusively occurs in adolescent males
Other red flags: bleeding from multiple sites, family history of bleeding disorder, easy bruising, bleeding after dental work
Posterior epistaxis is more common in adults / hypertensive bleeders
Investigations: FBC, coagulation, group and hold; contrast imaging for suspected mass
explanation.pearls: Adolescent boy with severe unilateral nose bleeds plus blocked nose equals JNA until proven otherwise (Source: BMJ Best Practice - JNA).

options.rationale: Severe recurrent unilateral epistaxis with nasal obstruction and visible posterior mass must not be treated as benign anterior bleeding. Would be correct only in true anterior Little area bleeding (Source: RCH CPG).
JNA is exceptionally vascular and clinic biopsy can cause life-threatening haemorrhage; imaging precedes biopsy and biopsy done under GA at theatre. (Source: ENT Society Australia).

Recurrent severe unilateral epistaxis with progressive nasal obstruction and a posterior nasal mass in an adolescent male is the classic JNA triad. Urgent ENT referral with contrast cross-sectional imaging is required; biopsy is performed in theatre after imaging and angiographic assessment if needed, per RCH CPG: Epistaxis and BMJ Best Practice.
Bilateral simultaneous septal cautery risks perforation and does not address posterior nasopharyngeal mass. (Source: RCH CPG).
TXA is an adjunct only; does not substitute for ENT assessment and imaging of suspected vascular tumour. (Source: ENT Society Australia).

explanation.summary: Phototherapy thresholds in Australia are read off a postnatal age vs SBR nomogram with separate lines for risk factors (prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis). A term low-risk infant with 340 micromol/L at 72 hours sits above the phototherapy line; exchange transfusion is reserved for levels nearing approximately 450 micromol/L despite intensive phototherapy or for clinical encephalopathy.
key_points: Threshold depends on postnatal age in hours and risk factors, not just absolute level
Conjugated bilirubin > 25 micromol/L or > 20 percent of total prompts cholestatic workup
Intensive phototherapy means high-irradiance light over maximal skin area
Re-check SBR 4 to 6 hours after starting phototherapy
explanation.pearls: Visible jaundice past the umbilicus in a term newborn always warrants a measured bilirubin; clinical estimation alone is unreliable.

options.rationale: SBR 340 micromol/L at 72 h in a term baby crosses the AU phototherapy threshold on the postnatal nomogram; conservative monitoring risks rising levels. Would never be correct above threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice).
Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not recommended; continuing feeds with phototherapy is preferred. Would never be correct as routine (Source: RCH CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines).

At 72 hours of age in a term infant with no risk factors, 340 micromol/L exceeds the Australian phototherapy line on the consensus nomogram and intensive phototherapy is started, with exchange transfusion considered if SBR approaches roughly 450 micromol/L despite intensive phototherapy, per RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice.

Exchange transfusion is for SBR approaching 450 micromol/L despite intensive phototherapy or for acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Would be correct at SBR approaching 450 or with neuro signs (Source: RCH CPG).
Conjugated fraction 8 is normal (under 20 percent of total or under 25 micromol/L) and does not indicate cholestatic workup. Would be correct only with elevated conjugated fraction (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Operational thresholds in Australian neonatal units are 2.6 mmol/L for at-risk asymptomatic infants and 2.0 mmol/L as the level requiring IV dextrose. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL under 2.0 mmol/L gets a 10 percent dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus plus infusion at 60 to 90 mL/kg/day, titrated to keep BSL above 2.6 mmol/L.
key_points: At-risk groups: late preterm, IDM, SGA, LGA, perinatal stress
BSL 2.0 to 2.6 mmol/L asymptomatic: feed plus or minus buccal dextrose gel and recheck
BSL under 2.0 mmol/L or any symptomatic infant: IV 10 percent dextrose 2 mL/kg then infusion
Always recheck within 30 minutes of any intervention
explanation.pearls: Glucose delivery in mg/kg/min equals (percent dextrose x mL/kg/day) divided by 144; an 80 mL/kg/day infusion of 10 percent dextrose delivers about 5.5 mg/kg/min.

options.rationale: BSL 1.8 is below operational threshold 2.6 for at-risk infants and requires active intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

A BSL below 2.0 mmol/L in an at-risk infant warrants immediate IV 10 percent dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus and maintenance infusion at around 80 mL/kg/day (delivering approximately 5.5 mg/kg/min of glucose), with rapid recheck, per RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia.
Enteral feeding is for BSL 2.0-2.6 in asymptomatic at-risk infants; below 2.0 requires IV dextrose. Would be correct at BSL 2.0-2.6 (Source: RCH CPG).

Glucagon is for refractory hypoglycaemia where IV access delayed/impossible and requires hepatic glycogen stores; not first-line in late-preterm IDM with IV access. Would be correct only with delayed IV access (Source: RCH CPG).
Buccal dextrose gel plus feeding is for BSL 2.0-2.6 in asymptomatic infants, not below 2.0; recheck always required. Would be correct at BSL 2.0-2.6 (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Since the 2015 ILCOR update, ANZCOR has recommended that vigorous newborns with meconium-stained liquor receive routine care without tracheal suctioning. Non-vigorous infants (poor tone, apnoea, HR less than 100 bpm) go to the resuscitaire and follow the standard algorithm; tracheal suction is only considered if ventilation is ineffective and meconium is suspected to obstruct the airway.
key_points: Vigorous = good tone, good cry or breathing, HR > 100 bpm
Routine intrapartum oro/nasopharyngeal suction on the perineum is not recommended
Non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn: dry, stimulate, then standard NRP
Tracheal suction only if PPV is ineffective and meconium obstruction is suspected
explanation.pearls: The change reduces delay to effective ventilation, which is the single most important resuscitation step.

options.rationale: A vigorous newborn with meconium-stained liquor does not require tracheal suctioning; routine care with drying, warming and observation is recommended, per ANZCOR Guideline 13.4 and the Australian NRP.

Routine tracheal suction of vigorous meconium-stained newborns is no longer recommended and may delay resuscitation. Would be correct only in non-vigorous newborn with airway obstruction (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).
PPV is indicated only with apnoea, gasping, or HR under 100, none of which apply. Would be correct in those situations (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).
Intubation is for ineffective bag-mask or specific indications; prophylactic CPAP/intubation not indicated in vigorous term newborn. Would be correct only with failed PPV (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).
Intrapartum oro/nasopharyngeal suctioning on the perineum is no longer recommended and does not reduce MAS. (Source: ANZCOR 13.4).

explanation.summary: NEC peaks in preterm infants in the second week of life. Bell staging: I suspected; IIA definite with pneumatosis intestinalis; IIB with portal venous gas or ascites; IIIA severe medical disease; IIIB perforation. IIA management is bowel rest, OG decompression, triple antibiotics (benzylpenicillin or ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole) for 7 to 10 days, parenteral nutrition, and serial AXR every 6 to 12 hours.
key_points: Pneumatosis intestinalis is pathognomonic for NEC
Portal venous gas suggests advanced disease (Bell IIB)
Free intraperitoneal air on lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral indicates perforation and surgery
Triple antibiotic cover for Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms
explanation.pearls: Falling platelet count and rising lactate are markers of deterioration and prompt surgical review even without radiographic perforation.

options.rationale: Continuing feeds in confirmed NEC (Bell IIA with pneumatosis) is contraindicated and risks progression to perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: NEC).
Advancing feeds is contraindicated; oral aminoglycosides not indicated for established NEC; bowel rest with parenteral broad-spectrum is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Surgery is for pneumoperitoneum, fixed bowel loop, palpable mass or deterioration despite medical therapy; Bell IIA without perforation is medical with surgical review on standby. Would be correct only with perforation or deterioration (Source: RCH CPG).

Bell stage IIA NEC (definite, with pneumatosis intestinalis) is managed medically with bowel rest, orogastric decompression, parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms (benzylpenicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole) and supportive care, per RCH CPG: Necrotising enterocolitis and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic.
Cefotaxime monotherapy does not adequately cover anaerobes; surgical review is mandatory at diagnosis. Would never be correct as sole therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: TTN results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, classically after elective caesarean without labour. It resolves within 24 to 72 hours with supportive oxygen and CPAP if needed. Key CXR differentiators: RDS = ground-glass with air bronchograms (preterm); MAS = patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation (term with meconium); pneumonia = focal consolidation; pneumothorax = hyperlucent hemithorax.
key_points: TTN: term, caesarean without labour, perihilar streaks and fissural fluid
RDS: preterm, diffuse ground-glass, surfactant deficiency
MAS: term post-dates, meconium liquor, patchy infiltrates
Pneumothorax: asymmetric breath sounds, hyperlucent on transillumination and CXR
explanation.pearls: If tachypnoea persists beyond 72 hours, reconsider the diagnosis.

options.rationale: TTN is managed supportively with non-invasive respiratory support (nasal high-flow or CPAP) titrated to keep SpO2 91 to 95 percent, gut rest until work of breathing settles, and IV maintenance fluids while waiting for fetal lung fluid to clear (usually within 24 to 72 hours). Persisting tachypnoea beyond 72 hours mandates reconsideration of the diagnosis (sepsis, cardiac, surfactant deficiency), per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress and Safer Care Victoria neonatal eHandbook.

Surfactant therapy is for respiratory distress syndrome (preterm, ground-glass with air bronchograms, surfactant deficiency); the CXR pattern and term gestation here are inconsistent with RDS, and surfactant is not indicated for TTN, per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress.

Empirical antibiotics in a term infant with negative maternal GBS, no fever, no prolonged ROM and a CXR pattern characteristic of TTN are not routinely required; antibiotics are reserved for clinical concern for sepsis or persisting illness beyond 72 hours, per RCH CPG: Early onset sepsis.

Weaning support and commencing feeds while the infant remains in significant respiratory distress (RR 78, grunting, FiO2 0.30) risks aspiration and worsens work of breathing; nil by mouth and continued support are appropriate until respiratory effort settles, per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress.

The infant is stable on non-invasive support with adequate saturations and a normal blood gas; intubation and tertiary transfer are reserved for failing non-invasive support, persistent hypoxaemia, or alternative diagnoses, per RCH CPG: Neonatal respiratory distress.

explanation.summary: Early-onset neonatal sepsis (less than 72 hours) is dominated by GBS and Gram-negatives, especially E. coli. Australian empirical therapy is benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) plus gentamicin. Late-onset sepsis (greater than 72 hours, particularly in the NICU) adds coagulase-negative Staphylococci, S. aureus and Gram-negatives, and typically uses flucloxacillin plus gentamicin or vancomycin in MRSA-prevalent units.
key_points: EOGBS empirical: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin
Late-onset: flucloxacillin plus gentamicin (community) or vancomycin plus gentamicin (NICU)
Add cefotaxime if meningitis is suspected or proven
Lumbar puncture should be done once the infant is stable enough
explanation.pearls: Cefazolin intrapartum prophylaxis is acceptable in non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; clindamycin is reserved for anaphylactic allergy with proven susceptibility.

options.rationale: Cefotaxime monotherapy is not standard empirical cover for EOS in AU; synergistic penicillin plus aminoglycoside is preferred. Would be correct only with cefotaxime added to a penicillin-aminoglycoside backbone with meningitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Early-onset neonatal sepsis (< 72 hours) is most commonly caused by group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli; the recommended empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic and RCH CPG: Early onset sepsis.

Flucloxacillin targets Staph aureus and is for late-onset sepsis with line infection, not first-line cover for EOGBS and E. coli. Would be correct for late-onset with line sepsis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Vanc plus cefotaxime is for late-onset hospital-acquired sepsis with meningitis suspicion or MRSA risk; not standard for early-onset community-presenting. Would be correct in late-onset (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Intrapartum cefazolin does not exclude sepsis with clinical deterioration; empirical antibiotics must be started. (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Congenital CMV is the leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children. Diagnosis requires viral detection (urine or saliva PCR) within the first 21 days of life to distinguish from postnatal acquisition. Symptomatic infants (CNS, hepatic, haematological or SNHL) benefit from 6 months of oral valganciclovir, with regular FBC for neutropenia and LFTs. All affected children need longitudinal audiology because hearing loss can be late-onset or progressive.
key_points: Saliva PCR is the first-line screening test; urine PCR confirms
Diagnostic window is the first 21 days of life
Treat symptomatic disease with valganciclovir 16 mg/kg BD for 6 months
Monitor for neutropenia, anaemia and transaminitis on treatment
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic congenital CMV with isolated SNHL is an area of active research; many AU centres treat with valganciclovir, but practice varies.

options.rationale: Symptomatic congenital CMV with end-organ involvement (microcephaly, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, intracranial calcifications, or sensorineural hearing loss) treated with oral valganciclovir 16 mg/kg BD for 6 months improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes; haematology and LFT monitoring is required because of neutropenia and hepatotoxicity, per RCH CPG: Congenital CMV and AAP Red Book.

Symptomatic congenital CMV warrants prompt antiviral; delaying to 12 months misses the window when valganciclovir improves outcomes. Would never be correct in symptomatic disease (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital CMV).

Six weeks IV ganciclovir was older regimen, superseded by 6 months oral valganciclovir (non-inferior, better neurodevelopmental/audiological). Would be correct only if oral not tolerated (Source: AAP Red Book).
CMV hyperimmune globulin is not standard postnatal therapy for symptomatic congenital CMV; oral valganciclovir is recommended. Would never be correct postnatally (Source: AAP Red Book).
Hearing rehab is part of care but does not replace antiviral, which improves hearing trajectories. Would never be correct alone (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Congenital syphilis is increasing in Australia, particularly in remote and Indigenous communities. Treatment of proven or highly probable disease (fourfold RPR titre difference, clinical features, abnormal CSF/long-bone films/LFTs) is IV benzylpenicillin for 10 days. Asymptomatic infants of inadequately treated mothers can sometimes receive a single IM benzathine dose if the full workup is normal.
key_points: Maternal treatment is inadequate if not benzathine penicillin, less than 4 weeks before delivery, or no fourfold drop in RPR
Long bone films show metaphysitis or periostitis; CSF VDRL confirms neurosyphilis
IV benzylpenicillin 30 mg/kg per dose for 10 days
Follow up RPR titres at 3, 6 and 12 months; expect fourfold decline
explanation.pearls: Antenatal screening in Australia now includes third-trimester syphilis serology in high-prevalence regions; a positive maternal test at 34 weeks should never be missed.

options.rationale: Single-dose IM benzathine is for infants with normal examination/investigations and adequately treated mothers; this infant has proven congenital syphilis. Would be correct only with normal exam/labs and treated mother (Source: Australian STI Guidelines).
Azithromycin is not recommended for congenital syphilis (resistance, CNS penetration); parenteral penicillin is only acceptable treatment. (Source: Australian STI Guidelines).
Treatment should not be delayed pending all confirmatory tests when clinical/serological/radiological findings establish probable congenital syphilis. (Source: RCH CPG).

Proven or highly probable congenital syphilis (fourfold higher RPR than maternal, clinical signs, abnormal radiographs or bloods) requires 10 days of IV benzylpenicillin 30 mg/kg per dose, dosed 12-hourly in the first week and 8-hourly thereafter, per RCH CPG: Congenital syphilis and Australian STI Management Guidelines.

Ceftriaxone has limited data in neonatal congenital syphilis and is not first-line; penicillin desensitisation should be performed if true allergy. Would be correct only with documented severe penicillin allergy after desensitisation failure (Source: Australian STI Guidelines).

explanation.summary: NAS from in-utero opioid exposure typically presents at 24 to 72 hours for methadone (later for buprenorphine). Non-pharmacological care (rooming-in, breastfeeding if not contraindicated, swaddling, low stimulation) is first. Pharmacological treatment with oral morphine begins when modified Finnegan scores remain at or above 8 for three consecutive measurements or two at or above 12 despite optimisation.
key_points: Methadone NAS peaks at 48 to 72 hours; buprenorphine later
Breastfeeding is encouraged unless co-use of cocaine, methamphetamine or untreated HIV
Morphine titration to Finnegan less than 8; wean by 10 percent every 24 to 48 hours
Phenobarbital is adjunctive for polysubstance or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: Naloxone in a baby of an opioid-dependent mother can precipitate seizures and is contraindicated even in apparent respiratory depression.

options.rationale: Breastfeeding is encouraged in stable methadone-maintained mothers and reduces NAS severity; switching to formula is not indicated. Would never be correct as routine (Source: RCH CPG: NAS).

Phenobarbital is adjunctive for polysubstance exposure or refractory NAS, not first-line monotherapy for opioid NAS where opioids are the agent of choice. Would be correct as adjunct in polysubstance NAS (Source: RCH CPG).
Naloxone is contraindicated in babies of opioid-dependent mothers (precipitates severe acute withdrawal/seizures). (Source: RCH CPG).
Persistent Finnegan 8+ requires inpatient monitoring and consideration of pharmacotherapy, not community follow-up. Would be correct only with Finnegan under 8 (Source: RCH CPG).

Three consecutive Finnegan scores at or above 8 (or two at or above 12) after maximal non-pharmacological care indicates pharmacological treatment; oral morphine is first-line for opioid-related NAS in Australia, typically starting at 0.04 to 0.05 mg/kg per dose 4-hourly, titrated to scores, per RCH CPG: Neonatal abstinence syndrome and Therapeutic Guidelines: Neonatal.

explanation.summary: Therapeutic hypothermia (whole-body or selective head cooling) reduces death and major neurodevelopmental disability in moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy. Eligibility: at least 35 weeks gestation, age less than 6 hours, evidence of perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia (cord pH 7.0 or below, base deficit 16 or higher, or APGAR 5 or less at 10 minutes, or ongoing resuscitation), and clinical or aEEG evidence of moderate or severe encephalopathy (Sarnat 2 or 3). Target temperature 33 to 34 deg C for 72 hours, rewarm at 0.5 deg C per hour.
key_points: Window: less than 6 hours of birth
Sarnat 1 (mild) does not require cooling; Sarnat 2 to 3 do
Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is first-line for neonatal seizures
Side effects of cooling: sinus bradycardia, thrombocytopenia, subcutaneous fat necrosis
explanation.pearls: Apparent shivering and decreased seizure threshold during rewarming are recognised; rewarm slowly and monitor aEEG closely.

options.rationale: Passive cooling to 35.5 degC does not provide target therapeutic range; servo-controlled cooling to 33-34 is required. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: ANZNN Cooling Protocol).
Normothermia is not the goal in confirmed moderate/severe HIE within 6 h; therapeutic hypothermia is evidence-based neuroprotection. (Source: ANZNN).

Term or near-term infants (at least 35 weeks gestation) within 6 hours of birth with evidence of perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia and moderate to severe encephalopathy (Sarnat 2 or 3) meet criteria for whole-body cooling to 33 to 34 deg C for 72 hours, with rewarming at 0.5 deg C per hour, per ANZNN Cooling Protocol and Cochrane: Cooling for HIE. Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is first-line for clinical seizures, per RCH CPG: Neonatal seizures.

Selective head cooling is alternative but duration is 72 h not 48, and AU/NZ units predominantly use whole-body cooling. Would be correct only with selective head cooling protocol at correct duration (Source: ANZNN).
Cooling must start within 6 h to be neuroprotective; waiting for MRI misses the window. (Source: Cochrane HIE).

explanation.summary: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is failure of the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance, producing right-to-left shunting through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, severe hypoxaemia and preductal-postductal SpO2 difference of 10% or more. Common antecedents include meconium aspiration, severe perinatal asphyxia, pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and pulmonary hypoplasia. Diagnosis is by echocardiogram showing right-to-left shunting, elevated pulmonary pressures, and a structurally normal heart - it is critical to exclude obstructed infradiaphragmatic total anomalous pulmonary venous return before treatment, because pulmonary vasodilators worsen pulmonary oedema in TAPVR. Management ladder: optimise ventilation (lung recruitment, PEEP, mild hyperventilation), correct acidosis, maintain adequate systemic BP (vasopressor support to drive shunt left-to-right), inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm. HFOV combines well with iNO. Sildenafil, milrinone and prostacyclin are adjuncts. ECMO is reserved for refractory disease with OI persistently above 25-40.
key_points: Differential cyanosis (preductal greater than postductal SpO2) suggests PPHN or coarctation
Echo must confirm shunt physiology and exclude structural heart disease before iNO
iNO 20 ppm is the standard starting dose
ECMO criteria: OI greater than 25 to 40 despite iNO and HFOV, plus reversible cause
explanation.pearls: In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm is first-line pulmonary vasodilator after optimising ventilation; rule out obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return on echo first - using iNO in obstructed TAPVR worsens pulmonary oedema dramatically (RCH CPG; RANZCN).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: PGE1 is for duct-dependent CHD; structurally normal heart with PPHN does not benefit and PGE1 can worsen pulmonary congestion. Would be correct in duct-dependent CHD (Source: RCH CPG: PPHN).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: PPHN with an oxygenation index above 20 in a term infant after optimisation of ventilation and surfactant warrants inhaled nitric oxide at a starting dose of 20 ppm; if response is inadequate or OI rises despite iNO, ECMO referral should be considered, per RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and BMJ Best Practice: PPHN.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: HFOV is useful adjunct to recruit atelectatic lung in MAS and may combine with iNO, but does not replace pulmonary vasodilator therapy in established PPHN. Would be correct as adjunct (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: ECMO is for refractory PPHN with OI persistently over 25-40 despite iNO and HFOV; bypassing iNO at OI 22 is premature. Would be correct at OI over 25-40 despite optimised therapy (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: Oral sildenafil is adjunctive or weaning therapy after iNO; not first-line in acute severe PPHN. Would be correct as weaning therapy (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease (transposition, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, severe Fallot, severe Ebstein) presents in the first hours to days with persistent cyanosis poorly responsive to oxygen. The hyperoxia test (PaO2 less than 150 mmHg / 20 kPa after 100 percent oxygen) supports cardiac cause. PGE1 0.05 microg/kg/min maintains the duct; lower doses (0.005 to 0.01 microg/kg/min) maintain an already open duct.
key_points: Hyperoxia test: PaO2 less than 150 mmHg suggests cardiac shunt
PGE1 side effects: apnoea (40 percent), fever, hypotension, jitteriness
Have intubation kit at bedside; transport by retrieval team
Always confirm with urgent echo before complex decisions
explanation.pearls: Differential cyanosis (preductal greater than postductal) suggests coarctation or interrupted arch; reverse differential cyanosis suggests TGA with coarctation.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease
RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: A cyanotic newborn who fails the hyperoxia test (PaO2 staying below 150 mmHg or 20 kPa) is presumed to have a duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart lesion until echo proves otherwise; PGE1 0.05 microg/kg/min maintains ductal patency, with awareness of apnoea, hypotension and fever, per RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Failed hyperoxia test indicates fixed right-to-left shunt; continued oxygen alone is inadequate and risks collapse if duct closes. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic CHD).
