source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: iNO is for PPHN with right-to-left ductal shunting on echo and structurally normal heart; presumptive PPHN before echo may worsen ductal-dependent CHD. Would be correct after echo confirms PPHN (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

options.rationale: Fluid bolus does not address the underlying shunt physiology; delaying echo risks ductal closure. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Closing duct in duct-dependent lesion is catastrophic; indometacin is for haemodynamically significant PDA in preterms without duct-dependent CHD. Would be correct only in haemodynamically significant PDA without ductal-dependency (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Causes of neonatal seizures, in rough order of frequency: HIE, ischaemic stroke and intracranial haemorrhage, infection (meningitis, encephalitis, sepsis), metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia, inborn errors), structural, and pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. A term infant without perinatal hypoxia and with normal initial bloods should prompt urgent MRI and LP. Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is the first-line antiepileptic in Australia.
key_points: Subtle seizures (eye deviation, cycling, lip smacking, apnoea) are common in neonates
First-line: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV load, repeat 10 mg/kg up to total 40 mg/kg
Second-line: levetiracetam or phenytoin; pyridoxine for refractory
Always seek the cause: imaging, LP, metabolic screen, glucose, electrolytes, ammonia
explanation.pearls: Perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke commonly presents as focal seizures in the first 72 hours of life in a previously well term baby; MRI with DWI is diagnostic.

options.rationale: Diazepam is not first-line in neonatal seizures and rectal route is unreliable; phenobarbital IV gives sustained levels and proven efficacy. Would never be correct in neonates (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures).
Ionised calcium 1.25 is within normal range; empirical calcium is not indicated and can cause arrhythmia if extravasated. Would be correct only with documented hypocalcaemia (Source: RCH CPG).
Pyridoxine is for refractory neonatal seizures unresponsive to standard antiepileptics; should not delay phenobarbital. Would be correct as second-line after phenobarbital failure (Source: RCH CPG).

Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV is first-line for confirmed neonatal seizures in Australian protocols; concurrently the cause must be sought (sepsis, metabolic, intracranial bleed or infarct, structural). MRI is preferred for parenchymal injury and stroke detection, per RCH CPG: Neonatal seizures and Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology.
This baby does not meet cooling criteria (no perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia, normal cord gas, normal APGARs). Would be correct only with HIE features (Source: ANZNN).

explanation.summary: Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (now vitamin K deficiency bleeding, VKDB) is preventable with prophylaxis. Classical VKDB occurs in days 1 to 7; late VKDB occurs from 2 weeks to 6 months and presents with intracranial haemorrhage in exclusively breastfed infants. IM vitamin K 1 mg as a single dose at birth is the gold standard; the oral alternative is 1 mg at birth, day 3 to 5, and 4 weeks. The historical leukaemia link from the 1990s has been refuted by multiple subsequent studies.
key_points: IM 1 mg single dose at birth is first-line
Oral regimen: 1 mg at birth, day 3 to 5, and 4 weeks; higher residual late VKDB risk
Late VKDB risk particularly in cholestasis (biliary atresia) and exclusive breastfeeding
Document consent process when families decline
explanation.pearls: If a baby on oral vitamin K develops cholestatic jaundice, switch to IM immediately.

options.rationale: NHMRC and RCH guidance recommends single-dose IM vitamin K 1 mg at birth as the most reliable prophylaxis against classical and late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB). When IM is declined, the recommended oral alternative is THREE 1 mg oral doses (birth, day 3 to 5, and 4 weeks) - not a single oral dose - with documented informed consent including the higher residual late VKDB risk, particularly with exclusive breastfeeding and undetected cholestasis, per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis and NHMRC Statement on Vitamin K.
A single oral dose does not provide adequate protection against late VKDB; the recommended oral regimen requires three 1 mg doses (birth, day 3 to 5, 4 weeks), per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis.

Vitamin K is required to prevent classical and late VKDB; the refutation of the leukaemia link does not eliminate the need for prophylaxis, and declining is not equivalent to safe practice, per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis and NHMRC Statement on Vitamin K.
Maternal supplementation does not provide adequate neonatal vitamin K stores or protect against late VKDB and is not a recommended substitute, per NHMRC Statement on Vitamin K.

Antenatal informed consent allows the family to consider evidence and ask questions in a low-pressure setting; deferring this discussion to the immediate postnatal period is not best practice and risks unprepared decision-making, per RCH CPG: Vitamin K prophylaxis.

explanation.summary: Preterm RDS is managed primarily with antenatal corticosteroids, early CPAP from delivery room, and surfactant delivered to those needing it. LISA delivers surfactant via a thin catheter while the infant continues spontaneous breathing on CPAP, reducing mechanical ventilation and bronchopulmonary dysplasia compared with INSURE (intubate, surfactant, extubate). Threshold for surfactant is typically FiO2 sustained above 0.3 (less than 28 weeks) or 0.3 to 0.4 (28 to 32 weeks).
key_points: Antenatal betamethasone halves RDS, IVH and neonatal mortality
Early CPAP at 6 to 8 cm H2O is first-line respiratory support
LISA / MIST reduces BPD versus INSURE in spontaneously breathing infants
Surfactant dose: poractant alfa 200 mg/kg initial; beractant 100 mg/kg
explanation.pearls: A second course of antenatal corticosteroids is considered if more than 7 to 14 days have elapsed and delivery remains likely within 7 days at gestation under 32 weeks.

options.rationale: AU threshold for surfactant in preterm RDS is sustained FiO2 over 0.3 (under 28 weeks) or 0.3-0.4 (28-32 weeks); ignoring 0.35 in 32-weeker risks worsening RDS. Would be correct only with FiO2 under threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Surfactant).
Prolonged ventilation after surfactant increases BPD risk in spontaneously breathing preterm; less invasive strategy preferred. Would be correct only in apnoea or failed CPAP (Source: ANZNN).

Postnatal corticosteroids in this context are inappropriate; antenatal steroids must be given to mother pre-delivery, and postnatal dexamethasone is for ventilator-dependent infants at risk of BPD. Would never be correct here (Source: RCH CPG).
Nebulised surfactant remains investigational and not recommended outside trials in AU; tracheal delivery is required for proven efficacy. (Source: RCH CPG).

In a preterm infant breathing spontaneously on CPAP, LISA (also called MIST in some AU centres) allows surfactant administration via a thin tracheal catheter while CPAP and spontaneous breathing continue, and reduces the rate of mechanical ventilation and BPD compared with INSURE, per RCH CPG: Surfactant administration and Cochrane: LISA versus INSURE.

explanation.summary: Roseola (HHV-6) classically causes 3 to 5 days of high fever in a well-appearing 6 to 24-month-old, with a blanching trunk-predominant rash erupting AS the fever resolves (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
key_points: Fever-then-rash pattern is the defining clinical clue (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
Self-limiting; no specific treatment beyond antipyresis and reassurance (StatPearls: Roseola).
Febrile convulsions occur in around 10 to 15% of cases during the fever phase (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
explanation.pearls: If a well child has a rash AS the fever breaks, think roseola; if the rash appears DURING fever with cough/coryza/conjunctivitis, think measles.

options.rationale: Fever-then-rash in a well 6 to 24-month-old (trunk-predominant blanching rash after defervescence) is classical roseola (HHV-6). Under NHMRC Staying Healthy and RCH guidance, roseola does not require formal childcare exclusion; exclusion ends once the child is afebrile and well, per NHMRC Staying Healthy and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

Measles requires fever PLUS cough, coryza or conjunctivitis with a cephalocaudal rash, none of which are present here; the well, post-defervescence trunk-predominant rash is roseola. Notification is required for measles but is not appropriate here, per NCIRS: Measles fact sheet and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.
Rubella shows tender suboccipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy with a face-first cephalocaudal rash, not the trunk-predominant post-defervescence pattern seen here, per RCH CPG: Rubella.

Scarlet fever has a sandpaper-textured rash with strawberry tongue, exudative pharyngitis and circumoral pallor; none are present and antibiotics are not indicated, per eTG: Group A streptococcal infection.

Roseola is self-limiting; antivirals are not indicated in immunocompetent infants, and there is no daycare-exclusion requirement beyond being afebrile and well, per RCH CPG: Viral exanthems and NHMRC Staying Healthy.

explanation.summary: Koplik spots, found on the buccal mucosa 1 to 2 days before rash onset, are pathognomonic for measles and allow earlier diagnosis and public health action before the typical caudal-spreading exanthem appears (NCIRS: Measles fact sheet).
key_points: Measles prodrome: fever + cough + coryza + conjunctivitis (the three Cs) (NCIRS: Measles).
Koplik spots appear 1 to 2 days BEFORE the rash (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
Rash starts at the hairline/face and spreads caudally over 3 days (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
Notifiable disease - urgent public health notification required at clinical suspicion (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
explanation.pearls: Suspect-then-isolate-then-test: place the child in a negative pressure single room with airborne and contact precautions and phone the public health unit before laboratory confirmation.

options.rationale: Measles is a notifiable disease in all Australian jurisdictions and clinical suspicion (especially with Koplik spots and an epidemiological link) triggers immediate isolation in a negative-pressure room with airborne and contact precautions and same-day phone notification to the public health unit BEFORE laboratory confirmation, to enable rapid contact tracing and PEP within the windows (MMR within 72 h, NHIG within 7 days), per CDNA: Measles SoNG and NCIRS: Measles fact sheet.

Waiting for laboratory confirmation before isolation and notification breaches Australian public health practice and delays contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis for susceptible contacts (the infant and pregnant parent in the bay), per CDNA: Measles SoNG.
Measles is airborne; droplet precautions alone are inadequate and a negative-pressure room with N95 respirator entry is required, per CDNA: Measles SoNG.

MMR is contraindicated in active suspected measles infection; vitamin A is recommended in confirmed cases of severe measles but does not replace isolation, notification, and inpatient assessment, and discharge before notification is unsafe, per WHO Measles guidelines and CDNA: Measles SoNG.

The clinical picture is classical measles, not bacterial sepsis or meningitis; antibiotics and LP are not indicated and isolation plus notification take priority, per RCH CPG: Febrile child and CDNA: Measles SoNG.

explanation.summary: For susceptible measles contacts, MMR within 72 hours is preferred in those eligible for live vaccine, but NHIG within 6 days is indicated in those for whom live vaccine is contraindicated: infants under 6 months, pregnant non-immune contacts, and severely immunocompromised patients (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).
key_points: MMR within 72h of exposure for eligible non-immune contacts (AIH: Measles).
NHIG within 6 days for pregnant non-immune, infants <6 months, severely immunocompromised (AIH: Measles).
Two documented MMR doses count as presumptive immunity in Australia (AIH: Measles).
Measles is notifiable - phone the public health unit on clinical suspicion (CDNA: Measles SoNG).
explanation.pearls: Pregnant non-immune contacts get NHIG, never MMR - live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

options.rationale: MMR is not used under 6 months because maternal antibody blunts the immune response and the vaccine is unreliable in this window; this infant should instead receive NHIG within 6 days. The action stated here would expose the infant to a live vaccine without conferring protection (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

Seroconversion takes around two weeks after a dose, so the MMR given five days ago is unlikely to be protective at this exposure - but a second early dose is not the standard PEP either; the child is over 12 months with a documented dose and is observed for prodrome with the routine 18-month MMR retained on schedule (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

MMR is a live vaccine and contraindicated in pregnancy. A non-immune pregnant contact within 6 days of exposure receives NHIG to attenuate or prevent maternal measles and its severe pregnancy complications (pneumonitis, prematurity, miscarriage). Her negative IgG on urgent serology confirms susceptibility (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles; CDNA: Measles SoNG).

MMR is a live vaccine and contraindicated in severe immunocompromise including induction chemotherapy; the action stated would carry vaccine-strain dissemination risk in a profoundly neutropenic child. The correct PEP for this contact is NHIG within 6 days (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

Two documented MMR doses meet the Australian definition of presumptive immunity; no further dose or NHIG is indicated. The action stated would be over-treatment of an already immune contact (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles).

explanation.summary: Severely immunocompromised susceptible children with significant varicella exposure should receive ZIG (zoster immunoglobulin) as soon as possible, ideally within 96 hours; live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in this group (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella).
key_points: Significant exposure = household OR >=1 hour indoor face-to-face OR shared room OR substantial hospital contact (AIH: Varicella).
Susceptible = no past disease, no vaccination, and seronegative if tested (AIH: Varicella).
ZIG first-line in immunocompromised, neonates, and non-immune pregnant women (AIH: Varicella).
Antiviral prophylaxis day 7 to 14 is an adjunct/alternative when ZIG unavailable (AIH: Varicella).
explanation.pearls: Neonates born to mothers who develop varicella from 7 days before to 2 days after delivery also need ZIG - very high mortality without it.

options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is live attenuated and CONTRAINDICATED in severely immunocompromised including those on induction chemo. Would be correct only in immunocompetent contacts (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Severely immunocompromised susceptible contacts (varicella IgG negative, no prior infection or vaccination) with a significant exposure should receive ZIG within 96 hours (preferably as soon as possible, but the AIH allows extension up to 10 days in some circumstances) to attenuate or prevent disseminated varicella (Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella).
Antiviral prophylaxis (days 7-14) is adjunct or alternative when ZIG unavailable; ZIG is preferred first-line. Would be correct when ZIG unavailable (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
Waiting for the rash forgoes the proven benefit of ZIG given before viraemia; disseminated varicella in immunocompromised carries significant mortality. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
Pre-treatment varicella IgG was negative documenting susceptibility; waiting for repeat serology delays ZIG and reduces effectiveness. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal septicaemia mandates immediate IV/IO ceftriaxone alongside fluid resuscitation - antibiotics must not be delayed by imaging or laboratory workup. Cultures are taken if access is fast; otherwise antibiotics go first (RCH CPG: Meningococcal infection).
key_points: Spreading non-blanching rash + shock = meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise (RCH: Meningococcal infection).
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV/IO without delay (eTG: Meningococcal disease).
Activate paediatric retrieval (NETS or state equivalent) early (RCH: Meningococcal infection).
Antibiotic prophylaxis for household and intimate contacts via public health unit (CDNA: Meningococcal SoNG).
explanation.pearls: If the petechiae are spreading WHILE you watch, you have minutes - antibiotics now, lines + fluids in parallel, retrieval call goes in before the third bolus.

options.rationale: This is meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise - rapidly spreading non-blanching rash with shock. Empirical IV (or IO if access difficult) ceftriaxone should be given as soon as access is obtained, ideally after cultures but NEVER delayed for them; fluid resuscitation, ABC support, and ICU/retrieval activation run in parallel (RCH CPG: Meningococcal infection; ANZCOR/APLS).

LP is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, or rapidly evolving purpura; CT-then-LP delays the only intervention that changes outcome. Would be correct only in stable patient with normal coags (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcal sepsis worsens mortality; cultures drawn only if access rapid, antibiotics must NOT wait. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Routine steroids are not the immediate priority and do not replace urgent antibiotics; stress-dose steroids may be considered later for refractory shock. Would be correct only later as adjunct in refractory shock (Source: ANZICS).
Even fully immunised children can develop IMD from non-vaccine strains or vaccine failure; the picture mandates immediate empirical therapy. (Source: CDNA IMD SoNG).

explanation.summary: Scarlet fever is group A streptococcal pharyngitis plus a toxin-mediated sandpaper-textured rash with strawberry tongue. First-line in Australia is phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg (max 500 mg) BD for 10 days (eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis).
key_points: Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue + flexural accentuation + circumoral pallor = scarlet fever (RCH: GAS).
First-line: penicillin V 10 days (eTG).
Severe penicillin allergy: macrolide (eTG).
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in high-ARF-risk settings have a different regimen and stricter follow-up (RHDAustralia).
explanation.pearls: Desquamation of fingertips and palms 1 to 2 weeks after the rash is a late clue if you missed the initial illness.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Group A streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days is first-line in non-high-ARF-risk Australian settings, but in high-ARF-risk settings (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in remote/regional areas, Maori and Pacific children) the preferred regimen is a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin to ensure compliance and prevent acute rheumatic fever, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline and eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

In an Aboriginal child from a high-ARF-risk remote setting with clinical scarlet fever (group A streptococcal pharyngitis with toxin-mediated exanthem), a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is the recommended Australian regimen to guarantee adherence and reduce ARF and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis risk, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline and eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
Amoxicillin is acceptable where penicillin V is unpalatable, but in high-ARF-risk settings an IM regimen is preferred to remove adherence as a failure mode, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline.

Cefalexin is broader-spectrum than necessary and reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy; it is not first-line in either standard or high-ARF-risk Australian settings, per eTG: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

Clinical scarlet fever with high ARF risk warrants immediate empirical antibiotics; awaiting culture results delays prevention of ARF and is not consistent with Australian guidance, per RHDAustralia ARF Guideline.

explanation.summary: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is an enteroviral infection (often coxsackie A16, less commonly EV71) causing low-grade fever, posterior-predominant oral ulcers and oval vesicles on palms, soles, and dorsa of hands/feet, often with nappy-area involvement in toddlers (RCH CPG: Viral exanthems).
key_points: Self-limiting; supportive care with hydration and analgesia (RCH: Viral exanthems).
Childcare exclusion: until all blisters have dried (NHMRC Staying Healthy).
EV71 strain can cause severe complications including aseptic meningitis, brainstem encephalitis, and acute flaccid paralysis (StatPearls: HFMD).
Differentiate from HSV gingivostomatitis: HSV = anterior/gingival, ill child, no acral lesions; HFMD = posterior oropharynx, acral lesions (RCH: Viral exanthems).
explanation.pearls: If a toddler refuses to drink because of mouth pain, accept dehydration is the real risk and admit for IV fluids - it is the only common reason HFMD comes back to ED.

options.rationale: Australian guidance (NHMRC Staying Healthy, RCH) recommends childcare exclusion until all blisters have dried (not just until afebrile). Red flags for severe enterovirus disease (especially EV71) include neurological signs (ataxia, myoclonus, irritability), persistent high fever beyond 3 days, persistent vomiting, and inability to maintain hydration, all of which warrant urgent reassessment, per NHMRC Staying Healthy and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease requires exclusion until blisters have dried under NHMRC Staying Healthy, not merely until afebrile; the lesions remain shedding virus, per NHMRC Staying Healthy.
Australian public health guidance does specify formal exclusion until blisters dry for hand-foot-and-mouth disease; no-exclusion advice is incorrect, per NHMRC Staying Healthy.
Aciclovir has no role in enteroviral HFMD; the diagnosis is not herpes simplex and antivirals are not indicated, per eTG: Herpes simplex and RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

She is clinically well, alert, perfused, and tolerating oral fluids in clinic; routine admission is not required and supportive outpatient care with explicit red-flag advice is appropriate, per RCH CPG: Viral exanthems.

explanation.summary: Pregnant women exposed to parvovirus B19 need serology to determine immune status; confirmed acute maternal infection in early-to-mid pregnancy triggers MFM-led MCA Doppler surveillance for fetal anaemia and hydrops (RANZCOG: Parvovirus in pregnancy).
key_points: About 50% of women of reproductive age are already immune (RANZCOG).
IgG positive / IgM negative = immune, reassure (RANZCOG).
IgG and IgM both negative = susceptible, repeat in 4 weeks (RANZCOG).
IgM positive = confirmed recent infection, refer MFM for serial MCA Doppler and ultrasound for hydrops (RANZCOG).
explanation.pearls: Highest risk for fetal loss/hydrops is exposure before 20 weeks; after 20 weeks the fetus has greater haematopoietic reserve and the fetal risk drops sharply.

options.rationale: Australian (RANZCOG) and KEMH guidance: serology first is the AU-recommended pathway. IgG positive / IgM negative confirms pre-existing immunity (around 50 percent of women) and no further action is needed. IgG and IgM both negative means susceptible: repeat serology in 4 weeks. IgM positive (or IgG seroconversion) is confirmed recent infection and triggers MFM referral for serial fetal ultrasound and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler velocimetry for at least 8 to 12 weeks, per RANZCOG: Parvovirus in pregnancy and KEMH: Parvovirus B19.

MCA Doppler surveillance is the correct AFTER-confirmation step but is unnecessary if she is already immune (around 50 percent prevalence) or if serology shows no infection; routine empirical Doppler before serology overcommits resources and is not the AU-recommended pathway, per RANZCOG: Parvovirus in pregnancy.

Amniocentesis is reserved for confirmed maternal infection with evidence of fetal compromise; it is invasive and inappropriate as a first-line investigation in an asymptomatic exposed contact, per RANZCOG: Parvovirus in pregnancy.

NHIG is not indicated for parvovirus B19 exposure in pregnancy; there is no proven prophylactic benefit and current Australian guidance recommends serology and surveillance instead, per Australian Immunisation Handbook.

Maternal parvovirus B19 infection can cause fetal anaemia and hydrops fetalis with the highest risk in the second trimester (around 9 to 20 weeks); discharge without serology at 18 weeks is unsafe, per RANZCOG: Parvovirus in pregnancy.

explanation.summary: Tinea corporis is a dermatophyte infection presenting as annular scaly plaques with active scaly raised borders and central clearing, common in contact sports through shared mats and equipment. First-line is topical terbinafine 1% twice daily for 1 to 2 weeks, plus equipment hygiene and treatment of affected teammates (eTG: Tinea).
key_points: Direct microscopy of skin scrapings positive for septate hyphae confirms dermatophyte (eTG: Tinea).
Topical terbinafine, miconazole, or clotrimazole BD x 2 weeks for limited disease (eTG: Tinea).
Oral antifungal for extensive disease, scalp, nails, or topical failure (eTG: Tinea).
Contact sport: do not return until lesions are no longer scaly and cannot be covered if competing (Sports Medicine Australia).
explanation.pearls: Pityriasis rosea looks similar but is scrape-negative and follows a Christmas-tree distribution along Langer's lines - and the herald patch precedes the eruption by 1 to 2 weeks, not 10 days.

options.rationale: Pityriasis rosea management; mycology positive here excludes pityriasis. Would be correct only with mycology-negative herald-patch-Christmas-tree pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Microscopy confirms septate hyphae - this is tinea corporis. Topical terbinafine 1% twice daily for 1 to 2 weeks (continuing for 1 week after clinical resolution) is first-line for limited disease, with lesion-edge application extending beyond the visible border (eTG: Tinea; RCH CPG: Tinea).

Oral antifungals are for extensive disease, scalp/hair (tinea capitis), nails, or topical failure; not for limited tinea corporis. Would be correct with extensive or scalp involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Topical steroid on tinea (tinea incognito) reduces inflammation transiently but worsens fungal growth and atypical spread; antihistamines do not treat infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Microscopy confirms fungal cause; antibacterial therapy inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN is a drug-induced, life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction with epidermal necrosis. Lamotrigine (especially with rapid titration or concurrent valproate) is one of the highest-risk agents. Stop the drug immediately, admit to burns/HDU, and engage ophthalmology early to prevent permanent ocular morbidity (eTG: Stevens-Johnson syndrome).
key_points: SJS: <10% BSA detachment; TEN: >30%; SJS/TEN overlap 10 to 30% (eTG: SJS).
Highest-risk drugs in children: lamotrigine, allopurinol, sulfonamides, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin), NSAIDs (eTG: SJS).
Mucosal involvement >=2 sites is required for SJS - eye involvement is the leading long-term morbidity driver (eTG: SJS).
Add to ADR / Lifetime Drug Alert / Australian Vaccine and Medicine Allergy Service notification (TGA).
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine titration too fast (or alongside valproate, which doubles the lamotrigine level) is the classic exam trigger - in real life, titration must follow product information to halve the SJS risk.

options.rationale: SSSS affects younger children (under 5), spares mucosae, no target lesions or drug history; carbamazepine is also an aromatic anticonvulsant that cross-reacts with lamotrigine in SCAR. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

EM has three-zone target lesions, acral, usually post-HSV; this case is dusky macules with sloughing and positive Nikolsky pointing to SJS. Half-dose lamotrigine continues the offending drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

HSV-associated EM has classic targets and minimal-to-modest mucosal involvement; diffuse dusky macules with bullae and Nikolsky in a child on a high-risk drug fits SJS. Would be correct only in HSV-associated EM (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Bullae plus positive Nikolsky sign plus involvement of at least two mucosal sites plus recent high-risk drug (lamotrigine, particularly with rapid titration or with concurrent valproate) is Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN spectrum. Immediate cessation of the offending agent, admission to a paediatric burns or HDU equivalent for fluid and skin care, and urgent ophthalmology review (ocular sequelae are the leading long-term morbidity) are mandatory (eTG: Stevens-Johnson syndrome; RCH CPG: Stevens-Johnson syndrome).
SJS has 5-15 percent mortality with delayed care and sight-threatening ocular sequelae; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Post-varicella invasive group A streptococcal infection with necrotising soft tissue infection and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is a paediatric emergency. Recognition rests on pain out of proportion to skin findings, focal anaesthesia, dusky skin, erythroderma, and rapid multi-organ failure. Resuscitate, broad antibiotics including clindamycin, and urgent surgical debridement (eTG: Necrotising soft tissue infection).
key_points: Pain out of proportion + focal anaesthesia + dusky skin + shock = nec fasc until proven otherwise (eTG).
Clindamycin is critical - inhibits exotoxin production (eTG).
Definitive treatment is surgical - imaging must not delay theatre (RCH CPG: Necrotising fasciitis).
iGAS post-varicella is a recognised pattern in Australian and international cohorts (CDNA: iGAS SoNG).
explanation.pearls: If you are not sure whether to call the surgeons, you already are - operative inspection is both diagnostic and therapeutic and there is no safer time than now.

options.rationale: Imaging must NOT delay surgical exploration in suspected nec fasc; diagnosis is surgical and operative inspection is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Atypical KD can mimic but pain disproportionate to skin findings, lactic acidosis, AKI, dusky soft tissue over healing varicella point to invasive bacterial supra-infection. Would be correct only with KD-specific features (Source: RCH CPG).

Disseminated varicella in immunocompetent child is rare; focal painful thigh with anaesthesia and toxin-mediated picture point to bacterial supra-infection. Would be correct only with disseminated VZV (Source: RCH CPG).
Scarlet fever has sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue, not shock/lactic acidosis/AKI/pain disproportionate to skin. Would be correct in scarlet fever pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Post-varicella, pain out of proportion to skin findings, focal anaesthesia, dusky skin, erythroderma, shock and multi-organ derangement (acute kidney injury, transaminitis, lactic acidosis) is invasive group A streptococcal infection with necrotising soft tissue infection plus streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Broad-spectrum cover (e.g. ceftriaxone) PLUS anti-staphylococcal (vancomycin) PLUS clindamycin (toxin suppression and ribosomal action) are essential, with urgent surgical debridement the definitive intervention - antibiotics do not penetrate necrotic tissue (eTG: Necrotising soft tissue infection; RCH CPG: Necrotising fasciitis).

explanation.summary: In a well pre-continent infant requiring confirmatory culture, clean catch is the preferred non-invasive method; bag specimens are inadequate, and SPA or catheter samples are reserved for unwell infants or failed clean catch (RCH CPG - Urinary tract infection).
key_points: Kass criterion: clean catch growth greater than 10^5 cfu/mL single organism = UTI
Catheter sample threshold: greater than 5 x 10^4 cfu/mL
SPA: any growth of a single Gram-negative organism is significant
Bag specimens used only for screening; positives must be confirmed
Bladder stimulation (suprapubic tap, paravertebral massage) improves clean catch yield
explanation.pearls: If the infant is septic and requires antibiotics within the hour, catheter or SPA is appropriate so cultures are not delayed.

sources.label: AAP - UTI in febrile infants 2-24 months

options.rationale: Bag specimens have ~60 percent contamination and Kass threshold cannot be applied; a positive bag must be confirmed. Would never be confirmatory; only useful as screening to be confirmed (Source: RCH CPG: UTI).

Catheter is for unwell infants needing immediate antibiotics or after failed clean catch; invasive and not first-line in well child whose mother can wait. Would be correct only in septic infant or failed clean catch (Source: RCH CPG).

In a pre-continent infant the RCH and NICE preferred non-invasive method is clean catch after perineal cleaning, often facilitated by bladder stimulation manoeuvres; growth of greater than 10^5 cfu/mL of a single organism meets Kass criteria for UTI (RCH CPG - Urinary tract infection; NICE NG224).

SPA is gold standard but invasive/painful and reserved for failed less-invasive collection or immediate sterile sample in septic infant. Would be correct in septic infant when other methods fail (Source: RCH CPG).
Nappy pad/cotton wool is unreliable for culture (contamination, cell lysis); not recommended for confirmatory specimens. Would never be confirmatory (Source: NICE NG224).

explanation.summary: Infants under 3 months with a positive urine require admission, blood culture, LP and IV penicillin plus gentamicin to cover E. coli, GBS and Listeria; oral therapy and outpatient management are unsafe (RCH CPG - Urinary tract infection).
key_points: Under 3 months UTI = admit, septic workup, IV antibiotics
Empirical regimen: IV benzylpenicillin + gentamicin
LP recommended given bacteraemia rate up to 10 percent and meningitis up to 2 percent
Switch to oral after 48 hours if culture sensitive and child improving
Total course typically 7-10 days
explanation.pearls: A positive urine in a young infant is not just a UTI; treat as occult bacteraemia until cultures return.

options.rationale: Outpatient oral is not appropriate in under-3-months with culture-suggestive UTI (high bacteraemia/meningitis risk). (Source: RCH CPG: UTI).
Antibiotics must not be withheld pending formal culture once urine microscopy is positive in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG).
Short stay with oral does not meet under-3-months pathway; IV plus LP are mandated regardless of clinical appearance. (Source: RCH CPG).

LP cannot be deferred in under-3-months with proven UTI (bacteraemia/meningitis risk), and ceftriaxone monotherapy omits Listeria cover. Would be correct only in over-3-months with selective workup (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Under 3 months with a positive urine result requires admission, blood culture, lumbar puncture and IV cover against E. coli, GBS and Listeria; benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the RCH and eTG empirical regimen (RCH CPG - Urinary tract infection; Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral after recurrent febrile UTI in a young child. DMSA at 4 to 6 months is the NICE NG224 recommendation and is not included in the RCH cascade. MCUG is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound.
key_points: RCH Melbourne recurrent-UTI imaging: renal tract ultrasound plus specialist referral
DMSA is a NICE construct not adopted by RCH
MCUG only after atypical features or abnormal ultrasound
CT and MAG3 are not screening tests for recurrent UTI
explanation.pearls: Recurrence and chronic constipation often go together; bladder-bowel dysfunction is a high-yield modifiable target.

options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral after recurrent febrile UTI in a young child; DMSA is part of the NICE NG224 algorithm and is not part of the RCH cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; DMSA is not part of the RCH recurrent-UTI imaging cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MCUG is invasive and is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; it is not the RCH first-line investigation in recurrent UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MAG3 renography is reserved for suspected obstruction or differential function questions, not as a screening test after recurrent UTI in the RCH pathway. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)
CT delivers significant ionising radiation and has no routine role in screening children for scarring or reflux. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Bag urine is a screening test only and cannot exclude or confirm UTI; clinical suspicion in a febrile pre-continent child requires clean catch or catheter sampling for diagnosis (RCH CPG - Urinary tract infection).
key_points: Bag contamination rate ~60 percent
Nitrites need >=4 hour bladder dwell to be reliable
Not all uropathogens reduce nitrate (eg Enterococcus, Pseudomonas)
Confirm any abnormal bag dip with clean catch or catheter sample
Symptoms + sterile-method culture, not bag urine, drive treatment
explanation.pearls: Trust the clinical picture more than the bag urine - a well child with negative bag and no fever may still need watchful waiting; a febrile child needs a reliable sample.

sources.label: AAP - UTI in febrile infants 2-24 months

options.rationale: Bag urine cannot reliably exclude UTI: nitrites require 4+ h bladder dwell (often negative in frequent voiders) and not all uropathogens reduce nitrates. (Source: NICE NG224; RCH CPG).
Empirical antibiotics should not be started on bag urine alone; reliable confirmatory sample is required first. (Source: RCH CPG).
Negative nitrites do not exclude UTI in infants (short bladder dwell, non-nitrate-reducing uropathogens). (Source: NICE NG224).
source_refs: AAP - UTI in febrile infants 2-24 months

options.rationale: Bag samples have ~60 percent contamination and do not meet Kass criteria; bag-urine culture cannot reliably exclude infection. (Source: RCH CPG).

Bag urine is not diagnostic. Australian guidance (RCH CPG: UTI, NICE NG224): bag urine is for screening only because of high contamination and unreliable nitrites; a clean-catch (or catheter/SPA if unwell) is required for diagnosis. Antibiotics should not be started on bag urine alone.

explanation.summary: Concentrated urine with FENa under 1 percent, low urine sodium and bland sediment in a clinically dehydrated child is prerenal AKI; failure to recover after volume restoration would suggest progression to ATN (RCH CPG - Acute kidney injury).
key_points: FENa <1% favours prerenal; >2% favours ATN (less reliable on diuretics)
Urine osmolality >500 in prerenal; ~300 (isosthenuric) in ATN
Urine Na <20 in prerenal; >40 in ATN
Bland sediment in prerenal; muddy brown casts in ATN
Urea:creatinine ratio >100:1 (mmol units) favours prerenal
explanation.pearls: Volume responsiveness within hours is the strongest confirmatory test for prerenal physiology.

options.rationale: Postrenal AKI requires sonographic evidence of obstruction (hydronephrosis, distended bladder); US is normal and bladder fills appropriately. Would be correct with hydronephrosis (Source: RCH CPG: AKI).

ATN typically has FENa over 2 percent, urine osmolality near plasma, and muddy brown granular casts; this child's urine is concentrated with FENa 0.4 percent. Would be correct with FENa over 2 and casts (Source: KDIGO 2012).

FENa under 1 percent, concentrated urine with osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg, low urine sodium and bland sediment with a normal renal ultrasound in a clinically dehydrated child indicate prerenal physiology with preserved tubular sodium reabsorption (RCH CPG - Acute kidney injury; KDIGO 2012 - AKI guideline).
AIN typically has pyuria, WBC casts, eosinophiluria and drug history; sediment bland and no offending medication. Would be correct with drug history and eosinophiluria (Source: KDIGO).
Glomerulonephritis has haematuria, RBC casts and proteinuria, often hypertension; sediment bland and no proteinuria/HTN. Would be correct with nephritic sediment (Source: KDIGO 2021).

explanation.summary: Suspected posterior urethral valves with obstructive AKI is managed by immediate small-calibre urethral catheterisation to decompress the bladder, followed by biochemical correction and definitive cystoscopic valve ablation once stable (RCH CPG - Posterior urethral valves; EAU Paediatric Urology Guidelines).
key_points: PUV is the commonest male infant obstructive uropathy
Antenatal clues: bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, thickened bladder, keyhole sign, oligohydramnios
First step: 8 Fr feeding tube as urethral catheter (avoid Foley)
Treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis, sepsis adjunctively
Definitive: cystoscopic valve ablation once stable
explanation.pearls: A Foley balloon can lodge in the prostatic urethra and worsen the obstruction; use a feeding tube or paediatric urinary catheter.

options.rationale: Definitive valve ablation is eventual treatment but only after resuscitation and bladder drainage; immediate priority is decompression. Would be correct only after stabilisation (Source: EAU Paediatric Urology).
Diuretics are contraindicated in postrenal AKI with downstream obstruction (worsens upper tract pressure) and won't lower K until obstruction relieved. (Source: KDIGO 2012).

The immediate intervention in suspected PUV with obstructive AKI and electrolyte derangement is catheter drainage (small-calibre urethral catheter, not a Foley balloon which can be held in the prostatic urethra) to relieve the obstruction and allow biochemical correction before valve ablation (RCH CPG - Posterior urethral valves; EAU Paediatric Urology Guidelines).

Nephrostomy is for failed bladder drainage, ureteric obstruction or supravesical pathology; bladder catheterisation is first-line in PUV. Would be correct only after failed bladder drainage (Source: EAU Paediatric).

Hyperkalaemia stabilisation is appropriate adjunctively but does not address the obstructive cause; without bladder drainage AKI and acidosis won't resolve. Would be correct as adjunct alongside catheter (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (no remission after 4-6 weeks daily prednisolone with or without IV pulses) requires renal biopsy and genetic testing before tailoring second-line immunosuppression, which is typically a calcineurin inhibitor in the absence of monogenic cause (KDIGO 2021 - Nephrotic syndrome).
key_points: Steroid resistance = no remission after 4-6 weeks high-dose prednisolone
Biopsy: FSGS most common; less often MCD, membranous, C3 glomerulopathy
Genetic panel: NPHS1, NPHS2, WT1, INF2, TRPC6
Monogenic SRNS poorly responsive to immunosuppression - kidney transplant has lower recurrence risk
Calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or ciclosporin) first-line second agent in non-monogenic SRNS
explanation.pearls: Always confirm compliance and exclude secondary causes (HBV, HIV, lupus, malignancy) before labelling steroid resistant.

options.rationale: Failure to remit after 4-6 weeks daily prednisolone defines steroid resistance; prolonging exposes the child to side effects without benefit. (Source: KDIGO 2021).

Calcineurin inhibitors are second-line but should be initiated AFTER biopsy and genetic results, since monogenic causes respond poorly. Would be correct after biopsy and negative genetic panel (Source: KDIGO 2021).

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome requires biopsy to characterise histology (commonly FSGS, less often MCD or membranous) and genetic testing for monogenic podocytopathies (NPHS1, NPHS2, WT1) which predicts response to second-line immunosuppression (KDIGO 2021 - Nephrotic syndrome; KHA-CARI - Nephrotic syndrome in children).

Rituximab is for frequently-relapsing/steroid-dependent and selected SRNS, only after biopsy and confirmation of histology/genetic status. Would be correct after biopsy in selected cases (Source: KDIGO 2021).
ACEi is adjunctive antiproteinuric in SRNS but immunosuppression cannot be ceased abruptly without confirmed histology. Would be correct as adjunct, not as primary withdrawal (Source: KDIGO 2021).

explanation.summary: PSGN is distinguished from IgA nephropathy and HSP by low C3 with usually normal C4, elevated streptococcal serology (ASO, anti-DNase B), and a 1-3 week latent period after pharyngitis (3-6 weeks after impetigo); IgA shows synpharyngitic haematuria and HSP has palpable purpura with joint involvement (RCH CPG - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
key_points: PSGN: low C3, latent 1-3 weeks post-pharyngitis, elevated ASO/anti-DNase B
IgA nephropathy: synpharyngitic (1-2 days), normal complement, raised IgA
HSP nephritis: purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, normal complement
Hypertension and oedema common to all three nephritic syndromes
C3 normalises within 6-8 weeks in PSGN; persistent low C3 suggests MPGN or lupus
explanation.pearls: Persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks in suspected PSGN should prompt biopsy to exclude C3 glomerulopathy or lupus nephritis.

options.rationale: Hypocomplementaemia (low C3 with usually normal C4 via the alternative pathway) following a recent streptococcal infection is characteristic of PSGN; both IgA nephropathy and HSP nephritis typically have normal complement (RCH CPG - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; KDIGO 2021 - Glomerular diseases).
Macroscopic haematuria with dysmorphic cells and RBC casts is shared across all three glomerulonephritides and does not discriminate. Would never be discriminating (Source: KDIGO 2021).
Synpharyngitic haematuria (1-2 days post-pharyngitis) is the hallmark of IgA nephropathy; PSGN has 1-3 week latency. Would be correct for IgA nephropathy (Source: KDIGO 2021).
Palpable purpura with arthralgia is defining for IgA vasculitis (HSP), not PSGN. Would be correct for HSP (Source: RCH CPG).
Elevated serum IgA supports IgA nephropathy not PSGN; PSGN is characterised by streptococcal markers and complement consumption. Would be correct only for IgA nephropathy (Source: KDIGO 2021).

explanation.summary: STEC-HUS is treated supportively with cautious fluids, RBC transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, hypertension control, and avoidance of platelets, antibiotics and antimotility agents; dialysis is added if indications develop (RCH CPG - Haemolytic uraemic syndrome).
key_points: Triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI
Avoid platelets unless major bleeding (microthrombus risk)
Avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents in STEC phase
Supportive cautious fluids; avoid overload in oliguric phase
Eculizumab in atypical HUS, not STEC-HUS
explanation.pearls: Antibiotics and loperamide are the two interventions students reflexively give for bloody diarrhoea that worsen outcomes in suspected HUS.

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in STEC-HUS may exacerbate microvascular thrombosis and is avoided unless active major bleeding or planned invasive procedure. Would be correct only for active bleeding (Source: Australasian Paediatric Nephrology).

Plasma exchange is for TTP and atypical HUS, not STEC-HUS where it has not shown benefit; reserved for diagnostic uncertainty pending ADAMTS13. Would be correct in TTP or atypical HUS (Source: Australasian Paediatric Nephrology).
Antibiotics for STEC are associated with increased HUS progression risk (toxin release) and not recommended once HUS is established. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS).

Management of STEC-HUS is supportive: cautious isotonic fluids to maintain euvolaemia (avoid overload in oliguric phase), red cell transfusion for symptomatic or severe anaemia (typically Hb <60-70 g/L), antihypertensive treatment, and avoidance of platelet transfusion unless active major bleeding because of microthrombus risk (RCH CPG - Haemolytic uraemic syndrome).
Antimotility agents are contraindicated in STEC (prolong toxin contact) and increase HUS risk/severity. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS).

explanation.summary: Dialysis indications in paediatric AKI follow AEIOU (Acidosis, Electrolyte, Ingestion, Overload, Uraemia); refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema and persistent anuria with rising urea collectively indicate immediate renal replacement (RCH CPG - Acute kidney injury).
key_points: Acidosis: pH <7.2 or bicarbonate <12 refractory to therapy
Electrolytes: K >6.5 not responding, severe hyper/hyponatraemia
Ingestion: dialysable toxins (salicylate, methanol, lithium)
Overload: pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics
Uraemia: encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding, urea >40 in children
explanation.pearls: Half of children with STEC-HUS require dialysis; early planning of access avoids emergent line insertion in coagulopathic patients.

options.rationale: Medical hyperkalaemia management provides temporary shift only and does not address overload/acidosis/anuria; failure to respond is itself a dialysis indication. Would be correct only as initial bridge to RRT (Source: KDIGO 2012 AKI).
Diuretics are unlikely effective in established anuric AKI and not a substitute for RRT when AEIOU indications are met. Would be correct only in non-anuric AKI (Source: KDIGO 2012).
Further fluid in established anuric HUS with rising weight, HTN and pulmonary oedema worsens overload. (Source: KDIGO 2012).

Renal replacement is indicated when any AEIOU criterion is met: refractory acidosis (pH <7.2, bicarbonate <12), refractory electrolyte derangement (K >6.5 not responding to medical therapy), fluid overload causing pulmonary oedema, uraemic symptoms, or oligo/anuria with biochemical deterioration; this child meets multiple criteria (RCH CPG - Acute kidney injury; Australasian Paediatric Nephrology - HUS guidance).
Resonium is slow and risks intestinal necrosis in unwell paediatric patients and does not address acidosis/overload. Would be correct only as adjunct in non-emergent setting (Source: KDIGO 2012).

explanation.summary: Atypical HUS is suggested by absent diarrhoeal prodrome, negative STEC testing, family history of unexplained renal failure or TMA, and low C3 with normal C4 reflecting alternative complement pathway activation; confirmation requires complement gene panel and treatment is eculizumab (Australasian Paediatric Nephrology - HUS guidance).
key_points: STEC-HUS: bloody diarrhoea, Shiga toxin positive, supportive treatment
Atypical HUS: no diarrhoea, STEC negative, complement dysregulation (CFH, CFI, MCP, C3)
Secondary TMA: drugs (calcineurin, quinine), pregnancy, malignancy, HIV
TTP: ADAMTS13 <10%, plasma exchange
Eculizumab indicated in atypical HUS, not STEC-HUS
explanation.pearls: Send complement genetics and CFH antibodies early in suspected atypical HUS - results take weeks and the diagnosis drives eculizumab decisions.

options.rationale: Atypical HUS classically lacks the bloody diarrhoea prodrome of STEC-HUS, has negative Shiga toxin testing, and frequently shows a family history of similar TMA or unexplained renal failure due to inherited complement regulatory protein mutations (Australasian Paediatric Nephrology - HUS guidance; KDIGO 2021 - Glomerular diseases).
The HUS triad is common to all HUS subtypes (STEC, complement-mediated, secondary). Would never be discriminating (Source: RCH CPG: HUS).
Hypertension occurs in both STEC and atypical HUS through volume and renin pathways. Would never be discriminating (Source: RCH CPG).
Normal ADAMTS13 excludes TTP but does not distinguish STEC from atypical HUS. Would discriminate from TTP, not between STEC and atypical (Source: KDIGO 2021).
Atypical HUS can be triggered by URTI but so can STEC; URTI alone is non-discriminating. Would never be discriminating (Source: Australasian Paediatric Nephrology).

explanation.summary: Acute PSGN is managed supportively with admission, sodium and fluid restriction, antihypertensive treatment, and a single course of oral penicillin; most children recover spontaneously with normalisation of C3 by 8 weeks (RCH CPG - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
key_points: Admit for monitoring of BP, fluid balance and renal function
Salt restrict to ~1-2 mmol/kg/day; fluid restrict to insensible + UO
Furosemide for fluid overload; CCB (eg nifedipine) or labetalol for severe hypertension
Single course of penicillin to eradicate residual GAS
Monitor C3 - persistent low at 8 weeks prompts biopsy
explanation.pearls: PSGN is overrepresented in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, often following skin sores; address scabies and impetigo at a community level.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in uncomplicated PSGN, which is supportive while complement normalises. (Source: RCH CPG: PSGN).

Biopsy is for atypical features (low C3 over 8 weeks, progressive AKI, nephrotic-range proteinuria, diagnostic uncertainty); classic clinical/serological PSGN does not need biopsy. Would be correct with atypical features (Source: KDIGO 2021).
Plasma exchange is not indicated in uncomplicated PSGN; ACEi can worsen AKI in acute oliguric phase and is not first-line antihypertensive in PSGN. (Source: KDIGO 2021).

Severe HTN over 99th centile with AKI warrants admission for monitoring, antihypertensive therapy and recognition of complications. Would be correct only in mild PSGN without severe HTN/AKI (Source: RCH CPG).

Acute PSGN management is supportive: admit for sodium and fluid restriction to manage circulatory overload, antihypertensive therapy (loop diuretic and/or calcium channel blocker for severe hypertension), and a single course of oral penicillin to eradicate residual group A strep colonisation (RCH CPG - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Hypospadias affects about 1 in 250 Australian male newborns and is identified on the neonatal check by ventral meatus, dorsal prepucial hood and chordee. Distal forms (glanular, coronal, subcoronal) make up around 70% and have excellent surgical outcomes when repaired in a single stage at 6-18 months. Even mild distal hypospadias is an absolute contraindication to neonatal circumcision because the prepuce is harvested for urethroplasty. Isolated hypospadias with bilateral descended testes does not warrant disorder-of-sex-development workup; karyotype, electrolytes and pelvic ultrasound are indicated only when associated with bilateral undescended testes, micropenis, or ambiguous external genitalia. All cases warrant routine paediatric urology referral and explicit documentation that ritual or medical circumcision must be deferred.
key_points: Hypospadias triad: ventral meatus, hooded foreskin, chordee
Distal (glanular/coronal) most common; proximal involves shaft/perineum
Avoid neonatal circumcision - foreskin needed for repair
Repair typically 6-18 months of age
DSD screen if proximal, bifid scrotum, or unilateral/bilateral UDT
explanation.pearls: A ventral meatus, dorsal hooded prepuce and chordee mean the foreskin is needed for two-stage urethroplasty - any neonatal circumcision burns the surgical bridge (RCH CPG; APSU).

sources.label: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Hypospadias contraindicates neonatal circumcision because the foreskin is required as tissue for urethroplasty. Would never be correct in any hypospadias (Source: RCH CPG: Hypospadias).

Hypospadias is a contraindication to neonatal circumcision because the prepuce is needed for urethroplasty. Karyotype and DSD workup are reserved for proximal hypospadias, hypospadias plus undescended testis, or bifid scrotum; isolated distal hypospadias with bilateral descended testes does NOT require karyotyping.
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Even partial circumcision compromises the prepuce needed for urethroplasty. (Source: RCH CPG).
Distal hypospadias with chordee requires paediatric urology assessment and family counselling, even with normal voiding. (Source: RCH CPG).

DSD workup is for proximal hypospadias, hypospadias with undescended testis or bifid scrotum, not isolated distal hypospadias with descended testes. Would be correct only in proximal/cryptorchid presentations (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

explanation.summary: Proximal hypospadias with a non-palpable gonad or bifid scrotum is treated as a DSD pending workup: karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, 17-OHP for CAH, electrolytes and androgen profile; sex assignment and surgery are deferred until the multidisciplinary team has a diagnosis (RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development).
key_points: DSD red flags: proximal hypospadias, bifid scrotum, non-palpable gonad(s), micropenis, clitoromegaly
Urgent investigations: karyotype, pelvic USS, 17-OHP, electrolytes, LH/FSH/testosterone
Salt-wasting CAH presents day 7-14 with vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, shock
Multidisciplinary team: endocrinology, urology, genetics, psychology, social work
Birth registration may be deferred while assignment decisions are made
explanation.pearls: A genital examination at birth missing one or both gonads in a phenotypic male is an emergency for endocrine assessment, not a routine paediatric problem.

sources.label: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Proximal (penoscrotal) hypospadias with a non-palpable gonad or bifid scrotum is a DSD and triggers urgent multidisciplinary workup including karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, 17-OHP for CAH, electrolytes and androgen profile; sex assignment is deferred pending the workup (RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Surgery cannot be planned until sex of rearing is determined; proximal hypospadias with non-palpable gonad is DSD until proven otherwise. (Source: RCH CPG: DSD).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: This is proximal hypospadias with cryptorchidism and bifid scrotum - highest-risk for DSD. Would never be correct in this presentation (Source: RCH CPG).
Glucocorticoid replacement is for confirmed/strongly suspected CAH with salt wasting; empirical steroids mask diagnosis. Would be correct only in confirmed/suspected adrenal crisis (Source: APEG).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Outpatient deferral risks missing salt-wasting CAH crisis in week 2 and delays MDT DSD workup. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

explanation.summary: An undescended testis that cannot be held in the scrotum should be referred for orchidopexy between 6 and 18 months; later surgery loses the fertility and malignancy benefit, and imaging adds little value (RCH CPG - Undescended testes).
key_points: Palpable UDT: inguinal orchidopexy 6-18 months
Non-palpable UDT: laparoscopic exploration
Retractile testis: stays in scrotum after manipulation - observe
Ascending testis: previously scrotal, now not - refer
Long-term risk: subfertility and 4-7x increased testicular cancer risk (location and timing dependent)
explanation.pearls: Examine in a warm room with warm hands - cremasteric reflex is brisk in toddlers and can mislead the unwary into reassurance.

options.rationale: Truly retractile testis stays in the scrotum after manipulation; this one does not, defining undescended/ascending testis requiring referral. Would be correct only with truly retractile testis (Source: RACS).

Australian and international guidelines recommend orchidopexy between 6 and 18 months for palpable undescended testes; surgery in this window preserves germ cell numbers and reduces long-term subfertility and malignancy risk compared with later intervention (RCH CPG - Undescended testes; RACS - Undescended testis position statement; EAU Paediatric Urology Guidelines).
Delaying beyond 18 months increases subfertility and malignancy risk; modern paediatric anaesthesia in infants is safe. (Source: RACS).
Hormonal therapy has low success/high relapse rates and is not recommended first-line in AU. (Source: EAU Paediatric Urology).
US does not reliably locate non-palpable testis and does not change surgical plan; imaging delays definitive management. (Source: RACS).

explanation.summary: A phenotypic male newborn with bilateral non-palpable gonads must be worked up urgently as a DSD with karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, 17-OHP and electrolytes to exclude virilised 46,XX CAH, partial androgen insensitivity or gonadal dysgenesis; surgery and sex assignment are deferred (RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development).
key_points: Bilateral non-palpable gonads = DSD until proven otherwise
Salt-wasting CAH presents day 7-14: vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, shock
Investigations: karyotype, pelvic USS, 17-OHP, electrolytes, LH/FSH/testosterone, HCG stimulation
Multidisciplinary input from endocrinology, urology, genetics, psychology
Defer birth registration if needed; ethics and family support essential
explanation.pearls: The cleanest way to flag this on the postnatal ward is to document the testes as palpable or not at every newborn check - the diagnosis is in the examination.

sources.label: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Bilateral non-palpable gonads in a phenotypic male is a DSD red flag requiring urgent multidisciplinary workup to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia (a virilised 46,XX female), partial androgen insensitivity, gonadal dysgenesis or anorchia; investigations include karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, 17-OHP, electrolytes and androgen profile with sex assignment deferred (RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development; RCH CPG - Undescended testes).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Bilateral non-palpable gonads in phenotypic male newborn is DSD until proven otherwise and risks missing salt-wasting CAH in week 2; outpatient deferral is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: DSD).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is eventual investigation for confirmed non-palpable testes but only after DSD has been excluded; operating without karyotype risks intervention on a virilised female. Would be correct only after DSD excluded (Source: RCH CPG).

Empirical steroid/mineralocorticoid is for biochemically confirmed/strongly suspected adrenal crisis; empirical without workup masks diagnosis. Would be correct only in confirmed crisis (Source: APEG).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

options.rationale: Bilateral non-palpable gonads is never normal; salt-wasting CAH can be lethal in week 2 if missed. (Source: RCH CPG).
source_refs: RCH CPG - Disorders of sex development

explanation.summary: Postnatal ultrasound for isolated mild/moderate antenatal hydronephrosis is performed after day 4 (and by 6 weeks) to avoid false reassurance from neonatal oliguria; severe or bilateral disease or suspected PUV requires earlier imaging (RCH CPG - Antenatal hydronephrosis).
key_points: SFU grading: 1 (pelvis only), 2 (calyces), 3 (calyceal dilatation), 4 (parenchymal thinning)
Mild/moderate isolated: USS days 4 to 6 weeks
Severe/bilateral/PUV-suspected: USS day 1-2 + paeds urology referral
Persistent hydronephrosis: MAG3 for obstruction, MCUG for VUR
Trimethoprim prophylaxis usually only for high-grade or VUR-confirmed disease
explanation.pearls: An infant with isolated mild-moderate antenatal hydronephrosis and normal newborn exam can often be discharged with an outpatient scan and surgical review.

sources.label: Society for Fetal Urology - Hydronephrosis grading

options.rationale: Imaging in the first 48 h underestimates hydronephrosis (physiological neonatal oliguria); routine MCUG not indicated for isolated SFU 1-2. (Source: RANZCR; RCH CPG).
Early scanning and routine MCUG are both inappropriate for isolated mild-moderate antenatal hydronephrosis. (Source: RANZCR).
Three-month deferral risks missing significant uropathy; SFU 2 should be assessed by 6 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG).
Symptom-driven imaging misses asymptomatic obstructive uropathy and VUR; all antenatally detected hydronephrosis needs postnatal confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG).

RCH CPG: Antenatal hydronephrosis recommends postnatal renal ultrasound after day 4 once neonatal oliguria resolves; for isolated SFU 1-2 by 6 weeks is appropriate. SFU 3-4, bilateral disease, or suspected PUV warrant earlier imaging in the first days of life, and MCUG is reserved for higher-grade or abnormal findings.
source_refs: Society for Fetal Urology - Hydronephrosis grading

explanation.summary: Localised upper-pole tenderness with a visible blue dot in a prepubertal boy with vertical testis and preserved cremasteric reflex is torsion of the appendix testis; management is conservative with analgesia and rest, and surgery is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty (RCH CPG - Acute scrotal pain).
key_points: Appendix testis is a Mullerian remnant at the upper pole
Blue dot sign: infarcted appendage visible through thin scrotal skin
Peak age 7-12 years; pain duration 1-2 days; spontaneous resolution
If exam unclear or torsion cannot be excluded, ultrasound or exploration
Cremasteric reflex preserved (lost in true torsion)
explanation.pearls: If you cannot confidently exclude testicular torsion clinically, treat the scrotum as a torsion and explore - the cost of a missed torsion is testis loss.

options.rationale: Torsion typically has sudden severe pain, nausea, high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex; this presentation does not fit. Would be correct in classic torsion presentation (Source: USANZ).

Subacute (12-48 hour) presentation in a prepubertal boy with localised upper-pole tenderness, visible blue dot, vertical lie and preserved cremasteric reflex is classic for torsion of the appendix testis. Australian management is conservative (analgesia, rest) because the appendage infarcts and the pain resolves; ultrasound with Doppler is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty.
Epididymo-orchitis has diffuse epididymal tenderness and positive urinalysis and is uncommon prepubertally without urinary anomaly. Would be correct with positive urinalysis (Source: RCH CPG).
Idiopathic scrotal oedema has painless/mildly tender pink scrotal swelling extending to perineum; no focal upper-pole tenderness or blue dot. Would be correct with that morphology (Source: RCH CPG).
Incarcerated hernia has tender groin lump extending into scrotum often with vomiting; examination here is intratesticular with no inguinal mass. Would be correct with groin lump (Source: RCH CPG).

explanation.summary: Recurrent stereotyped acute scrotal pain that resolves spontaneously, especially with a contralateral bell-clapper testis on examination, is intermittent torsion; normal Doppler after detorsion is falsely reassuring and the definitive treatment is bilateral scrotal exploration and orchidopexy (RCH CPG - Acute scrotal pain).
key_points: Intermittent torsion is a clinical diagnosis; imaging supports but cannot exclude
Bell-clapper anomaly is typically bilateral - bilateral fixation required
Doppler performed post-detorsion can show normal or hyperaemic flow
Heterogeneous echogenicity and reactive hydrocele on USS support recent torsion
Risk of next torsion event becoming non-detorting and ischaemic - elective exploration is curative
explanation.pearls: If a teenager describes repeated identical episodes of severe scrotal pain with self-resolution, book the theatre even if today's Doppler is normal.

options.rationale: Recurrent stereotyped acute scrotal pain with spontaneous resolution and contralateral bell-clapper is classic for intermittent torsion; normal Doppler does not exclude it. (Source: USANZ).
Observation delays definitive treatment and exposes the testis to recurrent torsion-detorsion injury; contralateral bell-clapper and history mandate operative exploration. (Source: USANZ).
MRI is not imaging of choice in suspected torsion and delays surgical exploration. Would never be correct as first step (Source: USANZ).

Recurrent stereotyped acute scrotal pain with spontaneous resolution is intermittent torsion; clinical diagnosis trumps imaging because Doppler is performed after detorsion and can be falsely reassuring. Bilateral fixation is required because the bell-clapper anomaly is typically bilateral, and the contralateral testis examination confirms it (RCH CPG - Acute scrotal pain; BMJ Best Practice - Testicular torsion; EAU Paediatric Urology Guidelines).

Negative urinalysis, no urethral discharge, no sexual activity and contralateral bell-clapper make epididymo-orchitis unlikely; antibiotics delay definitive management. Would be correct only with positive urinalysis and STI risk (Source: RCH CPG).
